The crying starts abruptly, lasts under a minute, and stops as suddenly as it began, after which he is embarrassed and says he was not feeling sad at all. He is sleeping well, eating well, works hard in physiotherapy, looks forward to visitors and laughs at jokes between the episodes. His PHQ-9 is 9, with 6 of those points coming from the crying and tearfulness items.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: PHQ-9 score 9 with most points from crying and tearfulness items, sleep and appetite preserved, interest and reactivity preserved, denies sadness during episodes
data_table.Examination: Mild dysarthria, right hand weakness with grade 4 power, no dysphagia, cognition intact on screening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at 30 mg at night and review his mood in six weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant option after stroke but the response in this syndrome is driven by serotonergic mechanisms at low doses, and six weeks of waiting is far longer than the few days in which improvement is usually seen. Sedation and weight gain also interfere with rehabilitation. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Involuntary crying that is brief, abruptly triggered and dissociated from felt sadness, in a man whose sleep, appetite, interest and reactivity are preserved, is post-stroke emotionalism rather than depression, and it responds to serotonergic antidepressants at doses lower than those used for depression. Response is usually apparent within one to two weeks, which is why review is scheduled early. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for depression after the discharge
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is valuable for genuine post-stroke depression, which this is not, given preserved reactivity, interest, sleep and appetite. Deferring to after discharge also leaves a distressing and socially disabling symptom untreated for weeks. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Reassure the family that no treatment is available for this symptom now
options.rationale: The symptom is treatable and often responds quickly, so reassurance without treatment leaves a family distressed and a patient avoiding social contact. Explanation matters, but it accompanies treatment rather than replacing it. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start quetiapine at low dose at night to settle the emotional outbursts
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no role in this syndrome and carry sedation, falls and cerebrovascular risks in older stroke survivors. They would be considered only for agitation with psychotic features, which is a different presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Emotionalism after stroke affects roughly one in five survivors in the first months and is frequently misread as depression, leading either to unnecessary full dose antidepressant courses or to no treatment at all. The distinguishing features are that episodes are brief, provoked by minor or sentimental triggers, and disconnected from the person's internal emotional state, while the core features of depression such as pervasive low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite disturbance are absent. Screening scales inflate scores in these patients because several items ask directly about crying. The mechanism involves disruption of serotonergic pathways modulating emotional expression, which explains why serotonin reuptake inhibitors work at lower doses and much faster than they do in depression. Explanation to the family is an important part of treatment, since the crying is often interpreted as suffering or as personality change.
key_points: Episodes are brief, easily triggered and dissociated from felt sadness.
Sleep, appetite, interest and reactivity are preserved, unlike in depression.
Depression scales overestimate severity because several items score crying itself.
Serotonergic antidepressants work at lower doses and within one to two weeks.
Family explanation reduces the distress caused by misinterpreting the crying.
explanation.pearls: Speed of response is diagnostic as well as therapeutic: improvement within one to two weeks on a low dose serotonin reuptake inhibitor supports emotionalism, whereas post-stroke depression typically needs four to six weeks and full antidepressant doses.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

subtopic_detail: new visual hallucinations with retained insight after a recent increase in dopaminergic therapy
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to see a 74-year-old man with an eight year history of Parkinson disease who has been seeing small animals in his living room for three weeks.

He describes cats and possums that move along the skirting board in the evening, knows they are not really there, and is not frightened by them. His neurologist increased his pramipexole six weeks ago because of worsening tremor, and he also takes levodopa with carbidopa three times daily. He takes no anticholinergic or sedative drug. He is afebrile with no urinary symptoms, his midstream urine culture is negative, his inflammatory markers are normal and his cognitive screening score is 26 out of 30, unchanged from a year ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg lying and 112/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Assessment: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight, no delusions, no fluctuation in attention, cognitive screening 26 out of 30 and unchanged from a year ago
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine culture negative, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Levodopa with carbidopa three times daily, pramipexole increased six weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review the hallucinations in a week
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking antipsychotics markedly worsen motor function in Parkinson disease, and risperidone in particular is avoided for this reason. If an antipsychotic becomes necessary after medication adjustment, quetiapine or clozapine are the agents used in this population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start haloperidol 0.5 mg as required for the visual hallucinations he has
options.rationale: Haloperidol is a potent dopamine antagonist and can precipitate severe rigidity and immobility in parkinsonian patients, making it the least suitable choice. Its usual role in delirium does not transfer to this population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reduce then withdraw the dopamine agonist before considering other drugs
options.rationale: Hallucinations in Parkinson disease are most often drug induced, and the recognised order of withdrawal starts with the agents that have the worst ratio of psychiatric effects to motor benefit, which means anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists before levodopa. The temporal link to the pramipexole increase makes it the obvious first target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop levodopa first and continue the dopamine agonist at the same dose
options.rationale: This inverts the recognised order: levodopa gives the greatest motor benefit per unit of psychiatric risk and is reduced last, while agonists are more strongly associated with hallucinations and impulse control disorders. Stopping levodopa first would cause disabling parkinsonism without addressing the likely cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start donepezil and increase the levodopa dose to improve his mobility
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors help hallucinations in the context of Parkinson disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies, but his cognition is stable and unimpaired on screening. Increasing levodopa at the same time would add to the dopaminergic load that is likely driving the symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Psychotic symptoms develop in a large proportion of people with Parkinson disease over time, and the earliest manifestation is typically formed visual hallucinations of people or animals with insight retained. The first step is always to look for precipitants, since infection, dehydration, metabolic disturbance and newly added drugs frequently unmask symptoms. When no precipitant is found, dopaminergic medication is reduced in a recognised order, removing anticholinergics first, then amantadine, then monoamine oxidase B inhibitors and dopamine agonists, and reducing levodopa last because it delivers the best motor benefit for its psychiatric cost. Antipsychotics are reserved for symptoms that persist or distress after medication adjustment, and only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable, with clozapine carrying the strongest evidence but requiring blood monitoring. Loss of insight, delusions or cognitive decline signal progression and warrant reassessment for an underlying dementia.
key_points: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight are the typical first psychotic symptom.
Search for infection, metabolic disturbance and new drugs before changing therapy.
Withdraw anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists before reducing levodopa.
Only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable antipsychotics in this population.
Loss of insight or cognitive decline suggests an evolving dementia.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about impulse control behaviours whenever a dopamine agonist is in use, since gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping and binge eating occur in up to 17 per cent of treated patients and are rarely volunteered without a direct question.

subtopic_detail: egodystonic intrusive images of harming an infant with full insight and avoidance of care tasks
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby. She asks her partner to take the baby out of the room, then tells you she has been having repeated images of drowning her daughter while bathing her.

She describes the images as horrifying and says they make her feel sick. She has stopped bathing the baby and hands her to her partner at bath time, and she has moved the kitchen knives to a high cupboard. She has no other unusual experiences, hears nothing, and does not believe anything is wrong with the baby or with herself beyond these thoughts. She sleeps when the baby sleeps, her mood is reactive, and she is breastfeeding successfully. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 14 with a negative response to the self-harm item, and she is adamant she would never act on the images.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 14 with negative self-harm item, intrusive images experienced as repugnant and alien, full insight, no hallucinations, no delusions, no elevated mood, sleep preserved
data_table.Examination: Infant thriving with appropriate weight gain, interaction warm and attuned, no neglect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent psychiatric admission and separate her from the infant
options.rationale: Separation is indicated when thoughts are ego-syntonic, driven by delusional beliefs or accompanied by a stated intent, as in postpartum psychosis. Intrusive images that the mother finds repugnant and actively avoids acting on carry a low risk of harm, and separation increases distress and damages attachment. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health guideline)

options.text: Start an antipsychotic and review her again in the clinic in one week
options.rationale: Antipsychotics treat psychotic phenomena, and she has none, with full insight and no hallucinations or delusions. They would add sedation and metabolic risk to a mother caring for a newborn without addressing the obsessional mechanism. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health guideline)

options.text: Advise that another adult supervise all care until the thoughts stop
options.rationale: Handing over care tasks is the avoidance behaviour that maintains the disorder, since it prevents the mother learning that the feared outcome does not occur. Formalising it as advice entrenches the very mechanism that therapy works to reverse. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health guideline)

options.text: Arrange psychological therapy for the intrusive thoughts and keep them together
options.rationale: Unwanted intrusive images of harm that are experienced as alien and repugnant, with full insight and avoidance behaviours, are perinatal obsessive compulsive symptoms, and the treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor added if symptoms are severe. Normalising the experience and keeping mother and baby together are both therapeutic. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health guideline)

options.text: Refer to child protection services because of the risk to the infant
options.rationale: The infant is thriving, well cared for and shows no sign of neglect, and the mother has taken protective action of her own accord. A statutory referral in this situation deters other women from disclosing the single most treatable perinatal symptom. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health guideline)

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of harm coming to the baby are reported by a large majority of new mothers and are only clinically significant when they become frequent, distressing and drive avoidance. The critical clinical distinction is between obsessional intrusive thoughts and psychotic ideation. Obsessional thoughts are ego-dystonic, repugnant to the mother, accompanied by full insight, and lead to avoidance of the feared situation, which is a protective pattern. Psychotic thoughts in postpartum psychosis are ego-syntonic, embedded in delusional beliefs such as the baby being possessed or better off dead, and are typically accompanied by disturbed sleep, elevated or perplexed mood and rapid fluctuation, which constitutes a psychiatric emergency. Misclassifying obsessional symptoms as psychotic leads to unnecessary separation and discourages disclosure, while missing psychosis is catastrophic. Treatment of perinatal obsessive compulsive symptoms is psychological therapy with exposure and response prevention, adding a serotonin reuptake inhibitor compatible with breastfeeding when symptoms are severe.
key_points: Intrusive thoughts of harm are near universal in new parents and only matter when distressing and disabling.
Ego-dystonic images with full insight and avoidance indicate obsessional symptoms.
Ego-syntonic thoughts with delusions, disturbed sleep and mood change indicate psychosis and are an emergency.
Avoidance of care tasks maintains the disorder and is a treatment target, not a safety plan.
Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is first line.
explanation.pearls: Ask the mother how she feels about the thought rather than only what the thought is: disgust and fear point to obsessional symptoms, while calm acceptance or a rationale for why the baby would be better off is the answer that mandates same day psychiatric assessment.

subtopic_detail: choosing between neuromodulation options when severe depression is accompanied by nihilistic delusions and food refusal
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 58-year-old man on the ward. He has had major depressive episodes before but nothing like this one, which has worsened over four months.

He has taken sertraline 200 mg daily for eight weeks and then venlafaxine 300 mg daily for eight weeks with lithium augmentation, both with documented adherence and no response. Over the last four days he has refused all food and fluid, saying his bowels have rotted away and that food would putrefy inside him. He speaks only in single words, moves slowly and has lost 8 kg in six weeks. His sodium is 149 mmol/L and his creatinine has risen from baseline. His wife is at the bedside and he has been assessed as lacking capacity to consent to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Assessment: Psychomotor retardation, near mutism, nihilistic delusions about the bowel, refusing food and fluid for 4 days, weight loss 8 kg in 6 weeks, assessed as lacking capacity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 149 mmol/L (135-145), urea 11.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer for a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation now
options.rationale: Magnetic stimulation is an option for treatment resistant depression after two failed adequate trials, but response takes several weeks of daily sessions and it is not established for psychotic depression or for a patient in acute physical danger. It also requires sustained cooperation that he cannot currently give. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add an atypical antipsychotic and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is standard for depression with psychotic features and would be appropriate in a physically stable patient, but four weeks is far too long when there is dehydration, rising creatinine and food refusal. It is frequently used alongside the definitive treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start ketamine infusions as an outpatient over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Ketamine and esketamine produce rapid effects in treatment resistant depression but the evidence base excludes psychotic depression, and outpatient management is unsafe for a man who is dehydrated and not eating. Outpatient delivery is the specific error here as much as the agent. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a two week washout period
options.rationale: A washout of two weeks followed by titration and a further response interval means more than a month without effective treatment, which he cannot survive in this state. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors retain a place in atypical and refractory depression in physically stable patients. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Arrange electroconvulsive therapy after assessing capacity and consent
options.rationale: Severe depression with psychotic features, food and fluid refusal and physical deterioration is the presentation with the strongest evidence for electroconvulsive therapy, which has the highest response rate of any treatment and works within one to two weeks. Because he lacks capacity, treatment proceeds under the substitute consent provisions of the relevant state mental health legislation. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

explanation.summary: The choice between neuromodulation treatments in resistant depression depends on urgency, psychotic features and physical state rather than simply on the number of failed drug trials. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation suits ambulatory patients with moderate to severe non-psychotic depression who have failed two adequate trials, requires daily sessions over four to six weeks and needs no anaesthesia. Electroconvulsive therapy is the treatment of choice when depression is life threatening, when there are psychotic features or catastrophic food refusal, when catatonia is present, or where a rapid response is required, with response rates in psychotic depression well above those achieved with medication. Its main burden is cognitive, chiefly transient anterograde amnesia and variable retrograde autobiographical memory loss, and right unilateral ultrabrief pulse stimulation reduces this. Capacity is assessed and documented, and where it is absent, treatment proceeds under state legislation with the required tribunal or substitute decision maker involvement.
key_points: Psychotic features, food refusal and physical deterioration favour electroconvulsive therapy.
Magnetic stimulation requires weeks of daily sessions and is not established in psychotic depression.
Electroconvulsive therapy has the highest response rate of any depression treatment.
Capacity must be assessed and documented, with state legislation governing substitute consent.
Right unilateral ultrabrief stimulation reduces the cognitive burden of treatment.
explanation.pearls: Depression with nihilistic delusions responds to electroconvulsive therapy in roughly 80 per cent of cases, substantially better than to an antidepressant and antipsychotic combination, and improvement in food and fluid intake is usually evident after the first two or three treatments.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: repetitive stealing of unneeded items preceded by tension and followed by relief in a financially secure adult
stem:
You are the psychiatrist assessing a 43-year-old primary school teacher referred by her lawyer after a second charge of shoplifting.

She has taken small items from supermarkets and chemists perhaps twice a month for four years. She describes mounting tension for an hour beforehand, a sense of release as she leaves the shop, then shame and self-disgust. She does not need the items, has never sold them, and keeps most of them in a cupboard or gives them to colleagues. Her household income is comfortable and her mortgage is nearly paid. She has not had periods of reduced sleep need, elevated mood, overspending or increased energy. She drinks two standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and scores 29 out of 30 on cognitive screening. Her memory, language and social conduct at work are unchanged over the four years.

data_table.Assessment: Tension before and relief after each episode, items not needed and given away or stored, no financial hardship, no hypomanic or manic episodes, no substance use, cognitive screening 29 out of 30
data_table.Examination: Physical examination unremarkable, mood euthymic with congruent affect, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the urge to relief cycle
options.rationale: Repeated stealing of objects not needed for use or value, preceded by tension and followed by relief and then shame, is an impulse control disorder, and cognitive behavioural approaches including covert sensitisation and imaginal desensitisation are the best supported treatment. Therapy targets the reinforcement cycle rather than the acquisitive act itself. (Source: RANZCP: Impulse control disorders)

options.text: Start lithium as the behaviour represents an undiagnosed bipolar illness
options.rationale: Stealing during mania occurs within an episode of elevated mood, reduced sleep need, increased energy and overspending, none of which she has had over four years. A mood stabiliser would treat an episodic illness whose episodes are absent. (Source: RANZCP: Impulse control disorders)

options.text: Arrange brain imaging and refer for assessment of frontotemporal disease
options.rationale: New antisocial conduct in middle age is a genuine presentation of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, but that diagnosis requires progressive change in personality, language or executive function, and her work performance, social conduct and cognitive screening are unchanged over four years. Insight and shame are also characteristically lost in that disorder and are prominent here. (Source: RANZCP: Impulse control disorders)

options.text: Advise that this is a legal matter and no clinical assessment is needed
options.rationale: The legal process runs in parallel but a treatable disorder is present and untreated relapse is likely, so declining assessment abandons both the patient and the court's interest in preventing recurrence. Clinical involvement does not excuse the offending, and the report should say so explicitly. (Source: RANZCP: Impulse control disorders)

options.text: Start a stimulant as the pattern suggests an attention deficit disorder
options.rationale: Impulsivity in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is pervasive from childhood across settings and is accompanied by inattention and restlessness, rather than being a single ritualised behaviour with an urge and relief pattern. Stimulants would not address the reinforcement cycle described. (Source: RANZCP: Impulse control disorders)

explanation.summary: Compulsive stealing is an uncommon impulse control disorder that is distinguished from ordinary theft by motive rather than by act: the items are not needed, not used and often given away or hoarded, and the behaviour follows a tension and relief pattern that resembles other behavioural addictions. It carries high rates of comorbid depression, anxiety, eating disorders and substance use, and shame usually delays presentation for years, with most people first assessed after legal proceedings begin. The important differentials are stealing during a manic episode, stealing driven by substance dependence or financial need, and new antisocial conduct as the presenting feature of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, which is separated by its progressive course and by the loss of insight and shame. Psychological treatment with covert sensitisation or imaginal desensitisation has the best evidence, and naltrexone has some support in reducing urges. Comorbidity should always be sought and treated.
key_points: Items are not needed, not used, and often given away or stored unopened.
The tension and relief cycle is what defines the disorder rather than the act of stealing.
Stealing within a manic episode is accompanied by elevated mood and reduced sleep need.
New antisocial conduct with lost insight and progressive change suggests frontotemporal disease.
Cognitive behavioural approaches have the best evidence, with naltrexone as an adjunct.
explanation.pearls: Ask what happened to the stolen items: giving them away, hoarding them unopened or returning them secretly points strongly to an impulse control disorder, while selling them or using them for their value does not.

subtopic_detail: planning the postpartum dose of an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser whose clearance rose through pregnancy
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has bipolar II disorder and has been well for three years on lamotrigine 200 mg daily.

At 24 weeks she developed early depressive symptoms with poor sleep and rumination. A lamotrigine level taken then was about 40 per cent below her pre-pregnancy level, and the dose was increased in steps to 350 mg daily, after which her symptoms resolved and she has been well since. She plans to breastfeed and to birth at 39 weeks. She has had no rash and no other adverse effects. She asks what should happen to her tablets once the baby is born.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: Euthymic, sleeping adequately, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, three years of stability before this pregnancy
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 350 mg daily, increased in steps from 200 mg at 24 weeks after the level fell about 40 per cent below the pre-pregnancy value
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her lamotrigine after the birth?

options.text: Continue lamotrigine 350 mg daily after the birth and review at six weeks
options.rationale: Clearance falls rapidly once the pregnancy ends, so a dose that produced therapeutic levels at 34 weeks produces supratherapeutic levels within days to weeks, with dizziness, ataxia, diplopia and rash. Six weeks of observation is long past the point where toxicity would appear. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Reduce towards the pre-pregnancy dose over the first two weeks after birth
options.rationale: Pregnancy induces glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine clearance, and that induction reverses over the first one to three weeks postpartum, so the dose is tapered back towards the pre-pregnancy dose over about two weeks with level monitoring and close symptom review. This avoids toxicity while keeping cover through the period of highest relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Stop lamotrigine at the birth and restart it if symptoms recur afterwards
options.rationale: The first weeks postpartum carry the highest relapse risk of a woman's life in bipolar disorder, so stopping a mood stabiliser at birth removes protection at the worst possible moment. Restarting also requires the slow titration that lamotrigine demands to limit rash risk, leaving her unprotected for weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Halve the dose immediately after the birth and stop breastfeeding as well
options.rationale: An abrupt halving overshoots in the opposite direction while clearance is still falling, and lamotrigine is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding provided the infant is monitored for rash, sedation and poor feeding. Cessation of breastfeeding is not required by this drug. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add sodium valproate after the birth and continue the current lamotrigine
options.rationale: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its level, which on top of falling postpartum clearance would compound toxicity and rash risk. Valproate is also avoided in women of reproductive age wherever an alternative exists. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is eliminated by glucuronidation, an enzyme system strongly induced by oestrogen, so clearance rises progressively through pregnancy and levels can fall by more than half by the third trimester, which is why breakthrough symptoms cluster in mid to late pregnancy. Dose increases guided by levels and symptoms are therefore expected. The corresponding risk sits on the other side of birth, because induction reverses within one to three weeks and a dose that was appropriate antenatally becomes toxic. The standard approach is to plan the postpartum taper before birth, returning towards the pre-pregnancy dose over about two weeks with level monitoring, rather than making a reactive change after symptoms of toxicity appear. This must be balanced against the postpartum period being the time of highest relapse risk in bipolar disorder, so prophylaxis is never stopped. The same oestrogen effect explains why combined hormonal contraception lowers lamotrigine levels and why levels rise during the pill free week.
key_points: Oestrogen induced glucuronidation roughly doubles lamotrigine clearance in pregnancy.
Levels can fall by half or more by the third trimester, causing breakthrough symptoms.
Induction reverses within one to three weeks after birth, risking toxicity on the antenatal dose.
Taper back towards the pre-pregnancy dose over about two weeks with level monitoring.
The postpartum period carries the highest relapse risk, so prophylaxis is not stopped.
explanation.pearls: The same interaction bites outside pregnancy: combined hormonal contraception halves lamotrigine levels, and levels rise sharply during the hormone free week, so a woman starting or stopping the pill needs a dose review just as a postpartum woman does.

subtopic_detail: multiple motor tics and one vocal tic for over a year in a nine year old with inattention
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9-year-old boy referred by his general practitioner. His parents say he has been blinking hard and jerking his head to one side on and off since he was six, and that about a year ago he started making a repeated throat-clearing noise. The movements come in bouts, wax and wane in severity, and are worse when he is tired or excited.

He tells you he can feel a build-up like an itch just before each one and can hold them back for a short time in class, after which they come out in a burst at home. His teacher reports he is inattentive, loses his place and does not finish work, and this predates the vocal noise by two years. He has friends, enjoys swimming and is not being teased. The tics do not interfere with his handwriting or his sleep, and he says they do not bother him much. Neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination is normal, and he takes no medication and uses no substances.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Tic history: Multiple motor tics from age six and a vocal tic for one year, waxing and waning, worse with fatigue
data_table.Premonitory features: Describes a premonitory urge with temporary voluntary suppression followed by rebound
data_table.Functional impact: Handwriting, sleep and peer relationships unaffected, inattention predating the vocal tic by two years
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and monitor his weight and prolactin level
options.rationale: Antipsychotics reduce tic severity but carry weight gain, metabolic and prolactin effects that are hard to justify for tics causing no functional impairment. They are reserved for severe or self-injurious tics that have not responded to behavioural treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose against the frequency of the tics
options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists are a reasonable pharmacological option and are particularly attractive where tics and inattention coexist, but they are second-line to behavioural therapy for tics that are not disabling. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that medication is reserved for impairment rather than for the presence of tics alone. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for atypical features such as abrupt onset with fixed rather than waxing and waning course, focal neurological signs, or tics beginning in adulthood. A typical developmental course with a normal examination does not warrant a scan. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Start methylphenidate and review whether the tics become more frequent later
options.rationale: His inattention may well warrant assessment and treatment in its own right, and stimulants are not in fact contraindicated in tic disorders as was once taught, but the lead-in asks about the tics and no formal attention deficit diagnosis has yet been established. Treating a presumed comorbidity before assessing it puts the sequence the wrong way round. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as first line therapy
options.rationale: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before 18 years meets criteria for Tourette syndrome, and behavioural therapy built on habit reversal training is first-line when tics are not severely disabling. It uses the premonitory urge he describes to train a competing response. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires at least two motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, persisting for more than a year with onset before 18 years, and it affects around 1 per cent of school aged children with a marked male predominance. The premonitory urge and the capacity for brief voluntary suppression followed by rebound are what distinguish tics from chorea, myoclonus, dystonia and stereotypies, and they are also the mechanism behavioural therapy exploits. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics combines habit reversal training, in which a competing response is performed at the moment of the urge, with function-based assessment and relaxation, and it has the best evidence base of any first-line treatment. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder each affecting a substantial proportion, and the comorbidity usually causes more impairment than the tics. Tics typically peak in early adolescence and improve substantially by early adulthood, so a prognosis discussion is a therapeutic intervention in itself.
key_points: Two or more motor tics plus one vocal tic for over a year defines Tourette syndrome.
A premonitory urge with suppressibility and rebound distinguishes tics from other movements.
Behavioural therapy with habit reversal is first-line when tics are not disabling.
Comorbid attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms usually cause more impairment than the tics.
explanation.pearls: The old teaching that stimulants must be avoided in tic disorders has not held up: randomised evidence shows methylphenidate does not worsen tics overall, and untreated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder causes more functional harm in Tourette syndrome than the tics themselves.

subtopic_detail: a six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eight months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has written asking for an assessment because the girl has not spoken a word at school since she started prep eight months ago. She nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and completes written work at the expected standard.

Her parents say she chatters constantly at home, tells long stories to her grandmother on the phone, argues with her older brother and plays imaginative games with him involving reciprocal turn-taking and pretend. She spoke her first words at 11 months and put sentences together before she was two. At the surgery she sits close to her mother, makes brief eye contact with you, smiles at a joke and shakes her head when you ask a question, but does not speak. Her mother says she also goes silent with unfamiliar adults at the shops and at birthday parties. She passed her newborn hearing screen and has had no ear infections.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Speech pattern: Fluent age appropriate speech at home, no speech at school for eight months, silent with unfamiliar adults
data_table.Developmental history: First words at 11 months, sentences before two years, passed newborn hearing screen
data_table.Social functioning: Reciprocal imaginative play with her brother, brief eye contact, smiles responsively in the consultation
data_table.Academic function: Written work at the expected standard, communicates by nodding, pointing and writing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for graded exposure therapy delivered jointly with her school
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations despite fluent speech elsewhere, lasting beyond a month of school and interfering with participation, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder. Graded exposure with stimulus fading delivered in partnership with the school is the first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before anything else
options.rationale: Autism is the near pair that families most often fear, and it is distinguished here by her reciprocal imaginative play, responsive smiling and normal social communication at home, since autistic social differences are present across all settings rather than confined to some. Situational specificity is the discriminating feature. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Start fluoxetine at a low dose and review her response in six weeks time
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have a role in selective mutism that has not responded to adequate behavioural therapy, or where severity prevents engagement with it. Starting medication before any psychological treatment has been tried inverts the recommended order. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Arrange audiology and formal speech pathology assessment of her language
options.rationale: Hearing and language assessment would be essential if speech were delayed or abnormal in every setting, but she achieved milestones early and speaks fluently at home. A passed newborn screen with normal home speech makes a primary language or hearing disorder very unlikely. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Advise the school to reward each spoken word with additional playtime
options.rationale: Contingent reward for speech raises the pressure on the very behaviour anxiety is blocking and commonly entrenches the silence. Effective behavioural programs reward participation and graded approach steps rather than speech itself in the early stages. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified among the anxiety disorders and is defined by a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally in others, lasting at least one month and not limited to the first month of school. It typically begins before age five but is usually identified when school entry makes the impairment visible, and it affects under 1 per cent of children with a female predominance. The core differentials are autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, hearing impairment and the transient silence of a child learning a new language, each separated by whether communication is impaired across all settings or only some. Treatment is behavioural and collaborative, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered by the school and family with specialist guidance, and crucially it rewards brave approach behaviour rather than speech itself. Pressure, bribery and public attention to the silence reliably make it worse, so a substantial part of the intervention is coaching the adults around the child.
key_points: Situational specificity separates selective mutism from autism and language disorder.
The child speaks fluently at home, which excludes a primary language or hearing problem.
Graded exposure with stimulus fading and school partnership is first-line treatment.
Rewarding speech directly raises pressure; reward participation and approach instead.
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the practical core of treatment: the child first speaks to a parent in an empty classroom, then a peer is quietly introduced into the room, then the teacher, with the audience widened only once speech is comfortable at the current step.

subtopic_detail: inner restlessness and pacing two days after a dose increase in a previously settled inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on the ward. A 24-year-old man admitted eleven days ago with a first episode of psychosis had his risperidone increased from 2 mg to 4 mg daily two days ago because he was still describing persecutory beliefs. Nursing staff have called you because he has been pacing the corridor since early morning and cannot sit through a meal.

He tells you the feeling is in his legs and that he has to keep moving or it becomes unbearable, and that it is worse when he sits still and eases when he walks. He says it started yesterday and that it is not the voices. His speech is normal in rate and form, he is not distractible, and his persecutory beliefs are described in the same terms and with the same conviction as at admission. There is no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity and no dystonia. His pulse rate is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Creatine kinase is 140 units/L (40-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, not distractible, persecutory beliefs unchanged in content and conviction
data_table.Subjective report: Restlessness localised to the legs, worse at rest and relieved by walking, onset the day after the dose increase
data_table.Neurological examination: No tremor, cogwheel rigidity or dystonia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 140 units/L (40-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence diazepam and continue the current dose of risperidone unchanged
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do help akathisia and are a recognised second-line option, which makes this the near pair, but leaving the causative dose unchanged treats the symptom while the cause continues. Dose reduction addresses the mechanism and benzodiazepines are reserved for when propranolol is contraindicated or ineffective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose and start propranolol for symptom relief
options.rationale: A subjective inner restlessness localised to the legs, relieved by movement, beginning within days of a dose increase and with an unchanged mental state is akathisia. Reducing the offending dose is the primary intervention and propranolol is the best supported symptomatic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the risperidone dose to treat the worsening psychotic agitation
options.rationale: Mistaking akathisia for psychotic agitation and escalating the antipsychotic is the classic anti-pattern, because it worsens the akathisia in a self-reinforcing cycle. His delusional content and conviction are unchanged, which is the evidence that the psychosis has not worsened. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start benzatropine to treat the emerging extrapyramidal adverse effects
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but are largely ineffective for akathisia, and they add cognitive impairment, constipation and urinary retention. The absence of tremor, rigidity and dystonia removes the indication anyway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add regular olanzapine at night in addition to his current treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy raises the total dopamine blockade and therefore the akathisia risk, while adding metabolic burden in a young man at the start of treatment. It compounds the cause rather than removing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, accompanied by an objective inability to remain still, and it appears within days to weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. It is among the most distressing of all antipsychotic adverse effects and carries a documented association with suicidal ideation and with treatment non-adherence, which is why recognising it matters more than its apparent mildness suggests. The diagnostic trap is that pacing, agitation and distress are also features of worsening psychosis, and the discriminators are the temporal relationship to a dose change, the patient's own localisation of the sensation to the limbs, relief with movement, and an otherwise unchanged mental state. Management begins with reducing or switching the antipsychotic, since akathisia is dose-related, with propranolol as the best supported symptomatic agent and benzodiazepines, mirtazapine or a switch to a lower-risk agent such as quetiapine or clozapine as further options. Anticholinergics, useful for parkinsonism and dystonia, are ineffective here and are a common prescribing error.
key_points: Onset within days of a dose increase with an unchanged mental state points to akathisia.
The sensation is localised to the limbs and relieved by movement, unlike psychotic agitation.
Dose reduction is primary; propranolol is the best supported symptomatic treatment.
Anticholinergics treat parkinsonism and dystonia but not akathisia.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia carries a recognised association with suicidal ideation, so a patient who becomes newly hopeless or impulsive within days of an antipsychotic dose increase is asked specifically whether the distress sits in the legs and eases when walking, before the agitation is attributed to the illness.

subtopic_detail: six months of feeling detached from oneself with fully retained awareness that the experience is not real
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 23-year-old apprentice electrician referred by his general practitioner. He says that since a frightening episode six months ago, when his heart pounded and he thought he was dying, he has felt as though he is watching himself from a few feet away, like a character in a film rather than the person doing the living.

He describes his hands as looking like they belong to someone else and says the street outside looks flat and drained of colour, as though painted on a backdrop. He is emphatic that he knows none of this is actually true and that it is his perception that has changed rather than the world, and he finds that distinction frustrating rather than reassuring. It is present for most of the day, most days. He smoked cannabis heavily for two years and stopped seven months ago, before the symptoms began, and uses no other substance and no alcohol. He has no hallucinations, no delusional beliefs and no thought disorder, his mood is anxious rather than low, and physical examination, thyroid function and a recent electroencephalogram are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Core symptoms: Persistent detachment from self with a sense of observing oneself, and a flat drained quality to the surroundings
data_table.Reality testing: Fully intact, with explicit awareness that the altered perception does not reflect external reality
data_table.Substance history: Cannabis ceased seven months ago before symptom onset, no other substance or alcohol use
data_table.Mental state: No hallucinations, delusions or thought disorder, anxious rather than depressed mood
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination, thyroid function and electroencephalogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a benzodiazepine to be taken whenever the detachment occurs
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines can deepen dissociative symptoms as well as causing dependence, and an as-needed regimen for a symptom present most of the day would mean near continuous use. Symptom-contingent dosing also reinforces the checking and monitoring that maintain the disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is warranted where there are focal neurological signs, an abrupt onset in later life or a history of head injury, none of which applies to a young man with a normal examination. Scanning first would delay treatment and risks an incidental finding that generates further anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the symptoms
options.rationale: Persistent detachment from the self and the surroundings with fully intact reality testing, causing distress and lasting months, is depersonalisation derealisation disorder. Psychological therapy with psychoeducation, grounding techniques and work on the catastrophic appraisals that maintain the symptoms is the first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic given the persistent unreal quality
options.rationale: Antipsychotics treat psychosis, which requires loss of reality testing, and he retains it completely by insisting the change is in his perception rather than in the world. Antipsychotics have no established efficacy in this disorder and add metabolic and extrapyramidal burden. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography to exclude temporal lobe epilepsy
options.rationale: Focal epilepsy can produce brief episodic dissociative experiences and is worth considering, which makes this the near pair, but seizure-related symptoms are stereotyped, last seconds to minutes and occur in discrete episodes rather than continuously for six months. The study has also already been performed and was normal. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation derealisation disorder is classified among the dissociative disorders and is defined by persistent or recurrent experiences of detachment from one's own thoughts, body or actions, or from the surroundings, with reality testing remaining fully intact throughout. Transient depersonalisation is extremely common, reported by up to half of the population at some point and particularly during panic, sleep deprivation or intoxication, but the disorder requires persistence and clinically significant distress or impairment. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and is frequently triggered by a panic attack, severe stress or cannabis use, and it can persist for years after the trigger has gone, as here. The intact reality testing is the feature that separates it from psychosis and is worth stating explicitly to the patient, because many fear they are developing schizophrenia and that fear itself amplifies the symptom. Treatment is primarily psychological, with cognitive behavioural approaches targeting symptom monitoring, avoidance and catastrophic interpretation, while medication is reserved for comorbid anxiety or depression since no agent has established efficacy for the dissociative symptoms themselves.
key_points: Intact reality testing separates this disorder from psychosis and should be named for the patient.
Panic, severe stress and cannabis are common triggers, and symptoms outlast them.
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting appraisal and monitoring is first-line.
No medication has established efficacy for the dissociative symptoms themselves.
explanation.pearls: Fear of impending madness maintains this disorder more than any other factor, so explicitly naming the condition and explaining that intact insight rules out psychosis is itself therapeutic and often reduces symptom intensity before any formal therapy begins.

subtopic_detail: recurrent replicative nightmares waking a veteran nightly despite improvement in his daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 44-year-old former soldier who has been taking sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months for post-traumatic stress disorder following a deployment. He has completed a course of trauma-focused therapy.

He tells you his daytime symptoms have improved substantially, with far fewer intrusive daytime images, less avoidance and a return to part-time work. What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes between one and three in the morning from the same dream, which replays a specific incident almost exactly as it happened, and he then lies awake for two hours. His partner says he does not shout, thrash, kick or leave the bed, and neither of them has ever been injured during the night. He drinks no alcohol, uses no cannabis and takes no other medication. His mood is reactive, he is not suicidal, and his physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Nightmare pattern: Replicative trauma-specific dreams waking him five or six nights weekly between 0100 and 0300 with two hours of subsequent wakefulness
data_table.Daytime symptoms: Substantially improved intrusions, reduced avoidance, returned to part-time work
data_table.Collateral from partner: No vocalisation, thrashing, kicking or leaving the bed, no injury to either partner
data_table.Treatment to date: Sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months, completed course of trauma-focused therapy
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe nightly temazepam to consolidate sleep and reduce awakenings
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder because they impair the emotional processing that trauma-focused therapy depends on, carry dependence risk in a population with high comorbid substance use, and have been associated with worse outcomes. They also do not reduce nightmare frequency. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Start quetiapine at night for its sedating and dream suppressing effect
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics are sometimes used off label for this purpose but the evidence is weak and the metabolic burden in a middle-aged man is real. Pharmacological augmentation follows rather than precedes a trial of the psychological treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Refer for polysomnography to assess for rapid eye movement behaviour
options.rationale: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder is the near pair worth excluding, since it also produces dramatic nocturnal events, and it is distinguished by dream enactment with vocalisation, thrashing and injury to the patient or bed partner, which the collateral history explicitly rules out here. Trauma nightmares occur without loss of atonia and do not need a sleep study. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders)

options.text: Refer for imagery rehearsal therapy targeting the recurrent nightmares
options.rationale: Nightmares frequently persist as a residual symptom after daytime post-traumatic symptoms have responded, and imagery rehearsal therapy, in which the patient rewrites and rehearses an altered dream narrative while awake, has the strongest evidence of any treatment for them. It is recommended ahead of adding further medication. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and review his sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: He has already had a substantial response at this dose across nine months, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have a modest effect on nightmares specifically, with some evidence that they suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can worsen dream disturbance. Further escalation is unlikely to target the residual symptom. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

explanation.summary: Nightmares are among the most persistent symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder and commonly outlast the daytime intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal that respond first to treatment, which makes residual nightmare disorder a distinct treatment target rather than evidence of overall failure. Trauma nightmares differ from ordinary bad dreams in that they frequently replicate the index event with unusual fidelity, occur in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, and produce full awakening with clear recall and autonomic arousal. The differential that must be excluded on collateral history is rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, in which loss of the normal muscle atonia allows the dream to be acted out with vocalisation, movement and injury, and which carries entirely different implications as a prodrome of synucleinopathy. Imagery rehearsal therapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence and works by having the patient select a recurrent nightmare, rewrite the narrative with a changed ending while awake, and rehearse the new version daily for around ten to twenty minutes. Australian guidance places it ahead of pharmacological options, with prazosin remaining a second-line consideration whose supporting evidence has become less consistent since the larger negative trials.
key_points: Nightmares often persist after daytime post-traumatic symptoms have responded to treatment.
Dream enactment with vocalisation or injury indicates rapid eye movement behaviour disorder instead.
Imagery rehearsal therapy rewrites and rehearses the dream while awake and is first-line.
Benzodiazepines are discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder and do not reduce nightmares.
explanation.pearls: Ask the bed partner specifically whether he moves, shouts or has ever hurt either of them during a dream: dream enactment points to rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder and a synucleinopathy prodrome, while a man who lies still and wakes to the same replayed scene has trauma nightmares.

subtopic_detail: confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after starting an antidepressant in a woman of seventy nine
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79-year-old woman at home by her daughter, who says her mother has been muddled about the day of the week for three days and had a near fall in the kitchen. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily three weeks ago for a depressive episode and reports her mood has lifted slightly.

Her other medications are amlodipine, atorvastatin and a thiazide she has taken for eight years without incident. She has had no cough, no urinary symptoms, no fever and no vomiting. On examination she is alert but disorientated to time, with normal power and no focal neurological signs, moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no peripheral oedema. Her pulse rate is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Sodium is 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Her sodium was 138 mmol/L eight weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert but disorientated to time, moist mucous membranes, no postural drop, no oedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Osmolality studies: Serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline and start hypertonic saline in a monitored setting
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures, marked obtundation or coma, and confusion with unsteadiness at 122 mmol/L does not meet that threshold. Continuing the causative drug would also guarantee recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose and repeat the sodium level again in two weeks
options.rationale: The effect is idiosyncratic rather than reliably dose-dependent, so dose reduction does not dependably correct it, and a two week interval is far too long to monitor a sodium of 122 mmol/L. This is the near pair to the correct answer and the distinction is that partial measures leave a symptomatic patient at risk of further falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch her to mirtazapine today and recheck the sodium in three days time
options.rationale: Switching antidepressant is a reasonable plan once the sodium has recovered and the depression still needs treatment, and mirtazapine carries a lower though not absent risk. Starting the replacement on the same day removes the ability to attribute any ongoing abnormality and skips the fluid restriction that actually corrects the sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start demeclocycline and continue the sertraline at her current daily dose
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is a third-line agent for chronic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis where the cause cannot be removed, with nephrotoxicity and photosensitivity as recognised problems. Here the cause is entirely removable, which makes pharmacological antagonism unnecessary. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the sertraline and commence fluid restriction with daily sodium checks
options.rationale: A euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L appearing three weeks after starting a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is drug-induced syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis. Withdrawal of the causative drug with fluid restriction and close biochemical monitoring is the treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are among the commonest drug causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, with the risk concentrated in the first four weeks of treatment and rising steeply with age, female sex, low body weight and concurrent diuretic use. The diagnosis requires hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia in a clinically euvolaemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine, a urine sodium above about 30 mmol/L, and normal thyroid and adrenal function, and a low urea with a low urate supports it. The main alternative in this age group is thiazide-induced hyponatraemia, which is why an eight year history of stable sodium on the same thiazide followed by an abrupt fall three weeks after a new antidepressant points to the newer drug. Correction must be controlled, with a rise of no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, because faster correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination with devastating and often irreversible consequences. Once the sodium normalises, an antidepressant with lower risk can be introduced with a sodium check at one to two weeks, and the depression itself still requires treatment.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first four weeks and rises with age, female sex and diuretic use.
Euvolaemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L defines the syndrome.
A stable sodium for years on the same thiazide points to the newly added drug.
Correction is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium two weeks after starting any selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor in a patient over 65 who is also taking a thiazide, because the combination multiplies the risk and the presentation is usually a fall or confusion rather than anything that looks biochemical.

subtopic_detail: abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds in a man in his fourth year of clozapine treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 500 mg daily for four years with good symptomatic control. Community staff report he has been off his food for five days, has vomited twice today and that his belly looks swollen.

He is drowsy but rousable and tells you his tummy has been aching and that he has not opened his bowels for nine days, which he says is not unusual for him. He takes no regular aperient. On examination the abdomen is grossly distended and tympanitic with generalised tenderness but no guarding, and bowel sounds are absent over four minutes of auscultation. There is no rigidity of the limbs and no tremor. His pulse rate is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. White cell count is 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Abdominal examination: Grossly distended tympanitic abdomen with generalised tenderness, no guarding, absent bowel sounds over four minutes
data_table.Neurological examination: Drowsy but rousable, no limb rigidity, no tremor
data_table.Bowel history: No bowel action for nine days, no regular aperient, two episodes of vomiting today
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), absolute neutrophil count 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal imaging, withhold clozapine and involve the surgical team
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds with gross distension, vomiting, tachycardia and a raised lactate in a patient on long-term clozapine is clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing to ileus, which carries a high mortality once obstruction or ischaemia develops. Urgent imaging, withholding the drug and surgical involvement are simultaneous rather than sequential steps. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Continue clozapine and start a stimulant laxative with review tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Aperients are the mainstay of prevention and of mild hypomotility, but giving a stimulant laxative into a possibly obstructed bowel with absent sounds risks perforation. Overnight review is far too slow for a patient with a raised lactate and hypotension. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Check the clozapine level and reduce the dose by a quarter this same evening
options.rationale: A clozapine concentration is useful in working out subsequent dosing but takes days to return and does nothing about a distended obstructed abdomen tonight. Dose reduction is too slow an intervention for an acute surgical problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Start an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids with a high fibre diet on the ward
options.rationale: Oral intake is contraindicated in a patient with absent bowel sounds and vomiting, and fibre without adequate transit worsens distension. Fibre supplementation is for prevention in an ambulant patient, not for an acute presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Withhold clozapine and repeat the full blood count before any imaging is done
options.rationale: Neutropenia is the clozapine adverse effect that monitoring programs are built around, and it is the near pair here, but his absolute neutrophil count is normal and haematological toxicity does not cause a silent distended abdomen. Deferring imaging to chase a normal blood count delays the diagnosis that matters. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility results from potent antagonism at muscarinic, serotonergic and adrenergic receptors in the enteric nervous system, and it affects a substantial minority of patients on the drug, with slowed colonic transit demonstrable in most. It is far less famous than agranulocytosis but kills more people, since case series consistently show gastrointestinal complications causing several times as many clozapine-related deaths as haematological ones, largely because it is recognised late. Late recognition has specific causes, in that patients on clozapine often have blunted pain perception and impaired symptom reporting, constipation is normalised by both patient and team, and no mandatory monitoring framework exists for bowel function in the way it does for the neutrophil count. Presentation ranges from chronic constipation to faecal impaction, paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation, and the transition can be rapid. Prevention is the practical message, with a baseline and regular bowel history, prophylactic aperients for anyone with reduced frequency, avoidance of additional anticholinergic drugs, and a low threshold for imaging when a patient on clozapine reports abdominal symptoms.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis does.
Blunted pain perception and normalised constipation lead to late presentation.
Absent bowel sounds with distension mandates imaging and surgical involvement, not laxatives.
Prevention relies on routine bowel history and prophylactic aperients rather than monitoring bloods.
explanation.pearls: Ask every clozapine patient how often they open their bowels at each review and start a regular osmotic aperient if it is less than every second day, because there is no blood test that detects the complication that most often kills them.

subtopic_detail: partition delusions about a neighbour in a woman of seventy eight with intact cognition and normal imaging
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 78-year-old widow referred after she called the police three times in a fortnight. She believes the man in the next unit comes through the wall of her bedroom at night to move her belongings and put chemicals in her tea, and she has stopped drinking anything he might have reached.

She describes hearing his voice through the wall commenting on what she is doing. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications accurately, cooks and shops independently, and her daughter confirms she has been sharp and organised until this began four months ago. On examination her Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 27 out of 30, attention and digit span are normal, and there is no fluctuation in her conscious level across a one hour interview. She has no visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism and no dream enactment. She wears two hearing aids that her daughter says stopped working months ago. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function, B12 and inflammatory markers are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Psychotic symptoms: Persecutory partition delusions involving the adjacent unit, auditory hallucinations through the wall, onset four months ago
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30, normal attention and digit span, no fluctuation in conscious level
data_table.Neurological examination: No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no dream enactment behaviour
data_table.Functional status: Independent with finances, medications, cooking and shopping
data_table.Investigations: Normal magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function, B12 and inflammatory markers
data_table.Sensory status: Wears two hearing aids that have not worked for months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy without any change to her medication
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a useful adjunct for distress and for coping with residual symptoms, but as sole treatment for florid persecutory delusions that have led to police involvement and to her refusing fluids it is inadequate. Her refusal to drink creates a physical risk that needs faster resolution. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start low dose amisulpride and arrange formal audiology assessment
options.rationale: Partition delusions with auditory hallucinations, preserved cognition and function, normal imaging and onset after 60 years describe very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis. Low dose antipsychotic treatment combined with correction of the sensory deprivation that contributes to symptom formation is the established approach. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat the psychosis of Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, both of which require cognitive impairment that is absent here with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 27 and full independence. Treating a dementia she does not have delays effective treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Treat as a delirium and screen for infection with cultures and further imaging
options.rationale: Delirium requires an acute onset over hours to days with impaired attention and a fluctuating conscious level, whereas this evolved over four months with normal attention and no fluctuation. The screening bloods and imaging are already normal. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start quetiapine at a low dose given her likely Lewy body sensitivity
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the correct choice when antipsychotic sensitivity from dementia with Lewy bodies is a concern, and this is the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that Lewy body disease requires fluctuating cognition, recurrent formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment, and all four are explicitly absent, so the sensitivity concern that drives the choice does not apply. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

explanation.summary: Psychosis presenting for the first time after the age of 60 is classified as very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis, and it differs from earlier onset schizophrenia in several consistent ways. Women predominate, negative symptoms and formal thought disorder are uncommon, cognition and premorbid function are typically preserved, and the delusional content is characteristically persecutory and spatially organised around the home, with partition delusions about people or substances passing through walls, floors and ceilings being close to pathognomonic. Sensory deprivation, particularly uncorrected hearing loss and to a lesser extent visual impairment, is a well replicated risk factor, and social isolation compounds it, so correcting the sensory deficit is a therapeutic intervention rather than an afterthought.
