The essential differentials are delirium, separated by the time course and by attention, dementia with psychosis, separated by cognitive testing and functional history, and dementia with Lewy bodies, separated by fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment. Response to antipsychotics is generally good but doses are a quarter to a half of those used in younger adults, and the increased mortality associated with antipsychotics in dementia makes accurate diagnosis before prescribing important.
key_points: Partition delusions involving walls, floors and ceilings are characteristic of the syndrome.
Preserved cognition and function separate it from dementia with psychosis.
Uncorrected hearing loss is a replicated risk factor and correcting it is part of treatment.
Antipsychotic doses are a quarter to a half of those used in younger adults.
explanation.pearls: Check whether the hearing aids actually work rather than whether they are worn: uncorrected hearing loss is one of the few modifiable risk factors in very late onset psychosis, and a dead battery has been the treatable contributor in more than one referral.

subtopic_detail: recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia in a toddler that stops entirely during a supervised admission
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the family of a 2-year-old girl admitted for the fourth time in three months with hypoglycaemic episodes. Each previous admission followed an ambulance call from home, and each time she recovered promptly and was discharged after a normal work-up.

During this nine-day admission, in which a nurse has been present at all cares and no food or drink has come from home, her glucose has remained between 4.2 and 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes. A sample taken during the last documented episode at home has now returned showing glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5) and beta-hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Cortisol and growth hormone responses were appropriate. Her mother, who trained as an enrolled nurse, has stayed at the bedside throughout, has asked repeatedly for further tests and has told several staff that a specialist interstate suspects a rare metabolic disorder. The treating team has been unable to verify that referral.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Inpatient course: Nine days with supervised cares and no external food, glucose 4.2 to 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes
data_table.Critical sample from home: Glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5), suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate
data_table.Counter-regulatory testing: Appropriate cortisol and growth hormone responses
data_table.Collateral: Unverifiable account of an interstate specialist referral, repeated requests for further investigation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with a continuous glucose monitor and review her in one week
options.rationale: Discharging the child back into the environment where the episodes occur, on the strength of a device that can be removed or its data disputed, returns her to a situation with a documented mortality. Covert surveillance and monitoring are not substitutes for statutory protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Offer the mother psychological therapy and arrange community follow up
options.rationale: Treatment for the perpetrating parent may well be part of the eventual plan, but it follows rather than replaces protection of the child, and engaging therapeutically first risks alerting the parent before safeguarding is in place. The child's safety is not contingent on the parent accepting help. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Report to child protection services and keep the child in hospital
options.rationale: High insulin with a suppressed C-peptide is chemically impossible in endogenous hyperinsulinism and proves administration of exogenous insulin, and episodes that occur only at home and cease under supervision complete the picture of factitious disorder imposed on another. Mandatory reporting with the child kept in a place of safety is the immediate step. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange a supervised fast with paired insulin and cortisol sampling now
options.rationale: A diagnostic fast is how endogenous hypoglycaemia is investigated, and it would be the right test if the mechanism were unknown. The paired sample already obtained has answered the question definitively, and a further fast exposes the child to deliberate hypoglycaemia for no diagnostic gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for insulinoma localisation imaging
options.rationale: An insulinoma is the near pair to consider, and it is excluded by the C-peptide, because a tumour secreting endogenous insulin releases C-peptide in equimolar amounts and the level would be high rather than undetectable. Insulinoma is also vanishingly rare at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Factitious disorder imposed on another, historically called Munchausen syndrome by proxy and described in child protection frameworks as fabricated or induced illness, involves a carer falsifying or inducing symptoms in a dependent for psychological rather than material gain. The perpetrator is usually the mother, health care backgrounds are over-represented, and the pattern typically includes recurrent presentations, symptoms witnessed only by the carer, findings that resolve when the carer is absent, unverifiable accounts of other specialists, and persistent pressure for further investigation. Insulin administration is one of the most commonly reported induction methods and is uniquely easy to prove biochemically, because exogenous insulin raises measured insulin while suppressing endogenous secretion and therefore C-peptide, a dissociation that no endogenous cause can produce. Mortality in reported series runs at around 6 to 10 per cent and long-term morbidity from unnecessary investigation and treatment is substantial, so protection precedes psychiatric formulation. The correct process is a mandatory report to the statutory agency with the child kept in a place of safety, a multidisciplinary meeting, a documented chronology assembled from source records rather than from the carer's account, and assessment of siblings, who are also at risk.
key_points: Raised insulin with suppressed C-peptide proves exogenous insulin administration.
Symptoms witnessed only by one carer and resolving under supervision is the pattern.
Mandatory reporting and a place of safety precede any therapeutic engagement with the parent.
Siblings are assessed too, and the chronology is built from source records not carer report.
explanation.pearls: Insulin and C-peptide are released in equimolar amounts from the beta cell, so a high insulin with an undetectable C-peptide during hypoglycaemia can only mean exogenous insulin, and in a two year old that single pairing is a child protection finding rather than an endocrine one.

subtopic_detail: a specific threat against a named person disclosed in a session by a patient with a history of violence
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 38-year-old man in an outpatient clinic for the eighth time. He has been attending for help with anger and relationship difficulties following separation from his partner. He has two previous convictions for assault, the most recent four years ago.

Today he tells you that his former partner's new boyfriend, whom he names and whose workplace and shift pattern he describes, is going to be dealt with this week. He says he has bought a knife for the purpose and that he has driven past the workplace twice. He is calm, coherent and consistent as he describes this and he repeats it when you check you have understood. On mental state examination his speech is normal in rate and form, there is no evidence of any delusion, hallucination or thought disorder, his mood is euthymic with a congruent affect, and his cognition is intact. He has taken no alcohol or other substance today. He tells you he has said this to you in confidence and asks you not to repeat it.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Disclosure: Named intended victim with described workplace and shift pattern, weapon obtained, two reconnaissance visits, stated timeframe of this week
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, no delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder, euthymic mood with congruent affect, intact cognition
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance taken today
data_table.History: Two previous convictions for assault, most recent four years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Arrange an involuntary admission under the mental health legislation today
options.rationale: Involuntary treatment criteria across Australian jurisdictions require a mental illness for which treatment is necessary, and his mental state examination shows no illness, with the risk arising from intent rather than from symptoms. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the mental health act manages risk arising from treatable illness whereas criminal justice manages risk arising from intent. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Discuss the disclosure with the treating team at the next case meeting
options.rationale: Team discussion is valuable and a second opinion is always worth having, but the stated timeframe is this week and a scheduled meeting introduces a delay the situation does not tolerate. Urgency is what converts a discussable concern into an immediate duty. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Contact the medical defence organisation before taking any other action
options.rationale: Medicolegal advice is worth obtaining and defence organisations are available urgently, but seeking it first places the clinician's exposure ahead of a named person's safety. The advice, when it comes, will be to disclose. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Notify the police and take steps to warn the person who was named
options.rationale: Australian privacy and health records legislation permits disclosure without consent where there is a serious and imminent threat to the life or safety of an identifiable individual, and every element that makes a threat credible is present. Warning the intended victim and notifying police is the recognised discharge of that duty. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Maintain confidentiality and document the disclosure fully in the case notes
options.rationale: Confidentiality is a strong obligation but it is not absolute, and it yields where disclosure is necessary to lessen a serious threat to an identifiable person. Thorough documentation is necessary but it protects the record rather than the person named. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

explanation.summary: Confidentiality in Australian practice is governed by the Privacy Act and its Australian Privacy Principles together with state and territory health records legislation, all of which permit use or disclosure of health information without consent where the clinician reasonably believes it is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to the life, health or safety of any individual. Australia has no direct statutory equivalent of the Tarasoff duty developed in American case law, but the professional and legal expectation converges on the same practical step when a threat is specific, credible and imminent. The features that make a threat actionable are a named or readily identifiable victim, expressed intent, a formulated plan, access to means, preparatory behaviour such as reconnaissance or weapon acquisition, and a stated timeframe, all of which are present in this presentation. Importantly the absence of mental illness does not remove the duty, and it does narrow the options, because involuntary treatment legislation cannot be used to detain a person who has no mental illness requiring treatment, leaving police notification and victim warning as the available routes. Practically the clinician informs the patient of the intended disclosure where it is safe to do so, discloses only the minimum information necessary, documents the reasoning contemporaneously, and seeks medicolegal and senior advice in parallel rather than beforehand.
key_points: Privacy legislation permits disclosure to lessen a serious threat to an identifiable person.
A named victim, a plan, access to means, reconnaissance and a timeframe make a threat actionable.
Absence of mental illness removes the mental health act as an option but not the duty to act.
Disclose the minimum necessary, document the reasoning, and seek advice in parallel.
explanation.pearls: Tell the patient you are going to disclose, unless doing so would increase the risk: it preserves what remains of the therapeutic relationship, it is expected under the privacy principles, and it is one of the first things asked about if the decision is later reviewed.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

subtopic_detail: repeated requests for rhinoplasty in a man who spends four hours a day checking mirrors
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 27-year-old man referred by a plastic surgeon who has declined to operate. He has had two previous rhinoplasties, the first at 21 and the second at 24, and says neither achieved what he wanted.

He tells you his nose is crooked and too wide and that people look at it on the train. He checks his profile in reflective surfaces for what he estimates as four hours a day, photographs his face from fixed angles each morning to compare, wears a cap pulled low and has stopped going to the gym or on dates. He resigned from a job requiring video meetings. He accepts that others tell him his nose looks normal but says they are being kind, and when you ask whether it is possible they are right he pauses and says probably not but he cannot be sure. There is no belief that he is being watched or persecuted, no hallucination, and no thought disorder. His mood is low with initial insomnia and he has thought about suicide if no surgeon will operate. The referring surgeon documented an anatomically normal nose.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Preoccupation: Estimated four hours daily of mirror checking and photographic comparison of a surgeon-documented normal nose
data_table.Functional impact: Resigned from work requiring video meetings, ceased gym attendance and dating, camouflages with a cap
data_table.Insight: Accepts reassurance is offered sincerely but cannot be certain his perception is mistaken
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with initial insomnia, no persecutory belief, hallucination or thought disorder, suicidal ideation contingent on surgical refusal
data_table.Surgical history: Two previous rhinoplasties at 21 and 24 with no relief of distress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Support the referral for rhinoplasty given the distress that he describes
options.rationale: Cosmetic procedures in body dysmorphic disorder leave the great majority no better or worse, the preoccupation commonly migrates to another feature, and dissatisfaction with surgeons is associated with litigation and rarely with violence. His two previous operations already demonstrate this pattern. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic for the overvalued ideas about his nose
options.rationale: Insight in this disorder runs on a spectrum and around a third hold their belief with delusional intensity, but that specifier does not change first-line treatment, which remains a serotonin reuptake inhibitor rather than an antipsychotic. Antipsychotic augmentation is considered only for inadequate response. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for supportive counselling and review his progress again in six months
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is markedly less effective than structured cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, and a six month interval is unsafe given the suicidal ideation he describes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the specific therapy targets the checking and reassurance-seeking that maintain the disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start a benzodiazepine for the anxiety and reassess him after four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines provide short-lived relief, do not treat the underlying disorder and risk dependence in a chronic condition. They may also function as a safety behaviour that maintains avoidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start a high dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with cognitive therapy
options.rationale: Preoccupation with a defect that others do not perceive, repetitive checking and camouflage behaviours and marked functional impairment define body dysmorphic disorder. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at the higher end of the dose range, combined with cognitive behavioural therapy including exposure and response prevention, are the established first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and affects around 2 per cent of the population, with far higher rates in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics where prevalence estimates reach 10 to 15 per cent. The diagnosis requires preoccupation with one or more perceived defects not observable or appearing slight to others, repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking or comparison, and clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is specified as good, poor or absent, and roughly a third hold the belief with delusional conviction, which does not alter the treatment pathway and should not be reclassified as a psychotic disorder. Suicidality is the reason this diagnosis matters so much in practice, since rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are among the highest of any psychiatric disorder, and the ideation is frequently contingent on whether a procedure will be performed. Cosmetic intervention is not effective treatment, with the great majority reporting no improvement or worsening and the preoccupation commonly shifting to a new body area, so declining surgery while actively offering psychiatric treatment is the clinically and ethically correct position.
key_points: Preoccupation with a slight or unobservable defect plus repetitive behaviours defines the disorder.
Around a third hold the belief with delusional conviction without changing first-line treatment.
Suicidality is high and is often contingent on whether a procedure is performed.
Cosmetic surgery rarely helps and the preoccupation commonly migrates to another feature.
explanation.pearls: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for body dysmorphic disorder are titrated to the upper end of the licensed range, as with obsessive compulsive disorder, and a trial is judged inadequate before 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose rather than at the four to six weeks used in depression.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: raised corrected calcium with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone after fifteen years of mood stabiliser treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for 15 years. She had three manic admissions before lithium was started and none since, and two previous attempts to switch her to other agents both ended in relapse within four months.

She feels well and has no bone pain, abdominal pain, polyuria or constipation. Her routine annual bloods show total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90) and estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2. Thyroid function is normal. A repeat set taken a fortnight later shows the same pattern. Her full blood count, liver function and serum protein electrophoresis are normal, and a myeloma screen is negative. She takes no thiazide, no calcium supplement and no vitamin D preparation, and she has had no recent immobilisation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Calcium studies: Total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)
data_table.Lithium and renal: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Other investigations: Normal thyroid function, full blood count, liver function and serum protein electrophoresis, negative myeloma screen
data_table.Confounders excluded: No thiazide, calcium supplement or vitamin D preparation, no recent immobilisation
data_table.Psychiatric history: Three manic admissions before lithium, none in 15 years, two failed switches with relapse within four months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for endocrine assessment and parathyroid imaging while continuing lithium
options.rationale: A corrected calcium near 2.88 mmol/L with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone, low-normal phosphate and a negative malignancy screen is parathyroid-driven hypercalcaemia, which in this setting is lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism. Endocrine referral with localisation imaging while lithium continues allows the parathyroid problem to be treated surgically without destabilising a mood disorder that has responded to nothing else. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease lithium abruptly and substitute sodium valproate at an equivalent dose
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium withdrawal carries a well documented rebound risk of mania within weeks, and hyperparathyroidism frequently persists after lithium is stopped because the glands have become autonomous. Stopping therefore risks relapse without reliably fixing the calcium. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Start cinacalcet now and continue lithium at the current dose and interval
options.rationale: Cinacalcet lowers calcium by increasing calcium-sensing receptor sensitivity and is genuinely useful when surgery is not an option, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that it is a medical holding measure rather than definitive treatment, and it is prescribed after endocrine assessment has established whether the disease is single-gland and operable rather than before. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure her, since the measured calcium is close to the reference range
options.rationale: Correcting for an albumin of 32 g/L adds roughly 0.02 mmol/L for every gram below 40, giving a corrected calcium near 2.88 mmol/L, which is clearly elevated rather than borderline. Reading the uncorrected value in a hypoalbuminaemic patient systematically understates the true calcium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose and repeat both results in one month before acting
options.rationale: Her lithium concentration is within the therapeutic range and the hypercalcaemia is not a dose-related toxic effect, so reducing the dose risks relapse without correcting the calcium. In a woman who has relapsed on two previous attempts to change treatment, that is a poor trade. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder)

explanation.summary: Lithium raises the set point at which calcium suppresses parathyroid hormone release by acting on the calcium-sensing receptor, so parathyroid hormone remains inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of a rising calcium, and with prolonged exposure the glands can become autonomous with multiglandular hyperplasia. Prevalence rises with duration of treatment and reaches roughly 10 to 15 per cent after a decade or more, yet it is frequently missed because calcium is not always included in routine lithium monitoring and because mild hypercalcaemia is asymptomatic. The biochemical trap in this case is albumin, since roughly 40 per cent of serum calcium is protein bound and a low albumin lowers the measured total calcium while leaving the physiologically active ionised fraction untouched, so a value that looks near-normal can conceal clear hypercalcaemia. An unsuppressed parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia localises the problem to the parathyroid glands and excludes the malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia that would suppress it, which matters because the alternative diagnoses have entirely different urgency. The management dilemma is that stopping lithium is not reliably curative once autonomy is established, while continuing it leaves the calcium elevated, and in a woman whose bipolar illness has failed two alternative agents the resolution is to treat the parathyroid disease surgically and keep the lithium.
key_points: Lithium raises the parathyroid calcium set point, leaving parathyroid hormone unsuppressed.
Correct calcium for albumin by about 0.02 mmol/L per gram below 40 before interpreting it.
An unsuppressed parathyroid hormone excludes malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.
Hyperparathyroidism often persists after lithium cessation, so stopping is not reliably curative.
explanation.pearls: Add corrected calcium to the annual lithium monitoring panel alongside renal and thyroid function, because lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism affects roughly one in eight patients after a decade of treatment and is asymptomatic until renal stones or bone loss have already occurred.

subtopic_detail: a prolonged repolarisation interval on opioid substitution therapy after a second drug was added
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man who has been stable on methadone 130 mg daily for three years, with no heroin use on supervised urine testing for 18 months and steady employment. Four weeks ago another doctor started escitalopram 20 mg daily for depression. He has had two days of vomiting and loose stools from a gastrointestinal illness that is now settling.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no seizures, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His electrocardiogram today shows sinus rhythm at 52 beats per minute with a measured QT interval of 520 milliseconds. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110). His liver function and thyroid function are normal, and he takes no other prescribed or over the counter medication. He tells you that stopping methadone is the one thing he does not want, because the last time his dose was cut he relapsed within a fortnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 52 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm at 52 beats per minute with a measured QT interval of 520 milliseconds
data_table.Electrolytes: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Methadone 130 mg daily for three years, escitalopram 20 mg daily started four weeks ago
data_table.Symptoms: No syncope, palpitations or seizures, two days of vomiting and diarrhoea now settling
data_table.Other investigations: Normal liver and thyroid function, no family history of sudden cardiac death

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cardiology review and insertion of an implantable defibrillator
options.rationale: Device therapy is for inherited or structural arrhythmia syndromes with sustained ventricular arrhythmia or high predicted risk, not for reversible acquired prolongation from drugs and electrolytes. Treating the reversible causes is expected to normalise the interval entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Correct the potassium and magnesium, cease escitalopram and repeat the tracing
options.rationale: At a rate of 52 beats per minute the RR interval is 1.15 seconds, so the rate-corrected interval is about 484 milliseconds rather than the alarming 520 measured, placing him below the 500 millisecond threshold at which methadone reduction is usually mandated. The reversible contributors, namely hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and a recently added serotonergic drug with its own repolarisation effect, are corrected first because doing so preserves the opioid treatment that is keeping him well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the methadone dose today and review the electrocardiogram next week
options.rationale: Halving a stable maintenance dose would precipitate withdrawal and, on his own history, relapse to injecting, which carries a far higher mortality than the arrhythmic risk being avoided. Dose reduction is the answer once the corrected interval exceeds 500 milliseconds with reversible causes already addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Cease methadone and transfer him to buprenorphine over the next few days
options.rationale: Buprenorphine has a much smaller effect on cardiac repolarisation and transfer is the right move for genuinely refractory prolongation, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that transfer destabilises a patient stable for three years and is reserved for when the interval remains prolonged after reversible contributors have been corrected. (Source: RANZCP: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Continue all current treatment and repeat the electrocardiogram in six months
options.rationale: Leaving a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L and a magnesium of 0.62 mmol/L untreated in a patient on a repolarisation-prolonging opioid accepts an avoidable risk of torsades de pointes. Electrolyte depletion after vomiting is precisely the setting in which these arrhythmias occur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Methadone blocks the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current and prolongs cardiac repolarisation in a dose-related way, with risk rising appreciably above roughly 100 mg daily, which is why baseline and follow-up electrocardiography is part of Australian opioid substitution practice. The interval that matters is the rate-corrected one, and at bradycardic rates the Bazett formula, which divides the measured QT by the square root of the RR interval in seconds, corrects downwards, so a raw QT of 520 milliseconds at 52 beats per minute yields a corrected value near 484 rather than the value that appears on first reading. Thresholds are conventionally an interval above 500 milliseconds, or a rise of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, as the point at which dose reduction, drug substitution or specialist referral becomes necessary. Risk is multiplicative rather than additive, so a moderately prolonged interval matters far more in the presence of hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, hepatic impairment, cytochrome inhibitors or a second prolonging drug, and escitalopram has its own dose-related effect that is greatest at 20 mg. The decision is genuinely a trade-off, since cutting or stopping methadone in a stable patient carries a real and quantified risk of relapse to injecting drug use with its own substantial mortality, so reversible contributors are corrected before the opioid is touched.
key_points: Bazett correction at a slow heart rate lowers the corrected interval below the measured QT.
Above 500 milliseconds corrected, or a rise over 60 milliseconds, triggers dose change or transfer.
Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and a second prolonging drug multiply the risk.
Destabilising effective opioid substitution carries its own substantial mortality.
explanation.pearls: Replace magnesium even when the level is only borderline in drug-induced repolarisation prolongation, because intravenous magnesium suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger torsades de pointes independently of whether the serum magnesium was low to begin with.

subtopic_detail: young woman with patchy scalp hair loss admitting to pulling hairs out when studying under pressure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student who has noticed thinning over the top and right side of her scalp for the past year. She wears her hair up to disguise it. With some embarrassment she tells you that she pulls hairs out one at a time, mostly in the evenings while studying, and feels a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards.

She says she is not trying to hurt herself and does not want to die. She does not eat the hair. She has always been a worrier but has no low mood, no weight change and sleeps reasonably well. On examination there are ill defined patches of shortened hair of varying lengths over the vertex and right parietal scalp, with no scaling, erythema, scarring or pustules, and the underlying skin looks normal. Eyebrows and eyelashes are intact. Thyroid function, iron studies and a full blood examination arranged by a colleague last month were all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Ill defined patches of hair of varying lengths over the vertex and right parietal scalp, no scaling, scarring, erythema or pustules
data_table.Distribution: Eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no body hair loss, no nail changes
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, iron studies and full blood examination all within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic with reactive affect, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence sertraline titrated to a therapeutic dose and review her response in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder, which trichotillomania sits alongside in the diagnostic grouping, so the reasoning is understandable. Trials in trichotillomania itself have been largely negative, which is why it is not first line. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine at a low dose with monitoring of weight and metabolic parameters
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics have some trial support in refractory cases and so are a real third line option rather than a nonsense answer. Starting one before any behavioural therapy exposes a nineteen year old to metabolic risk she does not need to take yet. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid to the affected areas and review her in eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats alopecia areata, the dermatological near pair, which produces smooth completely bald patches with exclamation mark hairs rather than broken hairs of differing lengths. There is no inflammatory process here to suppress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Arrange a scalp biopsy to distinguish scarring from non scarring patterns of alopecia
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for scalp hair loss where the clinical pattern is genuinely uncertain or scarring is suspected from erythema, scale or loss of follicular openings. A clear account of pulling with normal scalp skin makes the diagnosis without histology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training delivered by a psychologist experienced in this technique
options.rationale: Hairs of varying lengths in non scarring patches with premonitory tension and relief on pulling is trichotillomania, and habit reversal training is the intervention with the strongest evidence base. It combines awareness training with a competing response and is more effective than any medication studied. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders and involves recurrent pulling out of one's own hair with repeated attempts to stop, causing distress or impairment. Onset is typically in early adolescence and it is far more often reported by females in clinical samples. The scalp is the commonest site, followed by eyebrows and eyelashes, and the examination finding that distinguishes it from alopecia areata is hairs of differing lengths within irregular non scarring patches on normal underlying skin. Many patients describe a premonitory urge with tension relieved by pulling, while others pull automatically without awareness during sedentary activities, and the two patterns often coexist. Habit reversal training is first line, often within a broader cognitive behavioural framework, and N acetylcysteine has some supportive trial evidence as an adjunct; comorbid anxiety and depression should be treated on their own merits.
key_points: Hairs of varying lengths on normal non scarred skin distinguish it from alopecia areata.
Premonitory tension with relief after pulling is characteristic but not universal.
It is classified with obsessive compulsive and related disorders, not with self harm.
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication.
Ask about trichophagia, because swallowed hair can form a gastric bezoar.
explanation.pearls: Always ask whether the patient swallows the hair, because trichophagia can produce a trichobezoar extending through the pylorus into the small bowel, which presents with an epigastric mass and obstruction and needs surgical removal.

subtopic_detail: student falling asleep constantly whose knees buckle when he laughs at his friends' jokes
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20-year-old apprentice electrician who has fallen asleep at his workbench three times in the past month and has been warned by his supervisor. He says he sleeps eight hours a night, wakes unrefreshed, and feels an overwhelming need to sleep by mid morning that he cannot fight off, though a fifteen minute nap leaves him briefly clear headed.

He mentions that for the past year his knees have given way and his jaw has gone slack for a few seconds when he laughs hard with his mates, staying fully aware throughout. He also describes frightening moments on waking where he cannot move for half a minute. He drinks two standard drinks on weekends only, takes no medications, and has a body mass index of 22 kg per square metre with no snoring reported by his partner. His mood is good, he enjoys his sport and his weight is steady. Examination including neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, normal neurological examination, no goitre, Mallampati class 1 airway
data_table.Sleep history: Eight hours in bed nightly, unrefreshing, irresistible daytime sleep episodes, refreshing short naps, sleep paralysis on waking
data_table.Associated: Brief bilateral knee buckling and jaw slackness with laughter, fully conscious throughout

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a sleep physician for overnight polysomnography with a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Irresistible daytime sleepiness with refreshing naps, sleep paralysis and cataplexy triggered by laughter is narcolepsy type 1, and the diagnosis requires polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. Confirmation matters because it governs both treatment and driving advice. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence modafinil to control his daytime sleepiness and arrange review in three weeks
options.rationale: Modafinil is a mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is made and would genuinely help his symptoms. Starting it first removes the abnormality that the sleep latency test is designed to measure and, in Australia, prescribing is tied to specialist confirmation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange a home based sleep apnoea study and advise weight loss with sleep hygiene measures
options.rationale: Home studies are designed to detect obstructive sleep apnoea, the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness, but they do not record sleep stages properly and cannot diagnose narcolepsy. A slim young man with no snoring and an unobstructed airway is an unlikely candidate for apnoea. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant for atypical depression and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Hypersomnia is a feature of atypical depression, which is why this is considered, but he has good mood, preserved enjoyment of his sport and stable weight. Antidepressants do suppress cataplexy, so an empirical trial could partially mask the presentation and delay the real diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Request an electroencephalogram to characterise the episodes of loss of muscle tone
options.rationale: Electroencephalography investigates atonic seizures, the neurological near pair, in which consciousness is lost and there is no emotional trigger. Preserved awareness throughout an episode reliably triggered by laughter points away from epilepsy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, probably through an autoimmune process, and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood. The tetrad is excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations, though only sleepiness is universal and the full tetrad is present in a minority. Cataplexy is the near pathognomonic feature and is the abrupt loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness triggered by strong emotion, most reliably by laughter, affecting the knees, jaw and neck. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause and to demonstrate adequate sleep, followed by a multiple sleep latency test showing a mean sleep latency of eight minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. Management combines scheduled short naps and sleep hygiene with wake promoting agents such as modafinil, and separate treatment for cataplexy, and the driving and workplace implications must be addressed explicitly.
key_points: Sleepiness with refreshing short naps distinguishes narcolepsy from most other causes.
Cataplexy is emotion triggered muscle tone loss with preserved consciousness.
Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the tetrad but are not universal.
Diagnosis needs polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test.
Antidepressants suppress cataplexy and can obscure the diagnosis if started first.
explanation.pearls: A multiple sleep latency test shows a mean sleep latency of eight minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods in narcolepsy, and the prior overnight study must document at least six hours of sleep or the result cannot be interpreted.

subtopic_detail: woman with severe irritability and despair for the week before each period that lifts once bleeding starts
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old teacher who describes becoming a different person for about a week each month. She becomes intensely irritable, snaps at her partner and her students, feels hopeless and tearful, and sleeps poorly. She has twice taken sick leave because she could not face the classroom.

She says the change lifts within a day or two of her period starting and that she feels completely well for the following fortnight. On your advice she has kept a daily symptom diary through three consecutive cycles, which shows her symptom scores rising sharply about six days before each period, peaking on the two days before bleeding, and returning to baseline by the second day of bleeding, with a clear symptom free interval each cycle. She is not pregnant and uses condoms. She drinks alcohol rarely, takes no medications, and thyroid function and a full blood examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Symptom diary: Three consecutive cycles charted, scores rising six days premenstrually, peaking two days before bleeding, returning to baseline by day two of bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood examination within normal limits, urinary pregnancy test negative
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic today with reactive affect, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone taken in a continuous regimen
options.rationale: Drospirenone containing combined contraception has evidence in this condition and is a legitimate option, particularly when contraception is also wanted. It is second line to serotonergic therapy on effect size and would not be the first choice for a woman whose contraception is already settled. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with oestrogen and progestogen add back therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is highly effective and is used for severe treatment refractory disease, sometimes as a test before surgical management. It causes a hypo oestrogenic state with bone loss and is far too aggressive as an initial step. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms are not cleanly confined to the luteal phase or when a comorbid mood disorder is present. Given her documented symptom free fortnight, intermittent dosing achieves the same benefit with half the drug exposure. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken from ovulation until bleeding begins
options.rationale: A prospectively charted symptom cluster confined to the luteal phase with a clear symptom free interval is premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and serotonergic antidepressants are first line. Luteal phase dosing works because the response is rapid and not dependent on weeks of continuous treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Oral micronised progesterone taken through the second half of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Luteal progesterone was long prescribed for premenstrual symptoms but trials have consistently shown no benefit over placebo, and in some women progestogen exposure worsens mood. The intuition that a luteal problem needs luteal hormone does not hold. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a mood disorder in the DSM-5 classification, distinguished from ordinary premenstrual symptoms by severity and by functional impairment, and it affects around three to eight per cent of menstruating women. The diagnosis requires prospective daily symptom rating across at least two consecutive cycles, because retrospective recall is unreliable and about half of women who report the pattern do not show it when charted. The defining feature is a symptom free interval in the follicular phase, which separates it from premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying depressive or anxiety disorder, where symptoms persist at a lower level throughout. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and are unusual in this indication for working within a day or two, which is what makes luteal phase only dosing viable. Where these fail, options include combined hormonal contraception containing drospirenone, and in severe refractory cases ovarian suppression with add back therapy or bilateral oophorectomy.
key_points: Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for diagnosis.
A symptom free follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation of another disorder.
Serotonergic antidepressants work within one to two days in this condition.
Luteal phase dosing from ovulation to bleeding is as effective as continuous dosing.
Luteal progesterone supplementation has no benefit over placebo.
explanation.pearls: The rapid response of premenstrual dysphoric disorder to serotonergic medication, within 24 to 48 hours rather than the usual two to four weeks, is thought to reflect a direct effect on allopregnanolone metabolism rather than the mechanism that treats depression.

subtopic_detail: treating a colleague who discloses heavy drinking but has taken herself off the roster already
stem:
You are a general practitioner and a 34-year-old surgical registrar has made an appointment with you as a patient. She tells you she has been drinking a bottle of wine most nights for the past eight months since a relationship ended, and scores 22 on the alcohol use disorders identification test.

She tells you she has never operated or attended work while affected by alcohol, and that two weeks ago she recognised the problem, spoke to her director of training, and has been on planned leave since with no patient contact. She has arranged to see an addiction medicine specialist next week and wants your help with the interim management. She is tearful but engaged, denies suicidal ideation, and has no withdrawal symptoms today. Her liver function tests show a gamma glutamyl transferase of 96 U/L (5 to 35) with normal transaminases and bilirubin, and her full blood examination shows a mean cell volume of 99 fL (80 to 98).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: Gamma glutamyl transferase 96 U/L (5 to 35), transaminases and bilirubin within normal limits, mean cell volume 99 fL (80 to 98)
data_table.Mental state: Tearful but engaged with reactive affect, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, insight present
data_table.Occupational: Currently on planned leave with no patient contact, self reported to director of training, addiction medicine appointment arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action regarding her registration?

options.text: Continue treating her without notification, documenting the risk assessment in her record
options.rationale: Mandatory notification for an impairment requires a substantial risk of harm to the public, and a doctor who has removed herself from clinical work, disclosed to her employer and engaged with treatment does not meet that threshold. Documenting the reasoning protects both of you and preserves the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Telephone her director of training to confirm the details of her disclosure before proceeding
options.rationale: Contacting her employer without consent breaches the confidentiality she is entitled to as a patient, and her account is not in doubt. Verification would be relevant only if you doubted that the risk had actually been removed. (Source: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice)
source_refs: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.text: Decline to treat her and redirect her to the state doctors health service for all her care
options.rationale: Doctors health advisory services are an excellent adjunct and worth offering alongside her care, so recommending contact is reasonable. Refusing to treat a colleague who has approached you appropriately leaves her without a treating doctor at the point of greatest risk. (Source: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Make a mandatory notification to the regulator today because her drinking meets impairment criteria
options.rationale: Having a health condition, even a substance use disorder, is not by itself notifiable; the test is whether the practitioner is placing the public at substantial risk of harm. Notifying a colleague who has already removed the risk deters doctors from seeking help, which the guidelines explicitly warn against. (Source: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Advise her to make a voluntary self notification to the regulator as a condition of your care
options.rationale: Self notification is genuinely available and some doctors choose it, so raising it as an option is defensible. Making it a condition of treatment is coercive and adds a regulatory burden that her current arrangements have already made unnecessary. (Source: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

explanation.summary: Mandatory notification obligations under the National Law apply to four forms of notifiable conduct: practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, sexual misconduct, placing the public at risk of substantial harm through an impairment, and practising in a way that departs significantly from accepted standards. The 2020 amendments raised the threshold for treating practitioners specifically, so that notification is required only where there is a substantial risk of harm to the public, and the guidelines are explicit that the intention is to encourage practitioners to seek health care. Every state and territory except New South Wales and Western Australia applies this treating practitioner exemption in this form, and those two jurisdictions have their own separate arrangements. A practitioner who has identified her own problem, removed herself from clinical work, informed her employer and engaged with specialist treatment has substantially mitigated the risk. The treating doctor's role is then to provide good clinical care, document the risk assessment, and reassess if circumstances change, such as a return to work without adequate monitoring.
key_points: A health condition alone is not notifiable; the test is substantial risk of harm to the public.
Practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs is separately and always notifiable.
The threshold for treating practitioners was raised deliberately to encourage help seeking.
Document the risk assessment and the reasoning for not notifying.
Reassess if she returns to clinical work before treatment and monitoring are established.
explanation.pearls: The four categories of notifiable conduct are intoxication at work, sexual misconduct, impairment placing the public at substantial risk, and significant departure from accepted professional standards, and only the first of these is triggered by the substance itself rather than by a risk assessment.

sources.label: Ahpra and Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications
Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

subtopic_detail: older woman with failing central vision who sees detailed figures in period costume and knows they are not real
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 82-year-old woman brought in by her daughter, who is worried her mother is developing dementia. For the past three months she has been seeing small figures in old fashioned clothing walking along the skirting board of her lounge room, and sometimes brickwork patterns appearing across the wall.

She describes the images as vivid and detailed, lasting several minutes at a time, usually in the evening. She is quite clear that they are not really there and finds them curious rather than frightening, and she says they never speak to her. She has advanced age related macular degeneration and her corrected visual acuity is 6/60 on the right and counting fingers on the left. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications, cooks for herself, and scores 29 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen. She takes no anticholinergic medications, has no tremor or rigidity, no fluctuating attention and no dream enactment behaviour reported.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, normal gait, no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Vision: Corrected visual acuity 6/60 right and counting fingers left, advanced age related macular degeneration
data_table.Cognition: Standardised cognitive screen 29 out of 30, independent in all instrumental activities of daily living

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the nature of the phenomenon and refer for low vision rehabilitation services
options.rationale: Complex formed visual hallucinations with retained insight, intact cognition and no other modality involved in a person with severe visual loss is Charles Bonnet syndrome. Explanation alone relieves most of the distress, and optimising residual vision and environmental lighting reduces the frequency. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Request a urine culture with electrolytes and a computed tomography scan of the brain
options.rationale: This is the delirium screen, and delirium is always worth excluding when hallucinations are new in an older person. Delirium brings inattention, a fluctuating course and disorientation over hours to days, not three months of stable insightful imagery. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence donepezil for a presumed neurodegenerative cause and arrange memory clinic review
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors do reduce visual hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies, so the pharmacological logic is not absurd. A score of 29 out of 30 with full independence gives no basis for a dementia diagnosis to treat. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for dopamine transporter imaging and a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: This pathway investigates dementia with Lewy bodies, the near pair, which also causes vivid formed visual hallucinations in older people. That diagnosis requires fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism or rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and her cognition and examination are normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Commence low dose quetiapine at night and review her symptoms again in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment is for hallucinations arising from a psychotic or neurodegenerative process and carries stroke and mortality risk in older people. Treating a release phenomenon with retained insight exposes her to that risk for no benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Charles Bonnet syndrome is the occurrence of complex visual hallucinations in people with significant visual impairment, in the absence of psychiatric or neurological disease, and it is thought to arise from spontaneous activity in deafferented visual cortex. It affects a substantial minority of people with advanced macular degeneration, glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy, yet it is markedly under reported because patients fear being thought to have a psychiatric illness. The distinguishing features are that the hallucinations are purely visual, are often of people, faces, patterns or landscapes, and that insight is retained so the person knows the images are not real. They do not interact with the person, do not carry a persecutory meaning, and are not accompanied by hallucinations in other modalities. Management is chiefly explanation and reassurance, which most patients find sufficient, along with optimising remaining vision, improving lighting, and treating any social isolation; medication has a limited role reserved for severe persistent distress.
key_points: Complex formed visual hallucinations in the setting of significant visual loss.
Insight is retained and the images are silent and non interactive.
No hallucinations in other modalities and no cognitive impairment.
Explanation and reassurance are the primary treatment and are usually sufficient.
Antipsychotics carry stroke and mortality risk in older people and are not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Naming the condition to the patient is itself therapeutic: many people have concealed the hallucinations for months because they assume they are going mad, and simply being told this is a known consequence of eye disease removes most of the associated distress.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

subtopic_detail: child who talks freely at home but has not spoken at school in the eight months since starting
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has asked her parents to seek help. She has not spoken a single word at school since she started eight months ago, communicating only by pointing and nodding, though she joins in games with two classmates without speaking.

At home she is described as chatty, funny and bossy with her younger brother, and she speaks freely to her parents and grandparents. She spoke to you briefly in the waiting room while playing with her mother but has not spoken since you entered the room. Her parents report that she reached all her speech milestones on time and that her vocabulary and sentence structure are age appropriate at home. She makes eye contact with you, follows your pointing, brings a drawing to show her mother and looks to her for a reaction. There are no repetitive behaviours or restricted interests, her hearing was tested and normal last year, and there are no concerns about her learning.

data_table.Examination: Physically well, normal growth, no dysmorphic features, normal oromotor examination
data_table.Communication: Speaks freely at home with age appropriate vocabulary and sentence structure, mute at school for eight months
data_table.Social: Makes eye contact, follows pointing, shares enjoyment by showing, joins peer play non verbally
data_table.Investigations: Formal audiometry normal last year, no concerns regarding learning or motor development

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy using graded exposure with the school involved
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in a specific social setting while speaking normally elsewhere, for more than a month and interfering with schooling, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder. Graded exposure delivered in partnership with the school is the first line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer to a speech pathologist for assessment and treatment of an expressive language disorder
options.rationale: Speech pathology involvement is often valuable and speech pathologists frequently co deliver treatment for this condition, so this is not a wrong referral in itself. A language disorder would impair speech in every setting, and hers is entirely normal at home. (Source: RCH CPG: Speech and language delay)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Speech and language delay

options.text: Advise the school to reduce pressure on her to speak and review her progress in six months
options.rationale: Removing pressure to speak is a genuinely important component of management and stops the situation getting worse, which makes this partially right. Waiting without active graded exposure allows the avoidance to consolidate, and duration of untreated mutism predicts a poorer outcome. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence fluoxetine at a low dose and arrange paediatric review within the next four weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic medication has evidence in selective mutism and is used when behavioural treatment has failed or when the child is too anxious to engage with it. Starting it before any psychological intervention reverses the recommended order in a six year old. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment including a standardised observation schedule
options.rationale: Autism is the differential that must be considered in any child not talking at school, and the two can coexist. Shared enjoyment by showing, responsive eye contact, joint attention and normal reciprocal play at home argue against it here. (Source: RCH CPG: Autism spectrum disorder)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child consistently fails to speak in specific social situations despite speaking normally in others, most often being mute at school while fluent at home. Onset is usually between two and five years and it is frequently not recognised until school entry makes it obvious, by which time avoidance patterns are entrenched. Diagnosis requires the pattern to last at least a month, excluding the first month of school, and to interfere with education or social communication, and it must not be explained by a language disorder or a communication difficulty of autism. The condition is strongly associated with social anxiety disorder and with a family history of anxiety, and it is not a consequence of trauma or oppositionality, although both are commonly assumed. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered across home and school, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors reserved for children who cannot engage or who fail behavioural treatment.
key_points: Speech is normal in at least one setting, which excludes a primary language disorder.
Duration of at least one month beyond the first month of school is required.
It is an anxiety disorder, not oppositionality, shyness or a trauma response.
Graded exposure with school involvement is first line treatment.
Longer untreated duration predicts a poorer outcome, so do not simply wait.
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the technique that most often produces the first words at school: the child talks with a parent in an empty classroom, the teacher then enters at increasing proximity while the conversation continues, and the parent is gradually withdrawn once speech is maintained.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Speech and language delay

subtopic_detail: man with an evening urge to move his legs relieved by walking and a low ferritin on screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who cannot get to sleep. For the past year he has had a deeply unpleasant crawling sensation in both calves that builds during the evening while he sits watching television and forces him to get up and walk around. Walking relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns once he sits down again.

He is worst between about 9 pm and 1 am and says he is fine during the working day. His wife says his legs do not kick once he is asleep. He has no back pain, no radiation down the leg, and no numbness or weakness. He takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antipsychotics and drinks two cups of coffee before midday only. On examination pedal pulses are present and symmetrical, ankle reflexes are intact, and sensation and power are normal in both legs. His ferritin is 38 mcg/L (30 to 300), haemoglobin is 142 g/L (130 to 180) and transferrin saturation is 16 per cent (16 to 45).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical present pedal pulses, intact ankle reflexes, normal power and sensation in both lower limbs
data_table.Symptom pattern: Evening onset urge to move relieved completely by walking and returning with rest, no nocturnal limb jerking reported
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 38 mcg/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 16 per cent (16 to 45), haemoglobin 142 g/L (130 to 180), renal function and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence gabapentin at a low dose each evening and titrate the dose according to response
options.rationale: Alpha 2 delta ligands are an appropriate pharmacological first line for symptomatic restless legs and are preferred over dopamine agonists. They should follow rather than precede correction of iron deficiency, which can resolve symptoms without ongoing medication. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for a four week period with sleep hygiene advice provided
options.rationale: A hypnotic may help him fall asleep but does nothing for the sensory urge that is driving the problem, and dependence risk in a chronic condition is substantial. Sleep hygiene alone does not address a neurological sensorimotor disorder. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence pramipexole at a low dose each evening and review his response in four weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists relieve symptoms rapidly and were long used first line, which is why this remains a common answer. Augmentation, in which symptoms intensify and spread over months to years of treatment, has moved them down the ladder behind iron repletion and alpha 2 delta ligands. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine
options.rationale: This workup targets lumbosacral radiculopathy and peripheral neuropathy, the neurological near pairs, which give dermatomal or stocking distribution sensory loss and are not relieved within a minute of walking. His neurological examination is normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement taken with vitamin C and recheck the iron studies in twelve weeks
options.rationale: The urge to move with evening predominance and complete relief by walking is restless legs syndrome, and iron status is the first modifiable factor to address. A ferritin below 75 mcg/L warrants replacement in this condition even though it lies within the standard laboratory range. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome, also called Willis Ekbom disease, is diagnosed clinically on five criteria: an urge to move the legs usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, onset or worsening during rest, relief by movement, evening or night predominance, and the absence of a better explanation such as cramps or positional discomfort. Brain iron deficiency is central to the pathophysiology even when systemic iron stores appear adequate, because iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase in dopamine synthesis. This is why the treatment threshold for ferritin sits far above the usual laboratory cut off, at 75 mcg/L or a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent. Secondary causes to exclude include pregnancy, chronic kidney disease and drugs including antihistamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics and dopamine antagonist antiemetics. Where pharmacological treatment is needed after iron repletion, alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin have replaced dopamine agonists as first choice because of the risk of augmentation with long term dopaminergic treatment.
key_points: Five clinical criteria: urge, rest onset, movement relief, evening predominance, no better explanation.
Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in every patient at diagnosis.
Replace iron if ferritin is below 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation is below 20 per cent.
Alpha 2 delta ligands are now preferred over dopamine agonists for symptomatic treatment.
Review medications, since antihistamines and many psychotropics provoke the condition.
explanation.pearls: Augmentation is the specific hazard of long term dopamine agonist use in restless legs: symptoms begin earlier in the day, spread to the arms and trunk, and become more intense, and the paradox is that increasing the dose briefly helps before making it worse.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: older woman certain that mites live in her skin who brings in skin flakes sealed in a container
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman for the fifth time in three months about insects living under her skin. She has been treated twice with topical permethrin and once with oral ivermectin by a colleague and once by a dermatologist, with no change. She has fumigated her flat twice and has thrown out her mattress.

She places a small plastic container on your desk containing skin flakes, lint and a hair, and asks you to send it to the laboratory to prove the infestation. She is entirely certain about it, says the sensation of movement is constant, and will not consider any other explanation, though she holds no other unusual beliefs and there is no persecutory theme. She lives alone, manages her finances, and scores 28 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen. On examination there are linear excoriations and crusted erosions on the forearms and upper back, all within reach, with no burrows in the finger webs and no rash on the trunk. Full blood examination, renal function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and a urine drug screen are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Linear excoriations and crusted erosions on forearms and upper back confined to areas within reach, no burrows in finger webs
data_table.Cognition: Standardised cognitive screen 28 out of 30, independent in all instrumental activities of daily living
data_table.Mental state: Fixed unshakeable belief in cutaneous infestation, no other delusions, no hallucinations in other modalities, mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, renal and thyroid function, vitamin B12 and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for computed tomography of the brain and a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated when a late onset psychotic presentation comes with cognitive decline, focal signs or a rapid course, so it is a reasonable instinct in a 71 year old. A score of 28 out of 30 with full independence and an eight month single themed belief does not meet that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Examine the specimen with her, then explain there are no parasites and offer a further review
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a fixed delusion does not shift it and typically ends the therapeutic relationship, after which the patient consults elsewhere. Examining the specimen is right; stopping at contradiction leaves the condition untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Examine the specimen with her, then start low dose risperidone framed as treatment for the sensation
options.rationale: A single fixed unshakeable belief of infestation with intact cognition and no other psychotic features is delusional infestation, a somatic type delusional disorder, and antipsychotic treatment produces remission in a majority. Taking the specimen seriously and treating the distressing sensation rather than debating the belief is what secures adherence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence sertraline for an obsessive preoccupation and arrange psychology review within a month
options.rationale: Serotonergic treatment suits the patient who acknowledges the thought may be excessive, which defines an obsessional rather than a delusional presentation. She holds the belief with complete conviction, which places it outside the range that responds to this approach. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Send the specimen for microscopy and repeat the scabies treatment with a whole household approach
options.rationale: Repeat antiparasitic treatment is the correct response to genuine scabies, the near pair, which produces burrows in the finger webs and wrists, involves household contacts and itches worst at night. Four failed courses and lesions confined to reachable skin argue against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation, historically called delusional parasitosis or Ekbom syndrome, is a somatic type delusional disorder in which the person holds a fixed belief that they are infested by insects, worms or fibres. It is commonest in women over the age of fifty and characteristically presents to general practice and dermatology rather than to psychiatry, often after multiple failed courses of antiparasitic treatment. The specimen sign, in which the patient brings skin debris or lint in a container as proof, is highly characteristic and should be handled respectfully rather than dismissed. Secondary causes must be excluded, including substance use particularly stimulants, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, renal and hepatic failure, dementia and true infestation. Antipsychotic treatment, historically with pimozide and now more often with risperidone, olanzapine or aripiprazole, achieves substantial improvement in most patients, and the practical difficulty is engagement rather than efficacy, so treatment is best introduced as relief for the distressing sensation and the sleeplessness rather than as treatment for a false belief.
key_points: A single fixed somatic delusion with otherwise preserved functioning defines delusional disorder.
The specimen sign is characteristic and should be examined, not dismissed.
Exclude stimulant use, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, organ failure and true scabies.
Excoriations confined to skin the patient can reach is a useful physical clue.
Antipsychotics are effective; engagement rather than efficacy is the limiting factor.
explanation.pearls: Offer to examine the container under the microscope with the patient present rather than sending it away, because agreeing on what can be seen together preserves the alliance long enough to introduce treatment, whereas a laboratory report saying no organisms found is invariably rejected.

subtopic_detail: man eighteen months after his wife died who sets her place at the table and cannot accept she is gone
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 67-year-old man eighteen months after his wife of forty years died of pancreatic cancer. His daughter has encouraged him to come. He tells you he still sets her place at the dinner table each evening, has not moved any of her belongings, and spends several hours most days listening to voicemail messages she left him.
