He says he cannot accept that she is gone, feels that part of himself died with her, and avoids the shopping centre they used to visit because it is unbearable. He has withdrawn from the bowls club he attended for twenty years. He describes intense yearning every day rather than waves that come and go, and says life has no purpose without her. He does not feel worthless, his appetite and concentration are reasonable, and he still enjoys his grandson's visits. He denies thoughts of ending his life but says he would not mind if he did not wake up. He drinks two beers most evenings, the same as before she died, and takes no medications.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful when speaking of his wife, affect reactive to other topics, no psychomotor retardation, no guilt or worthlessness
data_table.Symptom pattern: Persistent daily intense yearning and preoccupation for eighteen months, identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders
data_table.Function: Withdrawn from bowls club and social contacts, maintains self care, shopping and finances
data_table.Risk: No active suicidal ideation or plan, passive wish not to wake, no prior attempts, protective relationship with grandson

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange admission to an older persons mental health unit for assessment of his suicide risk
options.rationale: Admission is warranted for active suicidal intent, plan or significant self neglect, none of which he has. A passive wish not to wake with preserved self care and a protective relationship does not justify removing him from his home. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at a therapeutic dose and review his response after six weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants are the right treatment when a major depressive episode is present or develops alongside the grief, and the two frequently coexist. He lacks pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness and guilt, and antidepressants have not been shown to treat the core grief symptoms themselves. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Reassure him that this is a normal response to losing a spouse and review him in three months
options.rationale: Grief of this intensity within the first six to twelve months is indeed expected and needs no intervention, so the instinct is a sound one at an earlier stage. Persisting at this severity beyond twelve months with social withdrawal and functional loss is what defines the disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer him to a community bereavement support group and encourage a return to his bowls club
options.rationale: Peer support and behavioural re engagement are valuable adjuncts and should be encouraged alongside treatment, so this is the closest wrong answer. Group support alone has not been shown to alter the course of established prolonged grief disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychotherapy specifically targeting the loss
options.rationale: Persistent intense yearning with identity disruption, disbelief and avoidance that is still severe and disabling at eighteen months meets prolonged grief disorder rather than normal bereavement. Grief focused psychotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence and outperforms general supportive counselling. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added as a formal diagnosis in DSM-5-TR and in ICD-11 to identify the minority of bereaved people, of the order of seven to ten per cent, whose grief does not follow the usual trajectory towards accommodation. The diagnosis requires the death of a close person at least twelve months earlier for adults, with persistent intense yearning or preoccupation on most days, together with symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, difficulty re engaging, emotional numbness, a sense of meaninglessness or intense loneliness. Normal grief characteristically comes in waves that become less frequent and less intense with time, while prolonged grief remains constant and disabling. The major differential is a major depressive episode, in which low mood is pervasive rather than focused on the deceased and worthlessness and guilt are prominent, and the two can coexist. Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring goals and relationships, has the strongest evidence and outperforms both interpersonal psychotherapy and antidepressant treatment for the core symptoms.
key_points: The diagnosis requires at least twelve months since the death in adults.
Persistent daily yearning with identity disruption and avoidance defines the syndrome.
Normal grief comes in waves that attenuate; prolonged grief remains constant.
Depression is distinguished by pervasive low mood with worthlessness and guilt.
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for the core grief symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Risk factors that predict prolonged grief disorder are worth eliciting at the time of a death: an unexpected or violent death, the loss of a child or spouse, high dependency on the deceased, and a lack of social support, and their presence identifies who to review deliberately at six and twelve months.

subtopic_detail: older man with abrupt memory complaints who answers most cognitive questions by saying he does not know
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74-year-old retired accountant brought in by his son, who is worried about dementia. The son says his father's memory problems began quite suddenly about four months ago, within weeks of the death of a close friend, and have been at much the same level since.

The patient himself is the one complaining, telling you repeatedly and with distress that his mind has gone and that he is a burden. During cognitive testing he answers I do not know to most questions with little apparent effort, but when you encourage him and give extra time he recalls two of three words and correctly names the prime minister. His son reports he has stopped going to the golf club, wakes at 4 am, has lost 5 kg and has stopped reading the newspaper he read daily for fifty years. He has never got lost driving, manages his own medications correctly, and has had no falls, hallucinations or tremor. Thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, renal function, calcium and a full blood examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, normal gait, no focal neurological signs, no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Cognitive testing: Frequent do not know responses with minimal effort, improves with encouragement and extra time, recalls two of three words on delayed recall
data_table.Collateral: Abrupt onset four months ago after a bereavement, plateaued since, early morning waking, 5 kg weight loss, withdrawal from usual activities
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, renal function, corrected calcium and full blood examination within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for formal neuropsychological testing before starting any treatment for his low mood
options.rationale: Neuropsychological assessment is genuinely useful in ambiguous presentations and will be worth arranging if he does not improve. Performed during an untreated depressive episode it underestimates ability across every domain, so the result will be misleading. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer for dopamine transporter imaging with a detailed sleep history taken from his partner
options.rationale: This targets dementia with Lewy bodies, which requires fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment behaviour. He has none of those features and his examination is normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at an appropriate dose and repeat cognitive testing after twelve weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt dated onset after a loss, prominent self reported deficits, do not know answers that improve with encouragement, and biological depressive features point to the cognitive impairment of depression rather than a neurodegenerative process. Treating the depression and retesting once the mood is better is the diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Commence donepezil for probable Alzheimer disease and arrange memory clinic review in three months
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease has an insidious onset over months to years with the family rather than the patient raising the concern, and patients characteristically confabulate or minimise instead of saying they do not know. Starting a cholinesterase inhibitor now treats the wrong diagnosis and leaves the depression untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer to a cognitive disorders clinic urgently
options.rationale: Structural imaging is part of a full dementia workup and would be indicated if focal signs, an unusual age or a rapid decline were present. Referring before a trial of antidepressant treatment risks a diagnostic label being applied to a reversible state. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: The cognitive impairment of depression in older people, long described as pseudodementia, produces genuine deficits in attention, processing speed and effortful recall that resolve or substantially improve when the mood disorder is treated. Several features distinguish it from a neurodegenerative dementia: the onset is relatively abrupt and can often be dated, frequently to a loss or stressor, and it plateaus rather than progressing. The patient is usually the one complaining and tends to emphasise and even exaggerate the deficits, whereas in Alzheimer disease the family raises the concern and the patient minimises it. On testing, do not know answers given with little effort that improve with encouragement contrast with the confabulation and near misses of Alzheimer disease. An adequate antidepressant trial with cognitive reassessment afterwards is both treatment and test, but these patients carry a substantially elevated risk of developing a true dementia within the following few years, so follow up must continue rather than stop at recovery.
key_points: Abrupt datable onset that plateaus, often after a loss or stressor.
The patient complains and emphasises deficits while the family is less concerned.
Do not know answers improving with encouragement, rather than confabulation.
Practical function, orientation and medication management are preserved.
Treat the depression and retest; these patients still carry an elevated future dementia risk.
explanation.pearls: Around half of older people whose cognition improves with antidepressant treatment go on to develop a true dementia within five years, so recovery is a reason to schedule annual cognitive review rather than to discharge the patient from follow up.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

subtopic_detail: man weeping uncontrollably at trivial remarks after a stroke who denies feeling sad while it happens
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old man ten weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. His wife raises that he bursts into uncontrollable sobbing several times a day, often triggered by something trivial such as a television advertisement or being greeted at the door.

The episodes last a minute or two, stop as abruptly as they begin, and he is mortified by them. He tells you clearly that he does not feel sad while it is happening and that the crying seems to come from nowhere and bears no relation to how he feels. Between episodes he says his mood is reasonable, he looks forward to his grandchildren visiting, he is engaging well with rehabilitation and is pleased with his walking progress. He sleeps well, his appetite is good and his weight is stable. He has a residual mild right arm weakness and mild expressive dysphasia. He denies any suicidal thoughts, and a cognitive screen is unremarkable for his dysphasia.

data_table.Examination: Mild right arm weakness with mild expressive dysphasia, no pseudobulbar dysarthria or dysphagia
data_table.Episode description: Abrupt stereotyped crying lasting one to two minutes, trivially triggered, terminating abruptly, several times daily
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic between episodes, reactive affect, preserved anticipatory pleasure, no guilt or worthlessness
data_table.Biological features: Sleep, appetite and weight all stable, engaging actively with rehabilitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy focused on emotion regulation strategies after stroke
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is effective for post stroke depression and anxiety and remains useful adjunctive support for the distress the episodes cause. Emotionalism is a neurological release phenomenon rather than a disorder of emotion regulation, so therapy alone does not reduce episode frequency. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Reassure the couple that this settles spontaneously and review his progress in three months
options.rationale: Emotionalism does become less frequent over the first year in many patients, so the natural history offered is broadly accurate. Several distressing episodes a day at ten weeks cause real social withdrawal, and effective treatment is available now. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to a full antidepressant dose over six weeks
options.rationale: Full antidepressant dosing and a six week horizon are what post stroke depression requires, and that is the near pair here. Emotionalism responds at lower doses within days to a fortnight, so this over treats and delays the assessment of response. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and review him in two weeks
options.rationale: Stereotyped brief crying disproportionate to and dissociated from the underlying mood is post stroke emotionalism, and serotonergic antidepressants reduce episode frequency substantially. The response is typically evident within one to two weeks and at doses below those used for depression. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Arrange urgent repeat brain imaging to exclude a new infarct in the brainstem or the pons
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is warranted for new focal deficits or a change in conscious state, neither of which is present, and his examination is stable. Emotionalism after a supratentorial stroke is a recognised consequence rather than a sign of new infarction. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Post stroke emotionalism, also called emotional lability or pathological crying and laughing, affects roughly one in five stroke survivors in the first six months and arises from disruption of corticobulbar pathways that normally inhibit brainstem motor programs for crying and laughing. The defining feature is the mismatch between the display and the felt emotion: episodes are abrupt, stereotyped, brief, triggered by minimal or unrelated stimuli, and the patient reports little or no corresponding sadness. This dissociation is what distinguishes it from post stroke depression, in which crying accompanies genuinely low mood, and where anhedonia, hopelessness, sleep disturbance and appetite change are also present. The two conditions frequently coexist, so both must be assessed rather than assuming one excludes the other. Serotonergic antidepressants are effective and characteristically work faster and at lower doses than in depression, and the improvement is often striking within the first fortnight; explaining the mechanism to the patient and family also substantially reduces the embarrassment and the social withdrawal that accompany it.
key_points: Abrupt stereotyped crying dissociated from the felt emotion defines emotionalism.
Post stroke depression brings pervasive low mood with anhedonia and biological features.
The two conditions commonly coexist and both must be assessed.
Serotonergic antidepressants work at lower doses and faster than in depression.
Explanation to patient and family reduces embarrassment and social withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: The speed of response is itself diagnostic: emotionalism typically improves within three to fourteen days of starting a serotonergic antidepressant, so a patient still crying unchanged at four weeks should prompt reconsideration of post stroke depression rather than a dose increase.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: man in his late fifties with new disinhibition and loss of empathy referred as late onset bipolar disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 58-year-old builder referred by his general practitioner with a question of late onset bipolar disorder. Over the past two years his wife has watched him change from a considerate man into someone who makes crude remarks to strangers, laughed when their neighbour described her husband's cancer diagnosis, and was formally warned at work for walking off a job site mid shift.

He now eats several packets of biscuits daily, has gained 12 kg, and insists on the same lunch at the same cafe at the same time each day and becomes agitated if this is disrupted. His wife says he is not elated, does not need less sleep and talks no faster than usual. He is unbothered by any of it and says his wife worries too much. His father developed a similar change at 60 and died in a nursing home at 66. On testing he scores 27 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen with intact orientation and recall, but he names only five animals in a minute and continues an incorrect response pattern after being corrected.

data_table.Mental state: No elevated or expansive mood, no pressured speech, no reduced sleep need, marked lack of concern about his situation
data_table.Behavioural change: Disinhibition, loss of empathy, carbohydrate craving with 12 kg weight gain, rigid daily routines
data_table.Cognitive testing: Standardised screen 27 out of 30 with intact orientation and delayed recall, verbal fluency five animals in one minute, perseverative errors
data_table.Family history: Father with a similar behavioural change from age 60, died at 66

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for couples therapy addressing the relationship strain and review his progress in two months
options.rationale: Relationship intervention treats a psychosocial cause of behavioural change and carer strain is certainly present and worth supporting. Attributing an organic frontal syndrome to relationship difficulty places the responsibility on a man who cannot modify his behaviour. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate as a mood stabiliser and arrange psychiatric review in four weeks
options.rationale: Mood stabilisation treats the mania that this presentation superficially resembles, which is why the referral was framed that way. Mania requires elevated or irritable mood with reduced sleep need and pressured speech, and the two year progressive course without any mood elevation excludes it. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging and refer for formal neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, hyperorality and compulsive routines with preserved memory and orientation but impaired verbal fluency and perseveration is behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia. Imaging for frontal and anterior temporal atrophy plus neuropsychology is the diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Request thyroid function with syphilis serology and a urine drug screen before any referral
options.rationale: Reversible causes deserve exclusion in any new neuropsychiatric presentation and these tests are part of a standard workup. They do not account for a two year progressive frontal syndrome with a matching family history, and relying on them alone delays the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence donepezil for a neurodegenerative process and arrange memory clinic review in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are for Alzheimer disease, the near pair, which presents with early episodic memory loss and preserved social conduct rather than the reverse pattern seen here. In frontotemporal dementia they are ineffective and can worsen behavioural symptoms. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest cause of dementia under the age of sixty alongside Alzheimer disease and is routinely misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder for two to three years before the correct diagnosis is reached. The diagnostic criteria require three of six features: early behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality and dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. The pattern of preserved orientation and recall alongside markedly reduced verbal fluency and perseveration is characteristic and is what a bedside screen such as a standardised cognitive test will miss, since those instruments are weighted towards memory. A family history is present in up to 40 per cent, with mutations in the C9orf72, MAPT and GRN genes accounting for most inherited cases. There is no disease modifying treatment, so the value of early diagnosis lies in behavioural management, carer support, decisions about work and driving, and access to younger onset dementia services and financial planning.
key_points: Personality and conduct change with preserved memory is the reverse of Alzheimer disease.
Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality and dysexecutive testing.
Standard cognitive screens are insensitive because they weight memory and orientation.
A family history is present in up to 40 per cent of cases.
Cholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective and may worsen behaviour in this condition.
explanation.pearls: Verbal fluency is the single most useful bedside test when frontotemporal dementia is suspected: naming fewer than eleven animals in a minute is abnormal, and the discrepancy between a near normal memory score and a poor fluency score is what separates it from Alzheimer disease at first assessment.

subtopic_detail: older woman who became confused and unsteady three weeks after her antidepressant was started
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79-year-old woman at home by her son. Three weeks ago you started her on sertraline for a depressive episode and she had begun to sleep and eat a little better. Over the past four days she has become vague and muddled, has been unsteady on her feet with two near falls, and vomited twice yesterday.

She has hypertension treated with indapamide, which she has taken for six years, and no other medical history. She has not had diarrhoea, fever, cough or dysuria, and there has been no change to her fluid intake. On examination she is drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop in blood pressure, jugular venous pressure not elevated and no peripheral oedema. Chest is clear and the abdomen is soft. Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Thyroid function and a morning cortisol are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L
data_table.Additional: Thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits, medications sertraline for three weeks and indapamide for six years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the sertraline, arrange hospital admission and commence careful fluid restriction
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the sertraline started three weeks ago is the new variable. Withdrawal of the drug with fluid restriction under inpatient monitoring is the correct combination at this sodium and conscious level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the indapamide, arrange hospital admission and commence intravenous normal saline
options.rationale: Thiazide and thiazide like diuretics are a leading cause of hyponatraemia in older people and indapamide should certainly also be stopped, so half of this is right. It has been taken unchanged for six years while the sertraline is new, and saline in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis can lower the sodium further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange admission for computed tomography of the brain and an intravenous fluid challenge
options.rationale: A fluid challenge is the right test when hypovolaemia is the suspected mechanism, but she has moist membranes, no postural drop and a urine sodium of 52 mmol/L, all of which indicate euvolaemia. Imaging investigates a structural cause for confusion that her electrolytes already explain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch her to mirtazapine at an equivalent dose and repeat the electrolytes in one week
options.rationale: Mirtazapine carries a lower risk of hyponatraemia and is a sensible choice when her depression is retreated later, so the drug selection itself is defensible. Substituting one antidepressant for another without treating a sodium of 118 mmol/L leaves the acute danger unaddressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue current medications, restrict fluids to one litre daily and repeat electrolytes in two days
options.rationale: Outpatient fluid restriction with repeat testing is reasonable for mild asymptomatic hyponatraemia in a well patient. A sodium of 118 mmol/L with drowsiness, disorientation and vomiting is severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and carries a risk of seizure and cerebral oedema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Antidepressant associated hyponatraemia through the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis is a common and under recognised adverse effect, with the highest risk in the first two to four weeks of treatment and in people over 65, of low body weight, or taking diuretics. All selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors carry the risk and venlafaxine and mirtazapine carry it to a lesser degree. The biochemical diagnosis requires hypotonic hyponatraemia with a serum osmolality below 275 mmol/kg, an inappropriately concentrated urine above 100 mmol/kg, a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, clinical euvolaemia, and the exclusion of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Severity is driven by symptoms and by rate of fall rather than by the absolute number, and drowsiness, vomiting and confusion at 118 mmol/L constitute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring inpatient management. The correction rate must not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because of the risk of osmotic demyelination, and a baseline sodium should be checked before starting an antidepressant in an older person and repeated at two weeks.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first two to four weeks and in older, lighter, diuretic treated patients.
Diagnosis requires hypotonic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before attributing it to the drug.
Saline can worsen the sodium in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis.
Do not correct faster than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours because of osmotic demyelination risk.
explanation.pearls: Check a baseline sodium before starting an antidepressant in anyone over 65 and repeat it at two weeks, because the median time to symptomatic hyponatraemia is around 13 days and the presentation is usually non specific confusion or a fall rather than anything that points to the electrolyte.

subtopic_detail: first line pharmacotherapy for cyclical mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase on prospective ratings
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who has kept a daily symptom diary for the past two menstrual cycles at your request. She reports two years of irritability, low mood, tearfulness and a sense of being out of control, together with breast tenderness and bloating.

Her diary shows that the symptoms start about six days before each period, build until bleeding begins, and settle within two to three days of the onset of bleeding. Between the end of one episode and the start of the next she rates herself as entirely well and functioning normally at work. She has twice had to leave work early during the worst days and her partner says the arguments are now affecting their relationship. She takes no regular medication and uses condoms for contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination unremarkable at today's visit which falls in the follicular phase, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, haemoglobin within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, prospective daily ratings across two cycles confirm a symptom free interval of about two weeks in each cycle

lead_in: What would you first recommend as pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral pyridoxine at high dose with evening primrose oil daily
options.rationale: Pyridoxine has modest evidence for physical premenstrual symptoms at low dose but not for the mood syndrome, and doses above 100 mg daily carry a risk of peripheral sensory neuropathy with prolonged use. Evening primrose oil has not been shown to help. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill with a 24 day active regimen
options.rationale: A drospirenone containing pill with a shortened hormone free interval is an effective second line option and is a reasonable choice for a woman who also wants contraception. It has a lower response rate than the serotonergic option and is not the first recommendation when contraception is not being sought. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Cyclical oral micronised progesterone in the second half of the cycle
options.rationale: Luteal phase progesterone has been studied repeatedly for this indication and performs no better than placebo. In some women it reproduces the very symptoms it is intended to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sertraline taken either continuously or in the luteal phase only
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are the established first line treatment for this condition and are distinctive in that they work within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is what makes luteal phase only dosing a viable regimen. Roughly six in ten women respond. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Low dose lithium carbonate with monitoring of the serum level
options.rationale: The cyclical pattern superficially resembles a rapid cycling mood disorder, which is why a mood stabiliser can seem logical, but her mood returns fully to baseline for two weeks of every cycle and is tied to the menstrual cycle rather than running autonomously. Lithium has no established role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from ordinary premenstrual symptoms by the severity of the mood disturbance and by demonstrable impairment of work, study or relationships, and it is separated from an underlying mood or anxiety disorder by the presence of a genuinely symptom free interval in the follicular phase. Because retrospective recall is unreliable and over attributes symptoms to the cycle, the diagnosis formally requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles, which is both a diagnostic step and a therapeutic one since many women find the pattern itself clarifying. The underlying mechanism is an abnormal central response to normal cyclical fluctuations in ovarian steroids and their neuroactive metabolites rather than any abnormality of hormone levels, which is why measuring hormones is unhelpful. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and their rapid onset in this condition, quite unlike their three to four week latency in depression, permits continuous, luteal phase or symptom onset dosing. Second line options include a drospirenone containing combined oral contraceptive with a shortened hormone free interval, and ovarian suppression is reserved for severe refractory cases.
key_points: A symptom free follicular interval separates this from an underlying mood disorder
Prospective daily ratings over two cycles are required for diagnosis
Hormone levels are normal and measuring them does not help
Serotonergic antidepressants act within days here, allowing luteal phase dosing
Luteal phase progesterone performs no better than placebo
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants relieve premenstrual dysphoric disorder within 24 to 48 hours rather than the three to four weeks required in major depression, which is why dosing restricted to the 14 days before menstruation works and halves total drug exposure.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: targeting the household environment to reduce relapse risk after a first episode of psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an early psychosis service reviewing a 19 year old man six weeks after his first admission. He presented with four months of persecutory beliefs about his neighbours and has responded well to risperidone, with his beliefs now held without conviction and his sleep and appetite restored.

He has moved back in with his parents. In the family meeting his father describes him as lazy and says he could snap out of it if he made an effort, and his mother becomes tearful and says she checks on him several times each night. They argue about his medication most days. Both parents say they are frightened and want to know what they can do. He is taking his medication reliably and is not using substances.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows settled affect, no current perceptual disturbance, residual persecutory ideas held without conviction, insight partially retained, no thoughts of self harm
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on two occasions, adherence confirmed by dose administration aid counts, metabolic screen within normal limits at baseline

lead_in: Which intervention is most likely to reduce his risk of relapse over the next year?

options.text: Referral to a supported employment program with an individual placement
options.rationale: Individual placement and support improves vocational outcomes and is an important part of early psychosis care, but its demonstrated effect is on employment rather than on relapse. It sits alongside rather than ahead of the family work. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: An increase in the risperidone dose with review in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: He has already responded well at the current dose and is taking it reliably, so there is no pharmacological failure to correct. Raising the dose adds metabolic and extrapyramidal burden, which is itself a common reason young people stop medication and relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Addition of an antidepressant to target his negative symptoms and low mood
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a limited and inconsistent effect on negative symptoms, and no depressive syndrome has been described here. Adding a second psychotropic without a clear indication complicates the regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Referral of the patient alone for individual cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Individual cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis is recommended and helps residual symptoms and distress, so this is a genuine component of good care rather than a wrong treatment. It does not address the household environment, which is the specific modifiable factor operating here. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: A structured family intervention with psychoeducation and communication skills
options.rationale: Households with high levels of criticism, hostility or emotional overinvolvement carry a substantially higher relapse rate, and the pattern described in this meeting fits both the critical and the overinvolved forms. Structured family work delivered over several months reduces relapse and readmission by roughly half, an effect size comparable to maintenance medication. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Expressed emotion describes the level of criticism, hostility and emotional overinvolvement directed toward a family member with a psychotic illness, and it is one of the most consistently replicated predictors of relapse, with relapse rates in high expressed emotion households roughly double those in low expressed emotion households over the year following discharge. The concept is not about blame: families arrive at these patterns through fear and exhaustion, and attributions such as laziness usually reflect a lack of information about negative symptoms rather than indifference. Structured family intervention combines psychoeducation about the illness and its treatment, communication skills training, structured problem solving and crisis planning, delivered over at least six months and generally around ten or more sessions. Meta analyses show reductions in relapse and readmission of about half, which places it among the most effective single interventions available in early psychosis and is why it is recommended for every family in contact with a first episode service. It works alongside maintenance antipsychotic medication, individual psychological therapy and vocational support rather than replacing any of them.
key_points: High expressed emotion roughly doubles relapse rates over the first year
Criticism, hostility and emotional overinvolvement are the three components
Attributions such as laziness usually reflect misunderstanding of negative symptoms
Structured family intervention runs over at least six months and around ten sessions
Relapse and readmission fall by approximately half
explanation.pearls: Ask a carer what they think causes the person's inactivity: an answer framed as a character flaw rather than an illness feature identifies high expressed emotion at the bedside and predicts relapse more reliably than any symptom rating scale.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Orygen Youth Health Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: recording treatment preferences while a person retains capacity for use during future episodes of illness
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman on the ward. She has bipolar affective disorder and has had three admissions with mania over eight years, on each occasion declining lithium while unwell and accepting it again once she recovered.

She came in voluntarily ten days ago with early elevation of mood, which has now settled. She is sleeping normally, her speech is unpressured and she describes her mood as back to her usual self. She tells you she hates that decisions get made for her when she is unwell and asks how she can have a say in her own treatment next time. She understands her diagnosis, can describe what happens when she becomes unwell, and weighs up the options you discuss with her.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows euthymic mood, normal rate and form of speech, no grandiosity, no perceptual disturbance, insight intact, decision making capacity retained on assessment
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium level within the therapeutic range, thyroid function within normal limits, renal function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Support her to complete an advance statement of her treatment preferences
options.rationale: An advance statement is made while a person has capacity and records the treatment they would want, and would not want, if they later become unwell and lose it. Australian mental health legislation requires treating teams to consider such a statement and to give written reasons when they depart from it, so completing it now is the action that gives her genuine influence over future episodes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Apply now for a community treatment order to cover any future episode
options.rationale: A compulsory order can only be made when the statutory criteria are met at the time, which requires a current mental illness with the person unable to consent and a risk that cannot be addressed less restrictively. She is well and consenting, and a pre-emptive order is not lawful. (Source: Mental Health Act frameworks for Australian states and territories)
source_refs: Mental Health Act frameworks for Australian states and territories

options.text: Apply to the tribunal for a guardian to be appointed to make decisions
options.rationale: Guardianship transfers decision making away from the person and is reserved for those with enduring incapacity, usually from cognitive impairment or disability. Her incapacity is episodic and she currently has capacity, so this is a disproportionate response that achieves the opposite of what she is asking for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Record her wishes in the file and review them at her next admission
options.rationale: A file note carries no standing under mental health legislation and may not be found by a team meeting her in an emergency. The statutory instrument exists precisely so that her wishes carry weight rather than depending on whether someone reads the notes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Ask her family to make future treatment decisions on her behalf
options.rationale: Nominating a support person is a legitimate and valuable part of this planning, but a nominated person supports the individual to express their own will and preferences rather than substituting their judgement. Handing the decision to family bypasses her stated wishes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Australian mental health legislation has moved from a substitute decision making model toward supported decision making, reflecting obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The practical instruments that express this are the advance statement of preferences, made while the person has capacity and setting out the treatment they would and would not want in a future episode, and the nominated support person, who is appointed to help the person express their own will and preferences rather than to decide on their behalf. Treating teams must consider an advance statement and, in most jurisdictions, must record written reasons if compulsory treatment departs from it, which means the document shapes clinical decisions even though it does not bind them absolutely. The clinical value extends beyond the legal effect: the conversation itself identifies which aspects of previous admissions the person found most distressing, such as seclusion, a particular medication or the involvement of police, and often surfaces workable alternatives. Recovery oriented practice treats episodes of incapacity as interruptions in an ongoing relationship with an autonomous person rather than as a licence to disregard their preferences.
key_points: Advance statements are made while capacity is retained for use during later incapacity
Teams must consider the statement and usually give written reasons for departing from it
A nominated support person assists expression of the person's own preferences
Compulsory orders require the statutory criteria to be met at the time, not in advance
The planning conversation surfaces workable alternatives to distressing past interventions
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically which part of a previous admission the person found most distressing and what helped: answers such as a preference for olanzapine over haloperidol, or for a particular relative to be called before police, are exactly what an advance statement can make binding on the team's reasoning.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Mental Health Act frameworks for Australian states and territories

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for repetitive hair pulling presenting as patchy scalp hair loss
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 16 year old girl referred by a dermatologist. Her parents brought her to the dermatologist three months ago because of patchy hair loss on her scalp and were told it was probably an autoimmune condition.

The dermatologist found broken hairs of many different lengths within the patches, no scaling and no smooth complete bald areas, with normal skin throughout, and a fungal scraping was negative. Seen alone, she tells you she pulls hairs out one at a time while studying and while watching television, often without noticing at first. She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, says she has tried many times to stop, and is embarrassed about how her hair looks at school.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches of hair loss over the right parietal scalp containing broken hairs of varying lengths, no scaling, no erythema, no exclamation mark hairs, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no other skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Fungal scraping negative, full blood count within normal limits, iron studies within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at an antidepressant dose
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder itself but trials in hair pulling have been largely negative, which is one of the features that separates this condition from obsessive compulsive disorder despite their grouping together. It may still be used where a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Habit reversal training delivered by a trained psychologist
options.rationale: Behavioural treatment combining awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control has the strongest evidence for this condition and is recommended ahead of medication. Awareness training matters particularly here because much of her pulling is automatic and outside her attention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Oral N acetylcysteine at high dose with review in three months
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine has some supportive trial evidence in adults and is reasonably well tolerated, which makes it a recognised second line option. The evidence in adolescents is weaker and it is not used ahead of the behavioural treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Potent topical corticosteroid applied to the affected scalp areas
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats alopecia areata, which is the diagnosis she was originally given, and the two are separated by the examination findings. Areata produces smooth complete bald patches with tapered exclamation mark hairs, whereas broken hairs of differing lengths within an irregular patch indicate mechanical extraction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Low dose olanzapine with monitoring of weight and metabolic profile
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has been trialled in refractory cases but carries substantial metabolic risk in an adolescent. It is not a first line treatment for a condition with an effective and well tolerated behavioural option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified among the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and is defined by recurrent pulling of one's own hair resulting in hair loss, with repeated attempts to stop and associated distress or impairment. Onset is typically in early adolescence and it is considerably more common in females presenting to clinics. Pulling occurs in two modes that often coexist: a focused mode preceded by mounting tension and followed by relief or gratification, and an automatic mode occurring outside awareness during sedentary activities such as reading or screen time, which is why awareness training is a necessary first component of treatment. The distinction from alopecia areata rests on the appearance of the patches, since mechanical pulling leaves hairs broken at varying lengths within an irregularly shaped area of otherwise normal scalp, whereas areata produces smooth complete loss with tapered exclamation mark hairs. Trichophagia should be asked about directly because swallowed hair can form a gastric trichobezoar with a tail extending into the small bowel, a rare but surgically important complication.
key_points: Broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular patch indicate pulling, not alopecia areata
Pulling occurs in both focused and automatic modes, often in the same person
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Serotonergic antidepressants have largely negative trial evidence for this condition
Ask directly about swallowing hair because of the risk of a gastric trichobezoar
explanation.pearls: Always ask whether the person swallows the hair they pull, because a trichobezoar with a tail extending through the pylorus into the jejunum presents with vomiting and weight loss and requires surgical removal rather than any psychiatric treatment.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: sequencing specialist referral and concurrent mood treatment for a young person seeking gender related care
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17 year old patient who was assigned female at birth, identifies as male and uses he and him. He has lived as male at school and at home for two years with his family's support and has not previously been referred to any specialist service.

He describes five months of low mood, loss of interest in soccer which he used to play weekly, and broken sleep. He links the distress to chest development and to being repeatedly misnamed by a group at school. He has no plan or intent to harm himself and has never self harmed. He is attending school, has close friends, and is not using alcohol or other drugs. He asks you what medical options exist and says he wants to know what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows reactive but low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, iron studies within normal limits, no current medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence testosterone therapy in the general practice at today's visit
options.rationale: Gender affirming hormone therapy in a person under 18 follows assessment by an experienced multidisciplinary team, with consideration of fertility preservation and the relevant consent framework. Initiating it at a first general practice visit bypasses each of those steps. (Source: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health)
source_refs: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health

options.text: Treat the depression first and defer the gender discussion until it lifts
options.rationale: Sequencing care this way is intuitive because clinicians reasonably want a clear assessment, but the distress here is substantially driven by the very issues being deferred, so the depression is unlikely to lift while they remain unaddressed. Deferral is itself experienced as a barrier and is associated with disengagement from care. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary gender service and treat the low mood now
options.rationale: Assessment for gender related medical care in a person under 18 is undertaken by a multidisciplinary service, and referral should not wait for mental health difficulties to resolve because the distress is closely tied to the unresolved gender related concerns and to the bullying. Treating the depressive symptoms concurrently with psychological therapy and school advocacy addresses both strands at once. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

options.text: Advise that no step can be considered until he turns eighteen years old
options.rationale: Australian practice provides for assessment and, where appropriate, treatment of people under 18 through specialist services, and turning 18 is not a legal or clinical threshold for beginning assessment. A blanket deferral leaves the current distress untreated. (Source: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health)
source_refs: Australian Professional Association for Trans Health

options.text: Refer for therapy aimed at exploring whether this identity will persist
options.rationale: Therapy directed at changing or discouraging a person's gender identity is ineffective, is associated with worse mental health outcomes, and is prohibited by legislation in several Australian jurisdictions. Exploratory psychological support is part of specialist assessment, but it is not framed as testing whether the identity is genuine. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Trans and gender diverse young people have substantially higher rates of depression, anxiety, self harm and suicidal ideation than their peers, and the evidence indicates that this excess is driven predominantly by external factors including bullying, family rejection, misgendering and barriers to care rather than by gender identity itself. Family support and the ability to use one's name and pronouns are among the strongest protective factors identified. The Australian standards of care set out a multidisciplinary model in which assessment covers gender identity and its development, mental health, family and social circumstances, and fertility considerations, and in which psychological support, social affirmation, medical options and advocacy in school settings all sit within the same plan. Mental health treatment proceeds in parallel rather than as a prerequisite, because delaying access while waiting for symptoms to remit both prolongs distress and is associated with disengagement. Practices aimed at changing or suppressing gender identity are ineffective, are linked to worse outcomes and are unlawful in several Australian jurisdictions.
key_points: Excess mental illness in this group is driven largely by external stressors, not identity
Family support and correct name and pronoun use are strong protective factors
Assessment for those under 18 is multidisciplinary and includes fertility discussion
Treat mental health concerns in parallel rather than as a prerequisite to referral
Practices aimed at changing gender identity are ineffective and unlawful in several jurisdictions
explanation.pearls: Consistent use of a young person's chosen name across home, school and health settings is associated with a substantial reduction in depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation, which makes documenting the name and pronouns in the medical record a clinical intervention rather than an administrative one.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents
Australian Professional Association for Trans Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: managing an elevated mood syndrome emerging on high dose corticosteroid when the steroid must continue
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 58 year old man on the respiratory ward. He was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily eleven days ago for a severe exacerbation of an inflammatory lung condition and the respiratory team say he needs to remain on a substantial dose for now.

Over the past four days the nursing staff report he has slept about two hours a night, has been talking rapidly and constantly to other patients, and yesterday telephoned a real estate agent about buying an investment property he cannot afford. He tells you he has never felt sharper and that he has worked out how to fix the hospital's discharge system. He has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness and his urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Elevated and expansive mood, pressured speech with flight of ideas, grandiose plans without fixed delusional conviction, no perceptual disturbance, orientated to time place and person, attention intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, sodium within normal limits, glucose 11.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), C reactive protein falling, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in a week
options.rationale: Corticosteroids can produce depressive as well as elevated states, and an antidepressant would be considered for the former. Giving one during an elevated episode risks worsening it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the corticosteroid abruptly today and observe him on the ward
options.rationale: Stopping abruptly after eleven days of high dose therapy risks adrenal insufficiency and would allow the lung disease to flare, which is a worse outcome than the psychiatric syndrome being treated. Corticosteroids are reduced in a planned way, not stopped outright. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate with monitoring of the serum lithium level
options.rationale: Lithium has been used prophylactically in patients requiring repeated corticosteroid courses, which gives this option some basis, but it has a slow onset, a narrow therapeutic index and requires stable fluid balance and renal function in an acutely unwell inpatient. It is not the treatment for an episode that is already established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss dose reduction with the treating team and commence olanzapine
options.rationale: The disturbance is dose related, so reducing the corticosteroid to the lowest dose that controls the lung disease is the definitive step and must be negotiated with the treating team rather than decided unilaterally. An antipsychotic provides symptom control in the interim, and olanzapine has the best evidence in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose unchanged and review him again in one week
options.rationale: He is making financial commitments he cannot meet and has had four nights of severe sleep disruption, which represents active risk rather than a syndrome that can be observed. Waiting a week allows further irreversible decisions. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is strongly dose dependent, with risk rising sharply above the equivalent of about 40 mg of prednisolone daily and reaching close to one in five patients at doses above 80 mg. Onset is usually within the first two weeks of starting or increasing the dose. The presentation is more often elevated or mixed than depressive in the acute phase, while depressive syndromes are more characteristic of long term therapy and of the withdrawal period, and a hypoactive delirium can also occur, particularly in older patients. Importantly, a personal or family history of psychiatric illness is not a reliable predictor, so the absence of one offers no reassurance, whereas a previous episode on corticosteroid strongly predicts recurrence. Management prioritises reducing the dose to the minimum required for the underlying disease, which usually resolves the syndrome within days to weeks, with an antipsychotic used for symptom control in the interim and abrupt cessation avoided because of adrenal suppression.
key_points: Risk rises steeply above about 40 mg prednisolone equivalent daily
Onset is typically within the first two weeks of starting or increasing the dose
Elevated and mixed states predominate acutely, depression with chronic use and withdrawal
A negative psychiatric history does not predict who will be affected
Reduce the dose in negotiation with the treating team and never stop abruptly
explanation.pearls: A previous corticosteroid induced psychiatric episode is the single strongest predictor of another, so document it prominently and consider prophylactic olanzapine or lithium cover if a future high dose course above 40 mg prednisolone equivalent becomes necessary.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: distinguishing refreshing hypersomnolence with muscle tone loss from depressive hypersomnia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 22 year old university student referred with treatment resistant depression. He has had eighteen months of overwhelming daytime sleepiness, falling asleep in lectures, on the bus and once in the middle of a conversation with a friend.

He has completed adequate trials of two different antidepressants at therapeutic doses, and says that his mood lifted a little on the second but that the sleepiness was entirely unchanged. He sleeps eight to nine hours at night, wakes feeling refreshed, and says a fifteen minute nap leaves him clear headed for a couple of hours. He still enjoys music and seeing friends when he is awake enough. When you ask about his laughter, he describes his knees buckling and his jaw going slack for a few seconds when something strikes him as very funny.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, no retrognathia, Mallampati class 1, mental state examination shows mildly low but reactive mood with preserved interest and no anhedonia, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24, thyroid function within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, no snoring or witnessed apnoeas reported by his housemate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry and review the tracing in the clinic
options.rationale: Oximetry screens for obstructive sleep apnoea, the other major cause of excessive daytime sleepiness, and would be sensible if his history suggested it. He has a normal body mass index, no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and describes naps as refreshing, whereas sleepiness from apnoea is characteristically unrefreshed. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Trial of a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
options.rationale: Two adequate trials have already left the sleepiness untouched, and the features that would support a depressive hypersomnia are absent since he retains interest and wakes refreshed. A third trial repeats a strategy that has already failed for the dominant symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Measure thyroid function with iron studies and vitamin B12 levels
options.rationale: Screening for metabolic and haematological causes of fatigue is a reasonable general step and thyroid function and ferritin have already returned within normal limits. None of these tests explains the episodes of emotionally triggered weakness, which is the discriminating feature. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast within a month
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when a secondary cause is suspected, such as a hypothalamic or pineal region lesion, signalled by focal neurological signs, headache, visual change or endocrine disturbance. He has none of these and the yield in a typical presentation is very low. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, together with refreshing naps and preserved interest, points to a primary disorder of sleep and wake regulation rather than to depression. Overnight study followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test is the diagnostic standard, demonstrating a short mean sleep latency with early entry into rapid eye movement sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 arises from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, most likely through an autoimmune mechanism, and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, yet diagnostic delay commonly exceeds a decade and misdiagnosis as depression is among the commonest reasons, because both present with a young person who is sleepy, withdrawn and underperforming. Cataplexy is the near specific feature and consists of brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved, and it must be asked about directly because patients rarely volunteer it and often describe it only as weakness or as knees giving way. The remaining features are sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep. The discriminator against depressive hypersomnia is the quality of sleep and naps: in narcolepsy naps are brief and genuinely restorative and night sleep is not extended, whereas depressive hypersomnia produces long unrefreshing sleep, difficulty getting out of bed and naps that leave the person no better. Diagnosis rests on overnight polysomnography excluding other causes followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief emotion triggered bilateral tone loss with preserved consciousness
Patients rarely volunteer cataplexy, so ask directly about weakness when laughing
Refreshing brief naps distinguish narcolepsy from depressive hypersomnia
Antidepressant trials leave the sleepiness unchanged
Polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test is the diagnostic standard
explanation.pearls: Ask every sleepy young patient what happens to their body when they laugh hard: a description of jaw slackening, head nodding or knees buckling for a few seconds with full awareness is cataplexy and shifts the diagnosis from depression to narcolepsy in a single question.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: recognising drug induced inner restlessness that has been misread as worsening agitation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the ward about a 46 year old man with schizophrenia whose antipsychotic was changed to aripiprazole three weeks ago. The nursing staff have documented increasing agitation and have given two doses of an oral as needed antipsychotic over the past two days, after each of which they record that he became more unsettled rather than less.

He tells you that he cannot describe it properly but that he feels a dreadful restlessness inside, that he cannot stay in a chair and has to keep moving, and that it is there from the moment he wakes until he falls asleep. He paces the corridor and rocks from foot to foot while standing talking to you. He says his psychotic symptoms have actually improved and denies feeling frightened or angry with anyone.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Constant shifting of weight while standing, inability to remain seated for more than a minute, no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no orofacial dyskinesia, mental state examination shows settled thought content with improved delusional conviction
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30 to 300), full blood count within normal limits, creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the antipsychotic dose and commence propranolol for the symptom
options.rationale: Subjective inner restlessness with observable motor restlessness beginning within weeks of an antipsychotic change is drug induced akathisia, and dose reduction addresses the cause while a lipophilic beta blocker is the best supported symptomatic treatment. Recognising it matters because akathisia is associated with increased suicide risk and with treatment discontinuation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the antipsychotic dose to settle what appears to be agitation
options.rationale: This is the error the ward has already made twice, and the record that he worsened after each as needed dose is the clue. Treating akathisia as psychotic agitation escalates the very drug causing it and produces a cycle of increasing dose and increasing distress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence benzatropine and review the response over the next few days
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents are effective for drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but perform poorly for akathisia, which is the extrapyramidal syndrome they do not treat. He has neither tremor nor cogwheel rigidity to suggest parkinsonism. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a dopamine agonist taken in the evening before he goes to bed
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists treat restless legs syndrome, in which the urge is localised to the legs, is worst in the evening and at rest, and is relieved by movement. His restlessness is generalised and constant throughout the day, his ferritin is not low, and a dopamine agonist risks aggravating psychosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement and recheck the ferritin in three months
options.rationale: Iron deficiency drives restless legs syndrome and replacement is indicated when ferritin falls below about 75 micrograms/L. His ferritin is well above that threshold, so there is no deficiency to correct. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness accompanied by an inability to remain still, and it is among the most distressing adverse effects of antipsychotic medication. It is most common in the first weeks after starting or increasing a drug, and aripiprazole is notable for causing it despite otherwise favourable extrapyramidal tolerability. The central clinical danger is misattribution: the outward picture of a pacing, unsettled patient is easily recorded as agitation or as worsening psychosis, which leads to dose escalation or additional as needed antipsychotic and a worsening cycle, and a documented deterioration after each as needed dose is the pattern that should prompt reconsideration. Restless legs syndrome is the main differential and is separated by the localisation of the urge to the legs, the circadian worsening in the evening and at rest, relief with movement, and an association with low ferritin. Management is reduction of the causative dose or a switch to an agent with lower liability, with propranolol as the best supported symptomatic treatment and benzodiazepines or mirtazapine as alternatives, while anticholinergics are ineffective.
key_points: Akathisia combines subjective inner restlessness with observable motor restlessness
It appears within weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic
Misreading it as agitation leads to dose escalation and a worsening cycle
Anticholinergics treat parkinsonism and dystonia but not akathisia
Restless legs is localised to the legs, worse at rest in the evening, and linked to low ferritin
explanation.pearls: A patient who becomes more unsettled after each as needed dose of antipsychotic has akathisia rather than agitation, and propranolol 10 to 20 mg three times daily alongside dose reduction is the response, not another dose of the drug causing it.

subtopic_detail: acting on a markedly prolonged QT interval with correctable electrolyte abnormalities and additive drug effects
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 52 year old woman with schizoaffective disorder. She has been taking citalopram 40 mg daily and haloperidol, and over the past week she has had repeated vomiting attributed to a gastrointestinal illness and has eaten very little.

This morning she felt light headed on standing and the nursing staff obtained an electrocardiogram. She has no chest pain and no palpitations, has never had a syncopal episode, and has no known cardiac disease. A previous electrocardiogram taken on admission six weeks ago was reported as normal. Her results are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no murmur, heart sounds dual, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.05), corrected calcium within normal limits, creatinine mildly raised, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia at 58 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 510 milliseconds, no ischaemic changes, compared with 430 milliseconds six weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue both medications and repeat the electrocardiogram in a week
options.rationale: An interval above 500 milliseconds with ongoing electrolyte depletion and bradycardia represents a present risk of a malignant arrhythmia rather than a trend to observe. A week of unchanged treatment leaves every contributing factor in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Replace potassium and magnesium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are the fastest reversible contributors to the prolonged interval and both must be corrected promptly, with magnesium replaced even when the level is only modestly low because it stabilises the myocardium. Continuous monitoring is required at this interval because the risk of torsades de pointes rises steeply beyond 500 milliseconds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic alone and continue the antidepressant unchanged
options.rationale: Both drugs prolong the interval and their effects are additive, and citalopram is specifically dose dependent in this respect with 40 mg exceeding the maximum recommended dose for patients over 60 and carrying a regulatory warning at any age. Stopping only one leaves a substantial pharmacological contribution untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium only if torsades de pointes actually occurs
options.rationale: Magnesium is certainly the treatment once the arrhythmia has begun, which is why this option feels familiar, but withholding it until then forgoes the opportunity to prevent an event that can be fatal on first occurrence. Prophylactic correction of a documented deficiency is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
