options.text: Switch immediately to a different antipsychotic at an equivalent dose
options.rationale: A switch to a lower risk agent will form part of the plan, but choosing and titrating a new antipsychotic is a decision for the coming days rather than the immediate response. It does nothing about the electrolytes or the bradycardia, which are the acute drivers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Drug induced QT prolongation results from blockade of the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, and risk accumulates additively across contributing factors rather than resting on any single one. The relevant factors here are two QT prolonging drugs taken together, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and female sex, which independently confers a longer baseline interval. Absolute thresholds matter for action: an interval above 500 milliseconds, or an increase of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, marks a substantially increased risk of torsades de pointes, and this patient meets both criteria. Citalopram carries a specific dose dependent warning, with maximum recommended doses of 40 mg in adults and 20 mg in those over 60 or with hepatic impairment. Immediate management corrects the reversible physiological contributors, which means replacing potassium to the upper half of the reference range and giving magnesium even when only mildly low, with continuous monitoring, while rationalisation of the psychotropic regimen follows once the acute risk is controlled.
key_points: Risk accumulates additively across drugs, electrolytes, bradycardia and sex
An interval above 500 milliseconds or a rise above 60 milliseconds from baseline is the action threshold
Replace magnesium even when only mildly low because it stabilises the myocardium
Citalopram prolongs the interval in a dose dependent way with a specific maximum dose warning
Correct the reversible physiology first, then rationalise the psychotropic regimen
explanation.pearls: Replace potassium to the upper half of the reference range rather than merely into it when the corrected QT exceeds 500 milliseconds, and give magnesium regardless of a borderline level, because serum magnesium correlates poorly with total body stores.

subtopic_detail: involuntary movements and a suggestive family history in apparent treatment resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 41 year old man referred with eighteen months of low mood, irritability and loss of interest that has not responded to adequate trials of two antidepressants. He works as an accountant and has been placed on a performance review at work.

His wife says the bigger change is that he has become blunt to the point of rudeness with her family, has spent several thousand dollars on impulse purchases, and no longer initiates anything at home. She also mentions that he fidgets constantly, drops cups and cutlery, and that his walking has become unsteady in a way he does not seem to notice. He has never been prescribed an antipsychotic or any dopamine blocking medication. His mother died at 55 in a psychiatric hospital with what the family were told was early dementia.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Brief irregular involuntary movements of the fingers and face incorporated into voluntary gestures, motor impersistence with inability to maintain tongue protrusion for ten seconds, slowed initiation of horizontal saccades, wide based unsteady gait, no cogwheel rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, vitamin B12 within normal limits, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, full blood count within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial a third antidepressant from a different class for three months
options.rationale: Two adequate trials have failed and the presentation includes a progressive movement disorder and executive change that no antidepressant explains. Further sequential trials are the mechanism by which this diagnosis is typically delayed for years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Send the huntingtin gene test from the clinic today and phone the result
options.rationale: The test itself is the right test, which is what makes this tempting, but delivering a result of this kind without pre test counselling, assessment of the patient's understanding, and planning for how at risk relatives will be informed is contrary to established practice. Each of his children carries a one in two prior risk and their position must be considered before the result exists. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia)

options.text: Refer to a neurogenetics service for counselling before any genetic test
options.rationale: Progressive personality change with apathy and disinhibition, chorea with motor impersistence and slowed saccades, and a parent who died young with a psychiatric and cognitive illness together indicate an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. Testing for it carries profound implications for the patient, his children and his insurance and employment, so it is performed within a genetic counselling framework rather than ordered from a psychiatric clinic. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia)

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic to suppress the involuntary movements now
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents including tetrabenazine are used for functionally disabling chorea later in the illness, so this is a treatment on the right pathway at the wrong time. Starting one before the diagnosis is established obscures the movement disorder and risks it being reattributed to the drug. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review the report
options.rationale: Imaging may show caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns but this appears relatively late and a normal scan would not exclude the diagnosis. It is a supportive investigation rather than the step that resolves the question. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene, with full penetrance at 40 or more repeats and anticipation through paternal transmission. Psychiatric and behavioural change frequently precedes the movement disorder by years, and irritability, apathy, disinhibition and depression are the usual presentations, which is why these patients often reach a psychiatric service first and accumulate several failed antidepressant trials. The motor signs to seek deliberately are chorea, often absorbed into apparently purposeful gestures early on, motor impersistence demonstrated by inability to sustain tongue protrusion or a steady grip, and slowed or delayed initiation of saccades, which is one of the earliest reliable findings. A family history may be obscured, since a parent who died young of another cause, or whose illness was labelled as early dementia, alcoholism or a psychiatric disorder, is common. Testing is performed through a genetic service because the result determines risk for children and siblings who have not asked to know, and because suicide risk around the time of diagnosis is elevated.
key_points: Psychiatric and behavioural change often precedes chorea by several years
Motor impersistence and slowed saccades are early and easily missed signs
Chorea is initially incorporated into voluntary movements and looks like fidgeting
A parent labelled with early dementia or alcoholism may represent an obscured family history
Genetic testing proceeds through a counselling framework because relatives are implicated
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and hold it out for ten seconds, and to grip your fingers steadily: inability to sustain either, known as motor impersistence, appears early in Huntington disease and is often present before chorea is obvious enough to be noticed by the family.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: weighing a contested medication association against active suicidal ideation in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17 year old boy who is eight weeks into a course of isotretinoin prescribed by a dermatologist for severe nodulocystic acne that had scarred his cheeks and back.

His mother booked the appointment because he has stopped going to soccer training, spends most of his time in his room and has become monosyllabic at home. Seen alone, he tells you his mood has been flat for about five weeks, that he has stopped enjoying things he used to, and that he sleeps poorly. When you ask directly, he says that in the past fortnight he has sometimes thought that everyone would be better off without him, though he has no plan and has never harmed himself. He had a depressive episode at 15 that responded to psychological therapy alone.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Flattened affect with reduced spontaneous speech, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, passive thoughts that others would be better off without him without plan or intent, marked improvement in the acne itself
data_table.Investigations: Liver function within normal limits, fasting lipids within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and review the mood in two weeks time
options.rationale: A dose relationship has not been established for the psychiatric association, so halving the dose has no evidential basis for resolving the problem. It preserves the exposure while delaying definitive action. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the isotretinoin and start an antidepressant at the same visit
options.rationale: Adding a second medication while continuing a drug that requires cessation under its own product information leaves the possible contributor in place and complicates the picture. It also delays the specialist assessment that his suicidal thinking warrants. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the isotretinoin and review him in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: A four week interval is far too long for an adolescent who has expressed thoughts that others would be better off without him. Passive death wishes require assessment within days, not weeks. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Cease the isotretinoin and arrange an urgent mental health assessment
options.rationale: Whatever the strength of the causal evidence at population level, the product information directs cessation if significant mood change or suicidal ideation emerges, and the presence of active passive death wishes in an adolescent with a previous depressive episode makes continuing the drug indefensible. Stopping is reversible and the acne can be reconsidered once he is well. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure that the association is unproven and continue the treatment
options.rationale: It is correct that large cohort studies have not established causation and that severe acne itself carries a substantial risk of depression, so the reasoning behind this option is genuinely sound at population level. That evidence governs whether the drug should be prescribed at all, not what to do for the individual in front of you who has developed suicidal thinking while taking it. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: The relationship between isotretinoin and depression has been debated for three decades and the population level evidence does not establish causation, with large cohort and case crossover studies showing no increase in depression or suicide attributable to the drug, and several suggesting that mood improves as severe acne clears. Severe acne is itself independently associated with depression, social withdrawal and suicidal ideation, which confounds the comparison substantially. Despite this, both Australian product information and prescribing practice require that patients and families be counselled about mood change before starting, that mood be reviewed at each visit, and that the drug be ceased if significant psychiatric symptoms emerge, reflecting the asymmetry between a reversible pause in an elective treatment and the consequences of a missed adolescent depression. The practical skill being tested is holding these two things together: the population evidence determines whether the drug is reasonable to prescribe, while the individual presentation determines what to do next for this patient. Any adolescent expressing thoughts that others would be better off without them requires assessment within days regardless of what medication they are taking.
key_points: Population evidence does not establish a causal link with depression or suicide
Severe acne independently carries a substantial risk of depression, confounding the association
Product information nonetheless directs cessation if significant mood change emerges
Population level evidence governs prescribing, not the response to an individual event
Passive death wishes in an adolescent require assessment within days
explanation.pearls: Counsel about mood and ask about it at every isotretinoin review, and record the conversation, because the obligation to monitor and to cease on significant mood change holds under Australian product information regardless of what the epidemiological evidence shows about causation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: pursuing copper studies when caeruloplasmin sits within the reference range in a young person with psychiatric and movement signs
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23 year old man admitted under your team. Over ten months he has become increasingly irritable and disinhibited, has failed two university semesters after previously doing well, and four months ago was diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis at another hospital.

Risperidone was started at 1 mg daily and within a week he developed marked rigidity and a coarse tremor, which his previous team described as an unusually severe reaction to a low dose. His speech has become slurred over the past two months and his handwriting has shrunk and become untidy. His mother has noticed he drools on his pillow. He drinks alcohol rarely and his urine drug screen is negative. He has one older sister who is well.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Dysarthria with hypophonia, coarse proximal tremor of both arms on posture, cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, micrographia, drooling, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin within normal limits, international normalised ratio within normal limits, serum caeruloplasmin 0.21 g/L (0.20 to 0.60), haemoglobin within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the serum caeruloplasmin level in three months and reassess
options.rationale: This treats a result at the very bottom of the reference range as though it excludes the diagnosis, which is the central trap. Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation, oestrogen and pregnancy, and it sits within the reference range in a meaningful minority of affected patients, so a normal value never excludes the condition and repeating it answers nothing. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility sequences
options.rationale: Imaging may show characteristic changes in the basal ganglia and midbrain and is part of the assessment once the diagnosis is being pursued. The appearances are supportive rather than diagnostic and would not distinguish this from other causes of a young onset movement disorder. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Measure the total serum copper concentration on a fasting sample
options.rationale: Total serum copper is misleading because most circulating copper is bound to caeruloplasmin, so the total falls in parallel with the carrier protein and can appear low, normal or high depending on the balance between reduced carrier and increased free copper. It is not used as a diagnostic test. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper content
options.rationale: Hepatic copper quantification remains the reference standard and retains a role when non invasive testing is equivocal, which makes it the strongest competing answer. It is invasive, carries bleeding risk, and is not the appropriate first step when a urine collection and a slit lamp examination will resolve the question in most neurological presentations. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Collect a 24 hour urine sample for quantitative copper excretion
options.rationale: Basal 24 hour urinary copper excretion is the most useful screening test when the diagnosis is suspected in a symptomatic patient and is raised in almost all those with neurological presentations, which is exactly the group this man falls into. Combined with slit lamp examination for corneal rings, which are present in nearly every patient with neurological involvement, it establishes the diagnosis in most cases without invasive testing. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter, causing failure of biliary copper excretion and of copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin, with accumulation in liver, brain, cornea and kidney, and although it is fatal untreated it is treatable, which is why it must be actively excluded in any patient under about 50 presenting with an unexplained movement disorder, unexplained liver disease, or a psychiatric presentation accompanied by either. Psychiatric features are the presenting complaint in around a third and include personality change, disinhibition, mood disturbance and occasionally psychosis, and they characteristically precede the neurological signs. Two findings in this case should redirect the assessment: markedly disproportionate sensitivity to a low dose of a dopamine blocking drug, which reflects pre-existing basal ganglia injury, and mildly deranged transaminases with a normal bilirubin in a young person. The critical diagnostic pitfall is the caeruloplasmin: it is normal in roughly one in ten patients overall and more often in those with active inflammation, so a value within the reference range must never be used to close the question. Basal 24 hour urinary copper excretion above 1.6 micromol per day supports the diagnosis and slit lamp examination for Kayser Fleischer rings is positive in almost all neurological cases.
key_points: Exclude Wilson disease in anyone under 50 with unexplained movement or liver disease
Psychiatric features precede neurological signs in a substantial proportion
Severe extrapyramidal reaction to a low antipsychotic dose is a warning sign
A caeruloplasmin within the reference range does not exclude the diagnosis
Basal 24 hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination establishes most neurological cases
explanation.pearls: Kayser Fleischer rings are present in over 95 per cent of patients with neurological Wilson disease but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone, so a slit lamp examination is close to definitive in exactly the group that reaches a psychiatric or neurology clinic.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: choosing between behavioural therapy and dopamine blockade as the first treatment for tics that have become socially impairing
stem:
You are the registrar in a general paediatric and adolescent clinic seeing an 11 year old boy brought by his mother. Since he was seven he has had bouts of blinking, shoulder shrugging and head jerking, and for the past two years he has also made a repeated throat clearing noise. The movements wax and wane, shift between body parts and disappear when he is absorbed in building models.

His mother says two boys in his class have started imitating the noise and he now asks to eat lunch in the library. He is in the top group for reading, sleeps well and has no rituals, counting or checking. He is not distractible in class and his teacher reports no difficulty with sustained attention. He can hold the movements back for a few minutes but describes a build up of tension in his neck that only settles once he lets them out.

data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and right shoulder shrug during the consultation, throat clearing three times, neurological examination otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Reassurance alone with a planned clinic review in twelve months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with psychoeducation is right when tics are noticed but not causing distress or functional loss, which is not the case once a child is avoiding the playground and eating lunch alone. Deferring for a year leaves an impairing symptom untreated through a full school year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Referral for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy built on habit reversal, in which the child learns to recognise the premonitory urge and perform a competing response, is the recommended first treatment for impairing tics and outperforms watchful waiting without drug adverse effects. The premonitory urge he describes is what makes him a good candidate, since the technique depends on being able to feel the tic coming. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Low dose risperidone titrated slowly over the next four weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents do reduce tic severity but carry weight gain, sedation and extrapyramidal risk, so they sit behind behavioural therapy and are reserved for tics that remain disabling after it has been tried or is unavailable. Risperidone differs from clonidine in acting on the dopaminergic rather than the noradrenergic limb, which is why its adverse effect profile is metabolic rather than cardiovascular. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Clonidine at night with blood pressure checked at each review
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological choice when tics coexist with prominent inattention or hyperactivity, neither of which his teacher describes, and it still ranks behind behavioural therapy as an opening move. It would be correct if a drug were needed and there were comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. (Source: American Academy of Neurology: Treatment of Tics)
source_refs: American Academy of Neurology: Treatment of Tics

options.text: Aripiprazole commenced at low dose with metabolic monitoring
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the best evidence among the antipsychotics for tic reduction in children, but the same sequencing argument applies and behavioural therapy has not yet been offered. Starting it now exposes him to appetite and metabolic monitoring for a symptom that may respond to a time limited course of therapy. (Source: American Academy of Neurology: Treatment of Tics)
source_refs: American Academy of Neurology: Treatment of Tics

explanation.summary: Chronic tic disorder and Tourette disorder are diagnosed clinically from motor and vocal tics persisting beyond a year with onset before age eighteen, and no investigation is required when the examination is otherwise normal. Severity typically peaks between ten and twelve years and then declines through adolescence, so a large part of management is explaining the natural history to the family and the school. Treatment is driven by functional impact rather than by tic count, and a child who is coping needs education and school liaison rather than therapy. Comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder are present in roughly half of referred children and often cause more impairment than the tics themselves, so they are screened for at every visit. Medication is added only when behavioural treatment has failed or is not accessible.
key_points: Tics that wax, wane and migrate with a premonitory urge and suppressibility are typical rather than concerning
Treat on functional impairment, not on how many tics are counted in a consultation
Habit reversal based behavioural therapy is the first line treatment for impairing tics
Screen every child with tics for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms
Antipsychotics are second line and require weight and metabolic monitoring
explanation.pearls: The premonitory urge is the therapeutic handle: children old enough to describe that build up of tension, usually from about nine years, are the ones who can be taught a competing response, and eight to ten weekly sessions is the standard course.

sources.label: American Academy of Neurology: Treatment of Tics

subtopic_detail: managing amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea appearing on a stable antipsychotic dose when the prolactin sits in the drug induced rather than tumour range
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman in the community clinic. She has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for eight months after a first episode of psychosis and has been well, working part time and attending university.

Today she tells you her periods stopped four months ago and that she has noticed milk leaking from both breasts when she showers. A urine pregnancy test in clinic is negative. She has no headache, no change in her vision and no galactorrhoea before starting treatment. She takes no other medication and does not use cannabis or other substances. She is clear that she wants to stay on treatment because the psychosis frightened her.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky discharge, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1680 mIU/L (100 to 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when prolactin rises above roughly 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, when there is headache or visual field loss, or when the elevation persists after the offending drug is withdrawn, none of which applies here. Scanning first risks finding an incidental microadenoma and anchoring management on it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cross titrate from risperidone to aripiprazole over three weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most among the second generation agents, and switching to a partial dopamine agonist normalises prolactin in most patients within weeks while maintaining antipsychotic cover. This preserves the treatment she wants to continue rather than trading her remission for her cycle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add cabergoline weekly and continue the current risperidone dose
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist can lower prolactin but is working directly against the antipsychotic at the receptor it blocks, and carries a real risk of destabilising the psychosis. Cabergoline is the right drug for a true prolactinoma, which is the distinction from the drug induced picture here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her periods
options.rationale: Inducing a withdrawal bleed masks the hormonal abnormality without addressing the dopamine blockade that is driving it, and the galactorrhoea will persist. Oestrogen replacement has a place only when the causative drug genuinely cannot be changed and bone protection is the aim. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease antipsychotic treatment and monitor for symptom recurrence
options.rationale: Stopping treatment eight months after a first episode carries a high relapse risk and is not justified by a reversible endocrine adverse effect with an easy pharmacological solution. Guidance supports continuing an antipsychotic for at least one to two years after a first episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary, so any drug that blocks the D2 receptor releases that brake and raises prolactin. The degree of rise tracks the degree of blockade, which is why risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are the usual culprits while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are comparatively sparing. Sustained hyperprolactinaemia matters beyond the visible symptoms because the resulting hypogonadism reduces bone mineral density over years. The key interpretive step is the magnitude of the level: drug induced elevations usually sit below about 2000 mIU/L, whereas a macroprolactinoma generally drives prolactin far higher and comes with mass effect symptoms. Baseline prolactin before starting an antipsychotic makes this distinction much easier later.
key_points: Check a pregnancy test and thyroid function before attributing galactorrhoea to a drug
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are the high prolactin antipsychotics
Aripiprazole is a partial dopamine agonist and typically lowers prolactin toward normal
Image the pituitary only for very high levels, mass effect symptoms, or persistence after the drug is stopped
Untreated hyperprolactinaemic hypogonadism costs bone density over the long term
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole reduces antipsychotic induced prolactin within about four weeks and can be used as a low dose adjunct of 5 to 10 mg daily when the original agent must be kept for efficacy reasons.

subtopic_detail: interpreting dilute high volume urine with a rising sodium in a long term lithium patient whose glucose is normal
stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health service reviewing a 46 year old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar affective disorder for eight years with no admissions in that time. She tells you she is passing very large amounts of pale urine and is getting up three or four times most nights, and that she carries a two litre bottle everywhere because her mouth feels dry.

A measured collection shows a urine volume of 4.6 L over twenty four hours. She has not changed her dose and takes no diuretic, no antipsychotic and no other regular medication. After she was kept without fluids under supervision for six hours the urine remained dilute and her serum sodium rose further.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no postural drop, no goitre, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 148 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73m2, random glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), serum lithium 0.71 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8), urine osmolality 178 mOsm/kg (300 to 900)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence amiloride and review the ongoing indication for lithium
options.rationale: Lithium enters the principal cell through the epithelial sodium channel and disables the collecting duct response to antidiuretic hormone, and amiloride blocks that entry channel and is the specific agent for the resulting concentrating defect. Reviewing the indication runs in parallel because the defect becomes less reversible the longer lithium continues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence desmopressin nasal spray and recheck the sodium weekly
options.rationale: Desmopressin replaces antidiuretic hormone and only works when the deficiency is at the pituitary end, whereas here the hormone is present and the collecting duct cannot respond to it. That resistance is precisely what separates the nephrogenic form from the central form that desmopressin treats. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake to 1.5 L daily and repeat the electrolytes
options.rationale: Her thirst is the compensation that is keeping her sodium at 148 rather than far higher, so capping intake while the renal losses continue risks driving a dangerous hypernatraemia. Fluid restriction is the treatment for primary polydipsia, which the dilute urine and rising sodium during supervised deprivation have already excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test before altering any treatment
options.rationale: Polyuria with thirst does warrant excluding an osmotic diuresis, but a random glucose of 5.2 mmol/L alongside urine that is dilute rather than loaded with solute has already done that. An osmotic cause would produce a urine osmolality well above the serum value rather than the 178 mOsm/kg recorded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease lithium abruptly today and substitute sodium valproate instead
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium withdrawal carries a well described rebound risk of mania over the following months in a woman who has been stable for eight years, so any change is made as a slow taper with a planned alternative. Valproate is also a poor default choice in a woman of reproductive age given its teratogenicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus affects a substantial minority of long term users and is dose and duration dependent rather than a sign of toxicity, which is why it appears at therapeutic levels. The mechanism is downregulation of aquaporin two water channels in the collecting duct after lithium accumulates in the principal cell, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine even when antidiuretic hormone is abundant. Patients compensate by drinking, and the danger arises when illness, surgery or anything else interrupts access to fluid and the sodium climbs quickly. Separate from this, lithium causes a chronic interstitial nephropathy with a slow fall in glomerular filtration rate, so renal function is monitored at least six monthly. Early recognition matters because the concentrating defect is partly reversible if lithium is stopped within a few years but often permanent after prolonged exposure.
key_points: Polyuria at a therapeutic lithium level is a concentrating defect, not toxicity
Dilute urine that stays dilute during water deprivation separates it from primary polydipsia
Amiloride blocks the channel through which lithium enters the principal cell
Never fluid restrict a patient whose thirst is holding the sodium down
Monitor renal function and thyroid function at least every six months on long term lithium
explanation.pearls: Amiloride 5 to 10 mg daily reduces urine volume in lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus within about two weeks, and because it also reduces lithium clearance the serum lithium must be rechecked five to seven days after starting it.

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for compulsive sports betting presenting behind a complaint of insomnia and low mood
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38 year old carpenter who has booked a long appointment for three months of poor sleep and feeling flat. He falls asleep easily but wakes at two in the morning and cannot settle again.

When you ask what is on his mind at that hour he becomes tearful and describes betting on sport through an app on his phone. He has lost about forty thousand dollars over two years, has taken out a personal loan his partner does not know about, and has been putting larger amounts on to win back what he lost. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and uses no other substances. He denies any thoughts of ending his life and says he has tried three times to delete the app.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired and tearful, no psychomotor retardation, normal cognition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy directed at his gambling
options.rationale: Structured cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the erroneous beliefs about chance, the chasing behaviour and cue exposure has the strongest evidence in gambling disorder and is the recommended first treatment. Directing therapy at the gambling rather than at the mood symptom treats the disorder that is generating both. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start sertraline and review his mood symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: His low mood and early morning waking are plausibly secondary to mounting debt and concealment rather than an independent depressive episode, and antidepressants have not shown benefit for gambling disorder itself. This would be the right move if depressive symptoms persisted once the gambling was being treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe naltrexone daily and arrange liver function monitoring
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in gambling disorder and are considered when psychological treatment has been tried and failed, particularly where there is a strong urge component or a family history of alcohol use disorder. It is a second line addition rather than an opening move. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange financial counselling as the sole intervention for now
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a genuinely useful part of the package and Australian gambling help services provide it, but on its own it manages the consequence and leaves the behaviour that created it untouched. It belongs alongside psychological treatment, not instead of it. (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia)

options.text: Advise self exclusion from betting platforms and review in three months
options.rationale: Self exclusion and app blocking reduce access and are worth arranging, but he has already tried deleting the app three times, which shows that removing the means alone has not held. A three month gap also leaves a man with escalating secret debt unsupported. (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder sits with the substance use disorders in current classification because it shares the features of tolerance, withdrawal, preoccupation and continued use despite harm. It is rarely the presenting complaint, and most people reach a doctor through insomnia, low mood, relationship breakdown or a request for a medical certificate, so a single screening question about betting belongs in any assessment of unexplained distress in this age group. Suicide risk is markedly elevated in gambling disorder, particularly around the point of disclosure to a partner or a creditor, so risk assessment is repeated rather than done once. Australian services combine psychological therapy with free financial counselling and with self exclusion registers that cover venues and online platforms. Comorbid depression, alcohol use and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and are reassessed after the gambling is being treated.
key_points: Ask directly about gambling when insomnia or low mood has no clear explanation
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting chasing and chance beliefs is first line
Financial counselling and self exclusion support treatment but do not replace it
Suicide risk peaks around disclosure of debt and needs repeated assessment
Reassess mood after the gambling is addressed before diagnosing a depressive disorder
explanation.pearls: Chasing losses, the act of betting more to recover what was lost, is the single most specific feature of gambling disorder and appears earlier than the financial consequences that eventually bring people to a doctor.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: a child who talks freely at home but has never spoken at school, with normal language milestones and a normal hearing screen
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic seeing a 6 year old girl referred by her school. In the fourteen months since she started school she has not spoken a word to her teacher or to any classmate, although she will nod, point and hand over written notes.

Her parents bring a phone recording in which she is chatting and singing at length with her younger brother at home. Her milestones were normal, she joined words into sentences before two, and a formal hearing assessment last term was normal. She makes eye contact with you, brings a toy over to show you and plays reciprocally with her mother in the room. There are no repetitive behaviours and no restricted interests. She flushes and freezes when you ask her a direct question.

data_table.Examination: Mute with the examiner but socially engaged non verbally, cranial nerves and oromotor examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Pure tone audiometry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for graded exposure behavioural therapy delivered with the school
options.rationale: Selective mutism responds to a behavioural program that builds speech through a planned ladder of steps, moving from non verbal to whispered to spoken responses across widening settings, and it must be run where the mutism occurs rather than only in a clinic room. Involving the teacher is what converts a clinic gain into classroom speech. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer to speech pathology for assessment of expressive language delay
options.rationale: The recording of fluent conversational speech and singing at home establishes that expressive language is intact, which is the finding that separates selective mutism from a language disorder. Speech pathology has a role only where an additional articulation or language problem is suspected on top of the mutism. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer for a diagnostic assessment for autism spectrum disorder instead
options.rationale: Reciprocal play, spontaneous showing, normal eye contact and the absence of repetitive behaviours or restricted interests argue against autism, and the mutism here is situation bound rather than a pervasive social communication difficulty. Autism assessment would be warranted if the social differences were present at home as well. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence fluoxetine at low dose and review her progress in six weeks
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are reserved for children whose mutism persists despite an adequate behavioural program or who are too anxious to engage with one, so they follow rather than replace therapy. Starting a drug first in a six year old commits her to medication without testing the treatment most likely to work. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise the school to wait a further six months for her to settle in
options.rationale: A month or so of silence in a new setting can be normal adjustment, but fourteen months is well beyond that and the longer the mutism is established the harder it becomes to shift. Waiting also allows the school to accommodate around her silence in ways that entrench it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child who speaks normally in comfortable settings is consistently unable to speak in specific social situations, most often school, for at least a month beyond the first month of enrolment. The child is not choosing silence, and framing it to families and teachers as a freeze response rather than defiance changes how the adults around the child behave. Around a third of affected children also meet criteria for social anxiety disorder, and the rate of comorbid anxiety in parents is high. The practical risk of delay is that schools adapt by allowing written or non verbal responses, which relieves anxiety in the short term and reinforces avoidance over the long term. Prognosis with an early behavioural program is good, and most children gain functional classroom speech.
key_points: Normal speech in one setting excludes a language disorder as the explanation
Duration must exceed one month beyond the initial month of starting school
Treatment is graded exposure delivered in the setting where speech fails
Pressing a child to speak in the moment reliably increases the freeze
Medication follows an inadequate response to behavioural treatment
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading, in which a parent the child already speaks to is gradually joined in the room by the teacher before the parent withdraws, is the highest yield single technique and is usually where a school program begins.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: a young man seeking rhinoplasty for a defect others cannot see, with three hours daily of mirror checking
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 22 year old apprentice electrician who asks for a referral to a plastic surgeon. He believes the bridge of his nose is twisted and that people stare at it.

He spends about three hours a day checking his profile in mirrors and in the reflective glass of shop windows, takes photographs from different angles to compare, and has stopped going to his football club social nights. He has cancelled two family gatherings in the past month. He has no concerns about his weight, eats normally and his body mass index is 23 kg/m2. He accepts that his family and friends tell him his nose looks ordinary but says he cannot make himself believe it. On examination his nose is symmetrical with no deviation.

data_table.Examination: Nasal bridge straight and symmetrical, no septal deviation, no excoriation of the skin
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to a plastic surgeon for an opinion on corrective rhinoplasty
options.rationale: Cosmetic surgery in this setting rarely satisfies the patient and the preoccupation typically transfers to the operated site or to a new body part, with worsening distress afterwards. Surgery would only be appropriate if there were an objective deformity, which examination has excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence olanzapine at low dose for a fixed belief about his body
options.rationale: Poor insight is common in this disorder and does not by itself make the belief delusional or make an antipsychotic the right treatment, since these patients respond to the same therapy as those with better insight. An antipsychotic is considered only as augmentation when a serotonergic drug and therapy have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted to appearance concerns
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy incorporating exposure to avoided situations and prevention of mirror checking and reassurance seeking is the recommended first treatment and targets the maintaining behaviours directly. Perceptual retraining in front of a mirror is a specific component that ordinary anxiety focused therapy does not include. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him about his appearance and review again in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance is itself one of the behaviours that maintains the disorder, giving brief relief followed by renewed doubt and more checking, so repeating it in the consulting room strengthens the cycle. He has already told you that family reassurance does not hold. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine and arrange psychological review only if it fails
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor at the higher doses used for obsessive compulsive spectrum disorders is an effective treatment and is combined with therapy in moderate to severe illness, but it is not preferred over therapy as the sole opening move. This would be the right answer if therapy were unavailable or he declined it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with a perceived defect that is unobservable or slight to others, combined with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing, camouflaging or reassurance seeking. It typically begins in adolescence and is under recognised because patients present to dermatologists and surgeons rather than to mental health services. The nose, skin and hair are the most commonly targeted areas, and muscle dysmorphia is a recognised variant in young men. Suicidal ideation and attempts are substantially more frequent than in obsessive compulsive disorder, so risk assessment is part of every review. Insight is often poor and up to a third of patients hold the belief with delusional intensity, which changes neither the diagnosis nor the first line treatment.
key_points: The defect is absent or slight to an observer while the distress is severe
Repetitive checking, comparing or camouflaging is required for the diagnosis
Cosmetic procedures usually leave the preoccupation unchanged or worse
Cognitive behavioural therapy with response prevention is first line
Suicide risk is high and is assessed at every contact
explanation.pearls: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors for body dysmorphic disorder need obsessive compulsive range doses, for example fluoxetine 40 to 80 mg daily, and a twelve week trial before the response is judged, which is longer and higher than the usual depression trial.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: sleepiness on night duty with an inability to sleep during the day in a rotating roster worker whose sleep is normal on leave
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old intensive care nurse who has worked a rotating roster with blocks of four night shifts for the past eight months. She asks for something to help her sleep.

She describes lying awake until midday after a night shift, managing only three to four broken hours, and then fighting to stay awake from about three in the morning on the next shift. She has twice caught herself drifting at the wheel on the drive home. On her two week annual leave in April she slept seven to eight hours a night without difficulty and felt well. She does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Her partner sleeps in the same room and reports no kicking or restless movements.

data_table.Examination: Mallampati class 1, neck circumference 32 cm, no goitre, mood and cognition normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies including ferritin and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe zopiclone to be taken before each daytime sleep period
options.rationale: A hypnotic may lengthen the daytime sleep a little but does nothing for the sleepiness on shift, which is the part that is putting her at risk on the road, and tolerance and dependence follow regular use. Sedatives are a short term adjunct at most, not the opening move. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before any treatment is started
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when obstructive sleep apnoea, narcolepsy or a periodic limb movement disorder is suspected, and a body mass index of 22 with no snoring, no witnessed apnoea and no limb movements makes those unlikely. The normal sleep on annual leave points firmly to a circadian rather than an intrinsic sleep disorder. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Prescribe modafinil each night shift and arrange follow up in a month
options.rationale: A wake promoting agent reduces sleepiness during night work but is reserved for residual impairment after circadian and behavioural measures have been optimised, and in Australia its subsidised indications do not cover this disorder. It would be considered if the structured program below failed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Plan timed bright light, protected daytime sleep and a pre shift nap
options.rationale: Shifting the circadian clock with bright light early in the shift, dark glasses for the drive home, a blacked out and quiet sleep period with the phone off, and a planned nap before the shift is the first line package and addresses both the insomnia and the sleepiness. It also directly reduces the drive home risk she has already had two warnings about. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence melatonin at bedtime and review her sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: Melatonin taken before the daytime sleep can help consolidate it and is a reasonable adjunct, but used alone and at the wrong clock time it shifts the rhythm unpredictably and leaves the on shift sleepiness untreated. Its timing relative to the desired sleep period matters more than the dose. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is diagnosed when insomnia or excessive sleepiness is temporally linked to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period, persists for at least three months, and is not better explained by another sleep disorder. The discriminating history is that sleep normalises on leave or on a run of day shifts, which separates a circadian misalignment from a primary insomnia. Around a fifth to a quarter of shift workers meet criteria, and night shift, early morning starts and rapidly rotating rosters carry the highest risk. Drowsy driving on the commute home is the most immediate danger and should be asked about explicitly, along with an offer of alternative transport arrangements. Longer term associations include cardiometabolic disease and mood disorder, which is why roster design is part of management rather than an aside.
key_points: Sleep that normalises on annual leave points to a circadian rather than intrinsic disorder
Ask directly about drowsy driving on the commute home
Bright light early in the shift and dark glasses afterwards shift the clock in the wanted direction
Protect the daytime sleep period with darkness, quiet and a silenced phone
Hypnotics and wake promoting drugs follow rather than replace circadian measures
explanation.pearls: A planned nap of 20 to 30 minutes taken before the night shift, or in the first half of it, improves alertness without the deep sleep inertia that follows a nap longer than about 45 minutes.

subtopic_detail: persistent detachment and a flat unreal quality to the world after a single cannabis episode, with reality testing preserved
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 20 year old university student referred by his general practitioner. Eight months ago, at a party, he smoked a much stronger cannabis preparation than he was used to and felt intensely frightened for several hours.

Since that night he has felt, in his words, like he is watching himself from just behind his own shoulder, and says his hands sometimes look as though they belong to someone else. Colours seem washed out and the street where he grew up looks like a stage set. He finds all of this distressing and says he knows perfectly well that it is his own mind playing tricks and that the world has not really changed. He has not used cannabis or any other substance since that night. He has no gaps in his memory for events or for personal information, hears no voices and holds no unusual beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, reactive affect, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cannabis induced psychotic disorder with residual perceptual features
options.rationale: A substance induced psychotic disorder requires hallucinations or delusions, and it is the preserved reality testing that excludes it: he describes the experience as if rather than asserting that the world has changed. A drug episode is nonetheless the single most common trigger for the correct condition. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Persistent depersonalisation and derealisation disorder after cannabis
options.rationale: Persistent or recurrent detachment from one's own body or mental processes together with unreality of surroundings, with intact reality testing and clinically significant distress, defines this disorder, and cannabis is the commonest precipitant in young men. The absence of memory gaps, voices and unusual beliefs rules out the competing diagnoses. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Panic disorder presenting with prominent dissociative experiences
options.rationale: Depersonalisation is a recognised symptom during a panic attack, but it is then episodic and tied to discrete surges of autonomic arousal rather than continuously present for eight months. He describes no palpitations, breathlessness or crescendo fear episodes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Schizophrenia presenting with predominantly negative and odd symptoms
options.rationale: Negative symptoms involve genuine loss of volition, affect and speech output, whereas he is distressed by and fully aware of a change in the quality of his experience, which is a different phenomenon. His reactive affect and intact thought form argue against it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Post traumatic stress disorder of the dissociative subtype after a scare
options.rationale: The dissociative subtype sits on top of a full post traumatic syndrome, which requires re experiencing, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative cognitions and hyperarousal, none of which he reports. The frightening drug episode is a trigger for the dissociative state rather than an index trauma driving intrusions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation and derealisation disorder is common enough to affect roughly one to two per cent of the population yet is routinely misdiagnosed as psychosis, because clinicians hear the strangeness of the description rather than the preserved insight within it. The distinguishing feature is the as if quality: the patient knows the experience is generated by their own mind, which is exactly what a psychotic patient does not. Onset clusters in late adolescence and early adulthood, and cannabis, hallucinogens, severe anxiety and sleep deprivation are the usual precipitants. Explaining the phenomenon and its benign nature is itself therapeutic because much of the distress comes from fear of going mad. No drug is specifically approved, and treatment targets comorbid anxiety and depression alongside psychological therapy.
key_points: Intact reality testing is what separates this disorder from psychosis
Cannabis is the single commonest precipitant in young people
Absence of memory gaps excludes dissociative amnesia and identity disorder
Psychoeducation reduces the secondary fear that drives much of the distress
Treat comorbid anxiety and depression, which are present in most cases
explanation.pearls: Antipsychotics do not help this disorder and frequently worsen the subjective deadness, so a diagnostic trial of one is not a harmless way of resolving uncertainty about whether the presentation is psychotic.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: a severely neglected preschooler in foster care whose social reciprocity is improving with placement rather than remaining fixed
stem:
You are the registrar in a child development clinic seeing a 4 year old boy placed with a foster carer eighteen months ago. Before the placement he lived in conditions of severe neglect with several changes of caregiver.

The referral says he seldom goes to an adult for comfort when he falls and rarely responds when his carer tries to soothe him, and that he shows little positive emotion during play. His carer adds that in the past six months he has begun to bring her drawings unprompted, glances back at her when something surprises him, and has started feeding a toy dinosaur with a plastic spoon. His vocabulary and sentence structure are appropriate for his age and he understands two step instructions. He lines his cars up occasionally but plays with them as cars as well, and he has no repetitive mannerisms and no sensory aversions.

data_table.Examination: Subdued affect, limited comfort seeking, emerging shared attention with the carer, growth on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Hearing and vision screening both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with an associated language strength profile
options.rationale: Autism requires persistent deficits in social communication together with restricted or repetitive behaviours, and the emerging joint attention, spontaneous showing and symbolic pretend play since placement point away from it. The steady improvement in reciprocity as caregiving improved is the discriminator, since autistic social differences do not resolve with a change of carer. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Global developmental delay arising from prolonged early understimulation
options.rationale: Global delay requires significant impairment across two or more developmental domains, and his language, comprehension and growth are all age appropriate. Neglect can certainly cause delay, but here the deficit is confined to the attachment and emotional domain. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Disinhibited social engagement disorder following the early deprivation
options.rationale: The disinhibited form presents as overfamiliarity, with a child who wanders off with strangers and shows no reticence, which is the mirror image of the withdrawn picture described here. Both follow deprivation, but they are distinguished by whether the child approaches too readily or not at all. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Childhood depressive disorder with marked anhedonia and social withdrawal
options.rationale: Depression in a preschooler would show a change from a previous better state with disturbance of sleep, appetite and play, whereas his reduced positive affect has been present since infancy and is improving rather than worsening. The developmental history of pathogenic care is what reframes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reactive attachment disorder arising from grossly insufficient early care
options.rationale: A consistently inhibited and emotionally withdrawn pattern toward caregivers, minimal comfort seeking and response to comfort, and reduced positive affect in a child with a documented history of grossly inadequate care defines this disorder. The improvement with an adequate carer is characteristic and is exactly what distinguishes it from autism. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Reactive attachment disorder can only be diagnosed where there is a documented history of pathogenic care, meaning persistent social neglect, repeated changes of primary caregiver, or rearing in a setting that prevented selective attachments forming. The child must have a developmental age of at least nine months so that selective attachment would normally have been established, and the picture must not be better explained by autism. Distinguishing the two is the central clinical task and is often got wrong in both directions, with consequences for the services a child is offered. The practical test is responsiveness to improved caregiving: attachment difficulties soften over months in a stable placement whereas autistic social communication differences persist. Treatment is not individual therapy for the child but work with the caregiver to build sensitive, predictable, responsive care, and placement stability is the single most powerful intervention available.
key_points: A history of grossly insufficient care is a required criterion, not merely supportive
The withdrawn form is reactive attachment disorder, the overfamiliar form is disinhibited social engagement disorder
Improvement with a stable sensitive carer argues strongly against autism
Symbolic pretend play and spontaneous showing are evidence against autism
Treatment works through the caregiver relationship, not through therapy delivered to the child alone
explanation.pearls: Disinhibited social engagement disorder persists in a proportion of children even after attachment security is achieved with a new carer, whereas reactive attachment disorder characteristically remits once care improves, so the two differ in prognosis as well as presentation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: yearning and preoccupation sixteen months after a spousal death that has not moved despite an adequate antidepressant trial
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58 year old woman whose husband died sixteen months ago after a short illness. She was started on sertraline by a colleague six months ago and has taken 100 mg daily for the past four months without missing doses.

She describes an ache of longing for him that fills most of the day, spends hours going through his photographs and messages, and has not been able to open the door of his study. She says she still cannot take in that he is gone. She lights up describing her granddaughter's swimming carnival last weekend and went to it willingly. She eats normally, her weight is unchanged, she feels she was a good wife and she has no thoughts of harming herself. There is no psychomotor slowing and she is not self critical.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking of her husband, warm and reactive otherwise, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for a structured psychological therapy targeting her grief
options.rationale: Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines revisiting the death with graded approach to avoided reminders and work on restoring goals, outperforms antidepressants for this condition and is the recommended treatment. The avoided study door is precisely the kind of target the approach component addresses. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 150 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation is the right move in a depressive episode with a partial response, but her presentation lacks pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness and appetite change, and antidepressants have not been shown to reduce the core yearning and preoccupation of this condition. Four months at a therapeutic dose without movement is itself evidence the target is wrong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add low dose quetiapine at night to settle her ruminative preoccupation
options.rationale: Augmenting with an antipsychotic is a strategy for treatment resistant depression with an established diagnosis, not for grief, and it adds metabolic and sedative burden without addressing avoidance. Preoccupation with a deceased person is not the rumination of a depressive illness. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal bereavement and review in six months
options.rationale: Intense yearning with preoccupation, disbelief and avoidance persisting beyond twelve months after the death in an adult, at a level that impairs function, is past the boundary of expected grief and is a recognised disorder in its own right. Normalising it here delays effective treatment for a woman who has already waited sixteen months. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer her to a community bereavement support group as the only measure
options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are valuable alongside treatment, but trials show they do not resolve the established disorder and can reinforce avoidance if the group does not work with it. Generic support is not equivalent to a structured therapy with a defined protocol. (Source: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement)
source_refs: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder is defined by persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased, accompanied by features such as disbelief, identity disruption, emotional numbness, avoidance of reminders and difficulty re engaging with life, causing impairment and lasting beyond twelve months after the death in an adult. The twelve month threshold is deliberately conservative because most bereaved people improve without treatment, and only a minority of around one in ten develop the persistent form. The frequent clinical error is to treat it as a depressive episode, since the phenomenology differs: sadness is focused on the lost person rather than pervasive, self esteem is usually intact, and positive emotion remains accessible in other domains. That distinction matters because antidepressants do not treat the core symptoms whereas targeted psychotherapy does. Risk factors include a sudden or violent death, loss of a child or partner, and a pre existing anxiety or mood disorder.
key_points: The adult threshold is twelve months from the death, not six
Grief is focused on the deceased, whereas depressive anhedonia is pervasive
Preserved self esteem and preserved capacity for pleasure argue against a depressive episode
Avoidance of reminders maintains the disorder and is the main therapeutic target
Antidepressants do not reduce yearning and preoccupation on current evidence
explanation.pearls: Prolonged grief disorder requires the death to have occurred at least twelve months earlier in adults but only six months earlier in children and adolescents, which is a commonly missed distinction when assessing a bereaved young person.

Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement

subtopic_detail: the hypnotic itself as the cause of a fall in an older woman, and how to stop it without simply substituting another sedative
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 78 year old woman two weeks after she fell getting up to the toilet at three in the morning and fractured her left wrist. She has taken zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly for the past four years, started after her husband died.

She says the tablet no longer works as it once did and that she often feels foggy for an hour or two after waking. She lives alone in a single storey home, uses no walking aid, and her postural blood pressure, visual acuity and gait speed have all been checked and were normal. Her vitamin D and calcium are adequate and she is on a bisphosphonate. She has no other sedating medication, drinks no alcohol, and her cognitive screening score is normal. She is frightened of both falling again and of lying awake all night.

data_table.Examination: Left wrist in a cast, timed up and go test 10 seconds, no postural drop, Mini Mental State Examination 29 of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and corrected calcium all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her insomnia?

options.text: Substitute temazepam 10 mg at night as a safer hypnotic alternative
options.rationale: Temazepam carries the same fall, fracture and cognitive risks in older people as the non benzodiazepine hypnotics and appears on the same list of drugs to avoid in this age group, so the substitution changes the molecule without changing the hazard. Swapping between agents in the same class is a common way of appearing to act while leaving the risk in place. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the zopiclone tonight and advise that any rebound will settle
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal after four years of nightly use produces rebound insomnia and anxiety severe enough that most patients restart within days, and withdrawal seizures are described with hypnotics of this class. The direction is right but the rate is unsafe and self defeating. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Taper the zopiclone gradually alongside cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: A planned dose reduction over weeks to months, paired with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, achieves durable cessation in a substantial proportion of long term users and gives her a treatment for the sleep problem rather than only removing the drug. Offering the therapy at the same time as the taper is what makes her able to accept it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add prolonged release melatonin and continue her usual zopiclone dose
options.rationale: Prolonged release melatonin is a reasonable option in people over 55 and is useful as a bridge during a taper, but adding it while the hypnotic continues leaves her on the drug that is most likely to have caused the fall. It is an adjunct to withdrawal, not a reason to defer it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the zopiclone given her normal gait and vision assessments
options.rationale: A normal gait, normal postural blood pressure and normal vision do not neutralise the risk, they leave the sedative as the only modifiable contributor identified, and the fall occurred in the middle of the night when the drug effect is maximal. Continuing is the option that ignores the disconfirming negative workup. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

explanation.summary: Sedative hypnotics roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people, and the risk is present with the non benzodiazepine agents as much as with benzodiazepines despite the marketing distinction between them. A fall at night in someone taking a nightly hypnotic should prompt a medication review before an extensive falls workup, and a negative workup strengthens rather than weakens the case for deprescribing. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia at any age and its benefits outlast those of drug treatment, which is why it is offered as the replacement rather than as an afterthought. Tapering works best when the patient understands that rebound insomnia is expected, time limited and not evidence that the drug was necessary. Australian programs that combine a patient information leaflet with a planned taper achieve cessation rates well above usual care.
key_points: Non benzodiazepine hypnotics carry the same fall and fracture risk as benzodiazepines in older people
A night time fall in a hypnotic user points to the drug before it points to the gait
Switching within the sedative class does not reduce risk
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia outlasts drug treatment and is first line
Warn about expected rebound insomnia so it is not misread as relapse
explanation.pearls: Reduce the hypnotic by about one quarter of the original dose every one to two weeks, and expect rebound insomnia to peak in the first three to five nights after each reduction and settle within one to two weeks.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

subtopic_detail: new self directed hitting and food refusal in a non speaking adult with intellectual disability whose environment has not changed
stem:
You are the registrar in a community disability health service asked to see a 34 year old man with severe intellectual disability who does not use speech. Over the past three weeks he has begun hitting the side of his own head with an open hand, mostly in the evenings, and has become resistant at mealtimes.

His support workers report that his house, staff roster, day program and routine are all unchanged, and that no new medication has been started. He is still drinking his usual fluids and will accept yoghurt and soup, but pushes away the toast and apple he previously ate every day. He has lost 2 kg in three weeks. He is afebrile and his bowels are opening daily. The behaviour support practitioner has asked you to prescribe something to settle him before a functional assessment can be scheduled.
