data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 126/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Resists approach to the face, no external swelling, chest and abdomen unremarkable, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, C reactive protein and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence risperidone at low dose and review the behaviour in two weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing an antipsychotic for behaviour in intellectual disability before a physical cause has been excluded is the central anti pattern in this population and produces sedation, weight gain and a masked underlying illness. It has a place only once medical and environmental causes have been addressed and a behaviour support plan has failed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a functional behaviour assessment and await its recommendations
options.rationale: Functional assessment is a core part of management but is designed to analyse the environmental antecedents and consequences of behaviour, and it will not identify an untreated physical cause. Deferring to it here delays the examination that the pattern of the presentation is pointing toward. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Commence sertraline for a presumed underlying depressive presentation
options.rationale: Depression does present atypically in people who do not use speech and can show as behaviour change and reduced intake, but the selective refusal of hard foods while soft foods are accepted is a mechanical pattern rather than a loss of appetite. An antidepressant would be considered after a physical cause is excluded and the picture remained pervasive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Undertake a systematic physical examination including the mouth and ears
options.rationale: New behaviour in a person who cannot report symptoms is treated as pain or illness until proven otherwise, and the combination of self directed hitting at one site, refusal of foods that require chewing and preserved fluid intake points to an examination of the teeth, jaw and ears. Dental disease and otitis media are among the most frequently missed causes in this group. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start regular paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after one week
options.rationale: A trial of simple analgesia is a defensible step when pain is suspected but no source is found, and here the examination has not yet been done, so treating blindly risks partially masking a treatable infection. Analgesia belongs alongside a diagnosis rather than instead of looking for one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Diagnostic overshadowing is the tendency to attribute new symptoms in a person with intellectual disability to the disability itself rather than to an independent illness, and it is one of the main drivers of avoidable deaths in this population. People who do not use speech communicate pain through behaviour, so a change in behaviour carries the same weight as a new symptom would in anyone else. The commonest missed causes are dental disease, constipation, gastro oesophageal reflux, urinary tract infection, otitis media, fracture and epilepsy related phenomena. The pattern of the behaviour often localises the problem: hitting one side of the head, refusing foods that need chewing, or a new stoop while transferring each point somewhere. Australian practice standards require that physical causes be excluded and that psychotropic medication for behaviour be time limited with a planned review, because this group is heavily over prescribed antipsychotics.
key_points: Treat new behaviour in a non speaking adult as pain or illness until excluded
Selective refusal of hard foods with preserved fluids is a mechanical pattern, not anorexia
Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude dental abscess or dental caries
Functional behaviour assessment analyses environment and will not find a physical cause
Antipsychotics prescribed for behaviour need an explicit indication, a target and a review date
explanation.pearls: An unchanged environment makes an environmental trigger much less likely and shifts the odds decisively toward a physical cause, which is why asking about roster, housemate and routine changes is part of the medical assessment rather than the behavioural one.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: recurrent winter depressive episodes with oversleeping and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a high latitude Australian city
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman in Hobart in mid July. For the third consecutive year she has become flat, unmotivated and tearful from about May onward.

She sleeps ten to eleven hours and still wakes unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet food, and has gained 5 kg since April. She finds it hardest in the first hours of the day. Each of the two previous episodes lifted completely in September without treatment and she was fully well through summer, working and socialising normally. She has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending. Her thyroid function, ferritin and vitamin D have been checked this month and are normal, and she has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Slowed but reactive, no psychomotor retardation on formal testing, weight 74 kg
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, ferritin, vitamin D and full blood count all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg each morning and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is an effective treatment for this pattern of depression and is a legitimate alternative, but it is not preferred ahead of a treatment with an equivalent effect size, a faster onset and no systemic adverse effects. It becomes the choice if the first line treatment is declined, poorly tolerated or ineffective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe high dose colecalciferol weekly and reassess her mood in a month
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency is common at this latitude in winter and worth correcting when present, but hers has been measured this month and is normal, so supplementation has no target. Trials of vitamin D for depression have not shown benefit in people who are already replete. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange bright light therapy for thirty minutes soon after waking each day
options.rationale: Daily morning exposure to a 10 000 lux light box is the first line treatment for a depressive episode with a seasonal pattern, with response rates comparable to antidepressants and a typical onset within one to two weeks. Morning timing is the active ingredient because it advances the delayed circadian phase that underlies the oversleeping and morning worsening. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start agomelatine at night with liver function testing before and during
options.rationale: Agomelatine acts on melatonergic receptors and has a rational circadian mechanism, but it is a later line agent in Australian practice and requires liver function monitoring before treatment and at intervals through the first five months. There is no reason to accept that monitoring burden ahead of a non pharmacological first line option. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Begin lithium augmentation given the recurrent and periodic course she has
options.rationale: A periodic recurrent course raises the question of bipolarity, but she has never had a hypomanic or manic period and a seasonal unipolar pattern is not itself an indication for a mood stabiliser. Lithium augmentation is a strategy for treatment resistant depression, and she has had no treatment yet. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive disorder when episodes begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years, with full remission in between and with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non seasonal ones. The winter pattern characteristically shows atypical or reversed neurovegetative features, meaning hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain, which is the opposite of the classic melancholic picture. Prevalence rises with latitude, so the pattern is more often seen in Tasmania and southern Victoria than in Queensland. The differential includes hypothyroidism, iron deficiency and vitamin D deficiency, all of which are more prevalent in winter and all of which should be measured before the diagnosis is settled. Preventive light therapy started before the usual month of onset is an option for people with a highly predictable pattern.
key_points: Two consecutive years of seasonal onset and remission are required for the specifier
Winter pattern episodes typically show hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving rather than insomnia and weight loss
Bright light at 10 000 lux for about 30 minutes shortly after waking is first line
Check thyroid function, ferritin and vitamin D before settling on the diagnosis
Screen for a history of hypomania before treating any highly recurrent depression
explanation.pearls: Light therapy works only if the eyes receive the light, so the box sits at about an arm's length in the upper visual field while the person reads or eats breakfast, and response is usually apparent within one to two weeks rather than the four to six expected of an antidepressant.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: choosing between magnetic stimulation and electroconvulsive therapy after two failed antidepressant trials in a patient who is eating and not suicidal
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 45 year old plumber with a current major depressive episode of fourteen months. He completed twelve weeks of escitalopram 20 mg daily and then ten weeks of venlafaxine 225 mg daily, both taken as prescribed, with no meaningful change.

He has also had sixteen sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He is eating and drinking normally, has lost no weight, and continues to work three days a week although he says he is going through the motions. He denies any intent to end his life and has made no plans. He holds no delusional beliefs about guilt, illness or poverty, and there is no stupor, mutism or waxy flexibility. He has never had a seizure and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Reduced spontaneous speech, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
options.rationale: Remission rates fall substantially with each successive antidepressant switch, and after two adequate trials the yield from a third is low enough that guidelines move to augmentation or a neurostimulation treatment. A further switch would postpone an effective option by another three months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an urgent course of electroconvulsive therapy under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective treatment available and is the right choice for depression with psychotic features, catatonia, food and fluid refusal or high imminent suicide risk, none of which is present. Choosing it here means accepting general anaesthesia and cognitive adverse effects when a less burdensome option has not been tried. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
options.rationale: This is the treatment positioned for a moderate depressive episode that has failed two adequate antidepressant trials in a patient who is physically well and not at imminent risk, and in Australia it attracts a Medicare rebate at exactly this point in the sequence. It is given awake without anaesthesia and does not carry the cognitive burden of the seizure based treatment. (Source: Medicare Benefits Schedule Australia)

options.text: Augment the venlafaxine with lithium and monitor levels and renal function
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is an evidence based strategy at this stage and is a genuine competitor, but it requires ongoing level monitoring, renal and thyroid surveillance, and carries a narrow therapeutic index in a man who works with machinery and tools. It remains a reasonable option if the neurostimulation course does not achieve remission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a course of intravenous ketamine infusions in a day unit setting
options.rationale: Ketamine and esketamine produce rapid reductions in depressive symptoms and are most useful where speed matters, such as acute suicidality, which is not the situation here, and access in Australia is limited and largely unsubsidised. Its antidepressant effect also wanes within days to weeks without repeated dosing. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Treatment resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two antidepressants given at an adequate dose for an adequate duration with confirmed adherence, and establishing that those two trials really were adequate is the first task rather than a formality. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation delivers focal magnetic pulses to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex over a course of around twenty to thirty sessions on consecutive weekdays, without anaesthesia and without inducing a seizure. Australian Medicare subsidy became available in 2021 for an initial course in adults with a diagnosed major depressive episode who have failed two adequate trials, which makes the two trial threshold a practical as well as a clinical cut off. Electroconvulsive therapy remains more effective overall and stays the treatment of choice where the illness is life threatening or psychotic. Ordering these options wrongly either exposes a well patient to anaesthesia or leaves a severely ill one waiting weeks for a slower treatment.
key_points: Confirm dose adequacy, duration and adherence before labelling a trial as failed
Two adequate failed trials is the Australian threshold for subsidised magnetic stimulation
Psychosis, catatonia, food refusal or imminent suicide risk move the choice to electroconvulsive therapy
Magnetic stimulation is given awake, on consecutive weekdays, over four to six weeks
Lithium augmentation remains a valid alternative at the same point in the sequence
explanation.pearls: The seizure threshold matters in opposite directions for the two treatments: electroconvulsive therapy deliberately induces a seizure, whereas an inadvertent seizure is the principal serious adverse event of magnetic stimulation, so concurrent bupropion, tramadol or clozapine must be identified before a course begins.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: repugnant intrusive images of harming a newborn with preserved insight and checking behaviour, seven weeks after birth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman at her baby's seven week check. She asks to speak to you alone and then, with great difficulty, tells you that pictures keep coming into her mind of the baby slipping from her arms on the stairs and of a knife.

She describes the images as horrible and says they make her feel sick. She has started carrying the baby only on the ground floor, has moved the kitchen knives to a high cupboard, and checks the baby's breathing eight or nine times a night. She says she would never do any of it and that she cannot understand why her mind produces it. She is sleeping when the baby sleeps, is feeding the baby well and is delighted by him when he smiles. She is fully oriented, hears nothing others cannot hear, and holds no beliefs that the baby is abnormal or in danger from others.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and ashamed, fully oriented, no perceptual abnormality, warm and attuned interaction with the infant
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, full blood count and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for further observation
options.rationale: Admission is indicated for postpartum psychosis or for severe depression with impaired capacity to care for the infant, and the discriminating features of psychosis are absent: she is oriented, has no perceptual disturbance and holds no delusional beliefs about the baby. Hospitalising an egodystonic obsessional presentation amplifies the shame that already delayed her disclosure. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Notify child protection services and arrange supervised contact meanwhile
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm that are unwanted and repugnant to the mother carry no increased risk of harm to the infant, and the risk in this presentation runs the other way, toward mothers concealing symptoms because they fear exactly this response. Reporting would be warranted if the thoughts were ego syntonic or accompanied by delusional beliefs about the child. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Commence olanzapine at night and review her in the surgery within a week
options.rationale: An antipsychotic treats the psychotic presentation this is being mistaken for and does nothing for obsessional symptoms, while adding sedation to a woman caring for a newborn overnight. The distinction that determines the drug class is whether the thoughts are recognised as the mind's own product, which she states clearly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention
options.rationale: Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder responds to the same therapy as at other times, targeting the avoidance of the stairs and knives and the repeated checking that maintain the cycle, and explaining the benign nature of intrusive thoughts is itself therapeutic. Normalising the phenomenon while treating the compulsions is what allows her to resume ordinary care of her baby. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Reassure her that these thoughts are common and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm genuinely do occur in a large majority of new parents and saying so is an important part of the consultation, but she has crossed from a normal phenomenon into a disorder because avoidance and checking are now restricting her behaviour. Reassurance without treatment leaves the compulsions to entrench. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

explanation.summary: Unwanted intrusive thoughts of harm coming to an infant are reported by the large majority of new mothers and fathers and are not in themselves pathological, which is why the threshold for disorder rests on distress, avoidance and compulsive behaviour rather than on the content of the thought. Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder affects a few per cent of postpartum women and characteristically centres on contamination, checking and harm themes involving the baby. The critical safety distinction is between egodystonic obsessions, which the mother experiences as alien and repugnant and which carry no increased risk to the infant, and the ego syntonic thoughts of postpartum psychosis, which arise within a delusional framework and do carry serious risk. Getting this wrong in either direction is harmful: an unnecessary child protection referral drives concealment, while missing psychosis can be fatal. Women frequently take weeks to disclose these symptoms, so the disclosure itself should be met with normalisation before assessment continues.
key_points: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are alien and repugnant and do not predict harm to the infant
Postpartum psychosis is distinguished by delusions, perceptual disturbance, disorientation or confusion
Avoidance and checking behaviour are what convert a normal intrusive thought into a disorder
Exposure and response prevention is the treatment, not an antipsychotic
Punitive responses to disclosure drive concealment in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred serotonergic option if medication is added for perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder in a breastfeeding mother, because relative infant dose is low, and obsessive compulsive disorder needs the higher end of the dose range rather than the usual antidepressant dose.

subtopic_detail: a primigravida with panic level dread of giving birth requesting an elective caesarean at twenty four weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 32 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 24 weeks. She asks you to write to the hospital requesting a caesarean section.

When you ask what worries her she becomes breathless and tearful, and describes lying awake imagining tearing and bleeding. She has left two antenatal classes early, cannot watch a birth scene on television, and has been avoiding her sister who is also pregnant. This fear has been present since her teens and long predates this pregnancy. She has had no previous births and no gynaecological surgery or assault. The pregnancy itself is progressing normally with a cephalic presentation, normal growth and no medical complications. She has a supportive partner and is otherwise functioning well at work.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates, blood pressure 112/68, distressed when discussing labour
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal screening including morphology scan all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Write supporting an elective caesarean section to be booked at 39 weeks
options.rationale: Surgery may ultimately be the agreed plan, but booking it before the fear has been assessed and treated leaves the anxiety disorder untreated and it commonly resurfaces as severe postnatal anxiety or fear of a future pregnancy. Most women whose fear is treated no longer request caesarean by the time they reach term. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Commence sertraline now and review her symptoms again in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication has a place in severe perinatal anxiety, but a specific and treatable phobia of childbirth responds to targeted psychological work and drug treatment is not the first move for a woman who is functioning well otherwise. It would be considered if therapy were insufficient or a comorbid depressive episode emerged. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Reassure her that most first births are uncomplicated and review at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Statistical reassurance does not shift a phobic fear and often increases the sense of not being believed, which is why women with this condition frequently disengage from antenatal care. The avoidance of classes and of her pregnant sister shows the fear is already driving behaviour. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Refer to the obstetric anaesthetist to plan early epidural analgesia in labour
options.rationale: An anaesthetic plan is a valuable component of a birth plan for a frightened woman and may well follow, but it addresses pain rather than the phobic anxiety, and her fear centres on injury and loss of control rather than on pain alone. It belongs within a broader plan rather than as the first response. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer to perinatal mental health for therapy directed at her fear of birth
options.rationale: Structured psychological treatment for fear of childbirth, combining cognitive work and graded exposure with a continuity midwife relationship, reduces fear and reduces caesarean requests, and it is the recommended first response to this presentation. Referring now at 24 weeks leaves time for a course to be completed before term. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

explanation.summary: Severe fear of childbirth affects a small but significant proportion of pregnant women and is described as primary when it predates any birth experience and secondary when it follows a traumatic birth, the distinction mattering because the secondary form often carries post traumatic symptoms requiring trauma focused treatment. The fear is phobic in quality, with avoidance, anticipatory dread and autonomic arousal, and it is distinct from ordinary apprehension about labour. Untreated, it is associated with disengagement from antenatal care, requests for caesarean without medical indication, prolonged labour and higher rates of postnatal depression and post traumatic stress. Australian guidance supports listening to the request seriously while treating the underlying anxiety, and a woman who still requests caesarean after adequate counselling and treatment is entitled to have that request considered by a senior obstetrician. Continuity of midwifery carer is one of the few structural interventions shown to reduce fear and intervention rates.
key_points: Fear predating any birth experience is the primary form and is phobic in quality
Avoidance behaviour distinguishes a phobia from ordinary apprehension
Treat the fear before settling the mode of birth, not the other way round
Untreated fear of childbirth predicts postnatal depression and post traumatic symptoms
A persisting request after adequate treatment is escalated to a senior obstetrician rather than dismissed
explanation.pearls: Continuity of midwifery carer, meaning the same known midwife through pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period, reduces both fear of childbirth scores and the rate of instrumental birth, and is worth arranging at the same time as the psychological referral.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: documented heavy prenatal alcohol exposure with impairment across several neurodevelopmental domains but no facial features
stem:
You are the registrar in a child development clinic seeing a 7 year old boy who has lived with his grandmother since he was two. Child protection records that his mother drank heavily throughout the pregnancy are available and his grandmother confirms them.

His teacher describes him as unable to stay on task, out of his seat, and two years behind in numeracy despite intensive support. His grandmother says he will walk off with anyone who speaks kindly to him, cannot be trusted near the road, and cannot manage a morning routine even with a picture chart. He is warm, makes good eye contact and has age appropriate conversational language. His face is unremarkable, with normal philtrum, upper lip and palpebral fissures. His head circumference is on the second centile and his height and weight are on the twenty fifth.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference second centile, no dysmorphic facial features, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Hearing and vision screening normal, chromosomal microarray previously reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate for his inattention and overactivity
options.rationale: Stimulants are used in this population and often help the attention component, but starting one now treats a single domain and closes off the broader assessment that determines his schooling, his disability funding and his safety supervision. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is also frequently the label these children receive instead of the underlying diagnosis rather than alongside it. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder

options.text: Refer for a diagnostic assessment for autism spectrum disorder in the first instance
options.rationale: His warmth, eye contact and conversational language argue against autism, and the indiscriminate friendliness described here reflects impaired social judgement rather than a social communication deficit. Autism can coexist and would be examined within the broader assessment rather than ahead of it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Repeat the chromosomal microarray and add fragile X testing before proceeding
options.rationale: A microarray that was normal does not need repeating in the absence of new dysmorphic or regressive features, and fragile X typically presents with different features including large ears, macroorchidism and gaze aversion. Genetic testing addresses a differential that the documented exposure history has already made much less likely. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange school based behaviour support and review his progress in six months
options.rationale: Classroom supports are necessary and should continue, but two years of intensive support have not shifted his numeracy and a support plan built without knowing the underlying profile tends to target compliance rather than the executive and adaptive deficits driving it. Delay also postpones access to funded supports. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment across all domains
options.rationale: Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure with functional difficulties in attention, academic achievement, adaptive behaviour and social judgement requires formal assessment of the defined neurodevelopmental domains by a multidisciplinary team, which is the only way the diagnosis can be made. The absence of facial features does not exclude the condition and in fact describes the majority of affected children. (Source: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder)
source_refs: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder

explanation.summary: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is diagnosed in Australia using a national diagnostic guide that requires confirmed or unknown prenatal alcohol exposure together with severe impairment in at least three of ten specified neurodevelopmental domains, assessed by a multidisciplinary team. The three sentinel facial features of short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum and thin upper lip are present in only a minority of affected children, so a normal face is entirely compatible with the diagnosis and is one of the commonest reasons it is missed. Microcephaly, when present, is a marker of central nervous system structural abnormality and contributes to the assessment. Children are frequently labelled with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder in sequence, each capturing a fragment of the picture, which delays appropriate educational and disability support. Making the diagnosis changes management because it reframes behaviour as a brain based difficulty with cause and effect and adaptive function rather than as wilful non compliance.
key_points: Most affected children have no facial features at all
Diagnosis requires severe impairment in at least three of ten neurodevelopmental domains
Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure plus multidomain impairment mandates formal assessment
Indiscriminate friendliness and poor road safety reflect impaired social judgement and adaptive function
Sequential behavioural labels often mask the underlying diagnosis for years
explanation.pearls: Impairment must be severe, meaning at or below the third centile or two standard deviations below the mean, in three or more domains, which is why informal impressions of difficulty are not sufficient and standardised testing by the team is required.

sources.label: Australian Guide to the Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: a second relapse that followed stopping oral medication, and whether that history makes the illness treatment resistant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning discharge for a 26 year old man admitted three weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. This is his second admission in eighteen months.

On both occasions his housemate and his sister describe him as stopping his aripiprazole tablets several weeks before becoming unwell again, and on both occasions symptoms resolved within two to three weeks of restarting the same drug at the same dose. He is now free of hallucinations and no longer holds the persecutory belief. He says tablets remind him every morning that he is ill, and that he wants above all not to come back into hospital. He uses no substances and a urine drug screen on admission was negative. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms and his weight and metabolic screen are unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no perceptual abnormality, no thought disorder, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, fasting lipids and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is most likely to reduce his risk of a further relapse?

options.text: Increase the oral aripiprazole dose and continue it at the higher dose
options.rationale: The illness responded fully to the current dose on both occasions, so the problem is not insufficient dose but the period during which no drug was taken at all. Raising the dose adds adverse effect risk without changing the behaviour that produced the relapses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Transition to a long acting injectable antipsychotic before he is discharged
options.rationale: Where relapse is driven by lapses in taking oral medication rather than by lack of efficacy, a depot preparation removes the daily decision and makes any future lapse visible weeks before symptoms return. Starting it in hospital lets tolerability be observed and takes advantage of his own stated priority of avoiding readmission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence clozapine with the required haematological monitoring program
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant illness, defined as failure of two adequate trials of different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration with confirmed adherence, and the adherence criterion is exactly what is not met here. Calling relapse after cessation treatment resistance is the classic error that leads to clozapine being started inappropriately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange a weekly dose administration aid with pharmacy supervised dosing
options.rationale: A dose administration aid helps when the difficulty is forgetting, but he describes a deliberate choice to stop because the tablet is a daily reminder of illness, which a blister pack does not address. It is a useful adjunct in the right patient and the wrong tool for this one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Continue oral treatment and reserve an injectable agent for any third relapse
options.rationale: Each relapse carries a risk of incomplete recovery, loss of housing, work and relationships, and a longer duration of untreated symptoms, so waiting for a third episode has a real cost. Depot treatment was once positioned as a last resort but is now offered early where non adherence is the identified driver. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Relapse in schizophrenia most often follows cessation of antipsychotic medication, and distinguishing non adherence from genuine lack of efficacy determines the entire subsequent treatment pathway. Long acting injectable preparations reduce relapse and readmission compared with oral treatment in patients with a history of poor adherence, and the modern position is to offer them early rather than after repeated episodes. The practical advantage beyond the pharmacokinetics is that a missed depot appointment is a visible event that triggers outreach weeks before symptoms return, whereas a bottle of tablets left in a cupboard is invisible. Where a patient has already responded well to a particular oral agent, the corresponding depot formulation of the same or a closely related molecule is the logical choice. Clozapine remains reserved for true treatment resistance, and mislabelling non adherence as resistance exposes patients to agranulocytosis risk and an intensive monitoring burden for no benefit.
key_points: Full response to the same drug and dose twice over excludes lack of efficacy
Treatment resistance requires two adequate trials with confirmed adherence
Long acting injectables are offered early where non adherence drives relapse, not as a last resort
A missed depot appointment is a visible early warning that oral treatment cannot provide
Each relapse risks incomplete recovery and loss of social role
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole and paliperidone long acting injections both require an oral or loading overlap at initiation, typically fourteen days of oral cover for aripiprazole, so discharge before that overlap is complete leaves the patient effectively untreated.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: lifelong inattention in a woman referred with anxiety whose symptoms have not moved on an adequate antidepressant trial
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 27 year old graphic designer who was started on sertraline six months ago for anxiety and has taken 100 mg daily for the last four months. She says she feels no different.

She describes her worry as being almost entirely about work: unopened emails, three projects started and none finished, and a recent formal warning for a missed deadline. She loses her keys and wallet most weeks and has been late to every appointment she has made with you. Her mother has kept her old school reports, which from age eight describe a bright girl who drifts off, does not finish her work and needs constant redirection. She sleeps well, her mood is reactive and she has never had a panic attack or a period of avoidance of social situations. She drinks alcohol rarely and uses no other substances.

data_table.Examination: Engaged and articulate, tangential at times, no psychomotor change, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 150 mg daily and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Four months at a therapeutic dose without any change argues that the target is wrong rather than the dose, and her worry is a consequence of missed deadlines and lost possessions rather than free floating apprehension. Escalating would consume several more months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Generalised anxiety disorder requires excessive worry across multiple domains that is difficult to control, whereas her worry is confined to the consequences of disorganisation and would be a proportionate response to a formal warning. Therapy aimed at worry will not address the executive difficulties generating it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate and assess her response over four weeks
options.rationale: A therapeutic trial cannot substitute for a diagnosis because stimulants improve attention in people without the disorder, so a good response proves nothing. Stimulant prescribing in Australia is also restricted by state authority requirements that presuppose a formal diagnosis. (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment given her social difficulties
options.rationale: She describes no difficulty with social communication, no restricted interests and no sensory differences, and her workplace problem is task completion rather than social interaction. Autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder frequently co occur, but nothing here points to the former. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Gather the childhood school reports and refer for a structured ADHD assessment
options.rationale: Diagnosis in adults requires evidence that several symptoms were present before age twelve, and contemporaneous school reports are the strongest collateral available, so securing them before referral makes the assessment possible rather than inconclusive. Her reports already describe the predominantly inattentive pattern that is routinely missed in girls. (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder persists into adulthood in a majority of childhood cases and is substantially under diagnosed in women, who more often show the predominantly inattentive presentation without the disruptive overactivity that prompts referral in boys. Adults typically present with the secondary consequences rather than the core symptoms, most commonly anxiety, low mood, workplace underperformance, relationship strain or substance use, so the diagnosis depends on the clinician asking about lifelong function rather than current distress alone. Australian diagnostic criteria require several inattentive or hyperactive symptoms to have been present before age twelve, symptoms in two or more settings, and clear functional impairment, which makes childhood collateral essential rather than optional. School reports, old assessments and a parent interview carry more weight than adult self report, which is affected by current mood. An antidepressant that produces no change at an adequate dose in a person whose anxiety is entirely consequence driven is an important clue that the primary diagnosis has been missed.
key_points: Several symptoms must be documented before age twelve for an adult diagnosis
Girls and women more often show the inattentive presentation and are missed
Anxiety and low mood are frequently secondary to the functional consequences
A response to a stimulant does not establish the diagnosis in anyone
Collateral from childhood outweighs adult self report
explanation.pearls: The inattentive presentation without hyperactivity still requires six or more inattentive symptoms in those under seventeen but only five in those aged seventeen and over, a threshold drop that matters when assessing an adult against their own childhood history.

sources.label: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: an abrupt severe occipital headache with extreme hypertension two hours after aged cheese and cured meat in a patient on an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 52 year old man brought in by his wife from a wedding reception two hours ago. He has taken tranylcypromine for eighteen months for a depressive illness that failed several other treatments.

He developed a sudden pounding headache at the back of his head, followed by a thumping heartbeat, drenching sweat and neck stiffness that he describes as muscles rather than pain on flexion. His wife says he ate a grazing platter of aged cheddar, salami and prosciutto because he had forgotten which foods he was meant to avoid. He is fully alert with no focal neurological signs and no photophobia. A non contrast computed tomography scan of his brain performed on arrival shows no haemorrhage. He takes no other regular medication and used no recreational drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, blood pressure 215/125, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit, fundi show no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic change, troponin and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous phentolamine titrated against the blood pressure response
options.rationale: The crisis is driven by displaced noradrenaline acting on alpha adrenoceptors, and a short acting intravenous alpha blocker reverses that directly and can be titrated in small increments as the tyramine load is cleared. Its brief duration of action is the advantage, because the surge is self limiting and a long acting agent risks overshoot into hypotension. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol given in small increments until the pulse settles
options.rationale: Blocking beta receptors while alpha mediated vasoconstriction is unopposed raises systemic vascular resistance further and can worsen the hypertension, which is the same trap as beta blockade in a catecholamine secreting tumour. A beta blocker may be added only after adequate alpha blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine repeated once if the pressure remains above target
options.rationale: Sublingual short acting dihydropyridine produces an uncontrolled and unpredictable fall in pressure with reflex tachycardia and has caused stroke and myocardial infarction, so it is not used in any hypertensive emergency. An intravenous agent with a predictable dose response is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Oral captopril with hourly blood pressure monitoring in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: An angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor acts on a pathway that is not the one driving this crisis, and the oral route gives neither the speed nor the titratability needed at a pressure of 215 over 125. The mechanism mismatch is the key point rather than the route alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia before any antihypertensive is started
options.rationale: A thunderclap headache with neck symptoms and a normal early scan would ordinarily prompt this, but his stiffness is muscular rather than meningism, there is no photophobia, and the dietary history with a florid adrenergic syndrome supplies a complete alternative explanation. Leaving a pressure of 215 over 125 untreated while performing the procedure is also unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors block the intestinal and hepatic enzyme that normally degrades dietary tyramine, so a tyramine rich meal delivers a large load to the circulation where it acts as an indirect sympathomimetic and displaces noradrenaline from presynaptic vesicles. The resulting surge produces severe hypertension, occipital headache, palpitations, sweating and a stiff neck, typically within minutes to a few hours of the meal. The foods that matter are those in which protein has been aged, fermented or spoiled, principally matured cheeses, cured and fermented meats, soy products, broad bean pods, tap beer and yeast extract spreads, while fresh meat, fresh cheese and bottled beer are safe. The same displacement mechanism makes pseudoephedrine and other indirect sympathomimetics dangerous in these patients. Treatment is a short acting titratable alpha blocker, and the crisis usually resolves within a few hours as the tyramine is cleared.
key_points: Tyramine acts indirectly by displacing noradrenaline, so alpha blockade is the rational antidote
Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade worsens the hypertension
Aged, fermented and spoiled protein foods are the risk, not fresh equivalents
Indirect sympathomimetics such as pseudoephedrine carry the same danger as tyramine
Sublingual nifedipine is not used in any hypertensive emergency
explanation.pearls: The washout required before switching from an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor to a serotonergic antidepressant is fourteen days, because the enzyme must be resynthesised, and this applies in both directions except that fluoxetine needs five weeks before an inhibitor is started.

subtopic_detail: advising parents about episodes of screaming early in the night that the child cannot recall next morning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the parents of a 4 year old boy who have come without him because they are frightened by what happens at night.

They describe that about ninety minutes after he falls asleep he sits up and screams, his eyes are open but he does not seem to see them, he is sweaty with a racing heart, and he pushes them away when they try to comfort him. It lasts around five minutes and then he lies down and sleeps. In the morning he is cheerful and has no memory of it at all. It happens two or three times a week and always in the first part of the night. He started four year old kindergarten six weeks ago and has been going to bed later than usual. He is developing normally, has no daytime symptoms and there is no snoring.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and developmentally appropriate on parental report, no dysmorphic features described, tonsils not enlarged on a recent review, no daytime behavioural concerns reported by kindergarten
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the next three months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress slow wave sleep and are occasionally used for frequent, dangerous or highly disruptive parasomnias in older children after other measures have failed. They are disproportionate for a benign self limiting phenomenon in a preschooler and carry sedation and behavioural risks. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography to characterise the nocturnal episodes
options.rationale: Sleep studies are indicated when the history is atypical, when episodes are stereotyped and very frequent suggesting nocturnal seizures, or when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected as a trigger. This history is entirely typical and there is no snoring or daytime sleepiness. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Advise the parents to wake him fully during each episode and comfort him
options.rationale: Attempting to rouse a child during one of these episodes typically prolongs it and increases agitation and confusion, because he is in deep sleep rather than awake and frightened. The advice is to stay nearby and keep him safe without waking him. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Start an antidepressant to reduce the anxiety underlying the night time distress
options.rationale: Medication for anxiety would be considered where a child had daytime anxiety symptoms or nightmares related to a specific stressor or trauma. He has no daytime symptoms, and the episodes occur in deep sleep rather than arising from dream content. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Reassure the parents, advise on safety, and address his sleep schedule
options.rationale: These episodes arise from incomplete arousal out of slow wave sleep, which is concentrated in the first third of the night, and they resolve spontaneously as the child matures without any treatment. The practical advice is to keep the environment safe, avoid waking him, and correct the sleep deprivation caused by his later bedtime, since insufficient sleep increases slow wave sleep pressure and directly increases episode frequency. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

explanation.summary: Sleep terrors are a disorder of arousal from slow wave sleep and are common in preschool and early school aged children. The features that identify them are timing in the first third of the night, autonomic arousal with sweating and tachycardia, apparent unresponsiveness to comforting, and complete amnesia for the event the following morning. Nightmares are the main differential and differ on every one of those points, occurring in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, with the child fully awakened, consolable and able to describe the dream. Management is reassurance, safety measures such as securing stairs and windows, and attention to sleep deprivation, which is the commonest precipitant because it increases slow wave sleep rebound. Investigation and medication are reserved for atypical, injurious or very frequent episodes.
key_points: Sleep terrors arise from slow wave sleep and occur in the first third of the night.
Complete amnesia for the episode the next morning is characteristic and distinguishes them from nightmares.
Nightmares occur in the second half of the night with full waking, consolability and dream recall.
Sleep deprivation increases slow wave sleep pressure and is the commonest precipitant.
Attempting to wake the child during an episode prolongs and worsens it.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the child remembers the episode in the morning, because complete amnesia with timing early in the night identifies a sleep terror needing only reassurance and an earlier bedtime, whereas vivid recall late in the night points to nightmares and a different conversation entirely.

subtopic_detail: responding to escalating prescribed opioid use for chronic non cancer pain with declining function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47 year old man who has taken sustained release oxycodone for chronic low back pain for five years. He has inherited this prescription from a previous doctor and asks you today for an increase.

He is now on 80 mg of oral morphine equivalent daily, having started on 20 mg. He tells you the pain is no better than when he started and that he has stopped playing golf and has been off work for two years. He says he gets a few hours of relief after each dose and is watching the clock towards the end of the interval. He has run out early twice in the past four months. He drinks no alcohol and uses no illicit drugs, and a urine drug screen shows only his prescribed medication. He has not had a trial of any non pharmacological pain program. His imaging shows degenerative change only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficit in either leg, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, reflexes symmetrical, no saddle anaesthesia, no bladder or bowel disturbance, guarded lumbar movement
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for the prescribed opioid only, lumbar magnetic resonance imaging shows degenerative disc disease with no nerve root compression, liver and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the dose as requested and review his pain scores in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation would be considered where a clear analgesic benefit had been demonstrated and function was improving, which is the opposite of his trajectory over five years. Escalating in the face of declining function and no analgesic gain increases harm without any prospect of benefit. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Cease the opioid abruptly today and manage any withdrawal symptomatically
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after five years of continuous use produces severe withdrawal and commonly drives patients to illicit sources or to other prescribers, which is more dangerous than continued prescribing. Rapid discontinuation in this population is associated with increased overdose and suicide risk. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Negotiate a structured tapering plan with a broader pain management approach
options.rationale: Chronic non cancer pain that has not improved over five years while function has steadily declined indicates that the opioid is not delivering analgesia, and slow tapering at around ten percent of the dose every two to four weeks typically maintains or improves both pain and function. The taper must be paired with active substitutes, meaning a multidisciplinary pain program, graded exercise and psychological therapy, because withdrawing the drug without offering anything in its place is what makes these conversations fail. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Add a benzodiazepine to help with the muscle spasm and his difficulty sleeping
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids markedly increase the risk of respiratory depression and death, and this combination features in a large proportion of opioid related fatalities. They also have no role in chronic low back pain beyond a few days. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Discharge him from the practice and advise him to find another prescriber
options.rationale: Abandonment leaves a dependent patient without care and simply transfers the problem, and it is the response most likely to result in harm. The clinical situation calls for active management of a treatment that is no longer working rather than disengagement. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

explanation.summary: Long term opioid therapy for chronic non cancer pain has weak evidence of sustained analgesic benefit and clear evidence of harm including tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, endocrine suppression and overdose. The markers that this treatment has failed are present here: no reduction in pain over five years, progressive loss of function, clock watching before doses and early prescription exhaustion. Tolerance and opioid induced hyperalgesia both mean that escalating the dose will not restore benefit. The appropriate response is a negotiated, gradual taper, commonly around ten percent of the dose every two to four weeks with slower steps at lower doses, undertaken alongside a multidisciplinary pain approach combining graded activity, psychological therapy and non opioid analgesia. Abrupt cessation and discharge from care both increase the risk of overdose and should be avoided.
key_points: Long term opioids for chronic non cancer pain show weak analgesic benefit with substantial harms.
Loss of function, clock watching and running out early indicate the treatment is failing.
Opioid induced hyperalgesia means dose escalation may worsen rather than relieve pain.
Taper gradually, around ten percent every two to four weeks, with slower steps at lower doses.
Combining opioids with benzodiazepines markedly increases the risk of fatal respiratory depression.
explanation.pearls: Measure function rather than pain scores when reviewing long term opioid therapy, because a patient who has stopped working and stopped exercising while his pain is unchanged has already demonstrated that the drug is not working, and that is the argument for a taper rather than an increase.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence
Faculty of Pain Medicine, Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists

subtopic_detail: responding to a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval in an older patient whose antidepressant dose exceeds the age adjusted maximum
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 71 year old woman admitted with a fractured wrist after a fall at home. She has taken citalopram 40 mg daily for two years for recurrent major depression and her mood has been stable.

The orthopaedic team have sent an electrocardiogram because she described two episodes of feeling faint in the week before the fall. She takes no other regular medication apart from a thiazide diuretic for hypertension and a proton pump inhibitor. She has had no chest pain and no palpitations. Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and her magnesium is 0.62 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, and a tracing from three years ago showed a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 64/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no tremor or clonus, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Corrected QT interval 512 ms against 430 ms three years ago, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue citalopram at 40 mg and repeat the electrocardiogram in three months
options.rationale: Continuing unchanged would be defensible if the interval were mildly prolonged and stable with no symptoms, and a corrected QT of 512 ms with presyncope sits in the range where torsades de pointes becomes a real risk. Her dose also exceeds the maximum recommended above 65 years, so the exposure driving the prolongation is itself inappropriate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to amitriptyline at a low dose, which also treats her neuropathic pain
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium and potassium channels and prolong the QT interval more than most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so this would worsen the specific problem. They also carry anticholinergic and orthostatic effects that increase falls risk in an older woman who has just fallen. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop all antidepressant treatment permanently and monitor her mood in clinic
options.rationale: Complete withdrawal would expose a woman with recurrent major depression to a high risk of relapse, and the problem is drug and dose specific rather than a contraindication to the whole class. Effective alternatives with minimal effect on the QT interval exist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Halve the citalopram to 20 mg and take no other action on the abnormal results
options.rationale: Reducing to 20 mg does bring the dose to the maximum recommended above 65 years and is a necessary part of the answer, but it leaves the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia untreated. Those electrolyte abnormalities are independently arrhythmogenic and are contributing substantially to an interval of 512 ms. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Correct the electrolytes, cease citalopram and change to a safer antidepressant
options.rationale: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms with presyncope requires the offending drug to be withdrawn rather than reduced, and citalopram at 40 mg exceeds the 20 mg maximum recommended above 65 years because prolongation is dose dependent. Replacing potassium and magnesium is equally important since both deficits independently prolong repolarisation, and sertraline or mirtazapine can then continue her treatment with minimal effect on the interval. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Citalopram and its enantiomer escitalopram prolong the QT interval in a dose dependent way, which is why the maximum recommended citalopram dose falls to 20 mg daily above 65 years and in hepatic impairment or with interacting drugs. This woman has been taking twice that maximum. Her thiazide has produced hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and both independently prolong repolarisation, so the abnormal interval has several correctable contributors acting together. A corrected QT above 500 ms with presyncope is the threshold at which the culprit drug is ceased rather than merely reduced. Sertraline and mirtazapine have minimal effect on the interval and are appropriate substitutes, while tricyclics would make matters worse.
key_points: Citalopram prolongs the QT interval dose dependently, with a maximum of 20 mg daily above 65 years.
Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia each independently prolong the QT interval.
A corrected QT above 500 ms or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline is the threshold for ceasing the culprit drug.
Tricyclic antidepressants prolong the QT interval more than most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Sertraline and mirtazapine have minimal effect on cardiac repolarisation and are suitable alternatives.
explanation.pearls: Check the citalopram dose against age whenever you see a prolonged QT interval, because 40 mg is twice the recommended maximum above 65 years, and always replace potassium and magnesium at the same time since a thiazide induced deficit commonly contributes more to the interval than the antidepressant does.

subtopic_detail: recognising sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter in a young man referred with suspected depression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old university student referred by his mother because he sleeps all the time and she is worried he is depressed.

He describes falling asleep in lectures and once while sitting on a bus, and says brief naps leave him refreshed for an hour or two. He is not sad, is looking forward to the summer, has been going out with friends and has not lost interest in his hobbies. His appetite and weight are unchanged and he denies any thoughts of self harm. He mentions that when his friends make him laugh hard his knees buckle and his jaw goes slack for a few seconds while he stays fully aware, and that he sometimes wakes unable to move for half a minute and sees a figure in the doorway that is not there.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, normal power and reflexes, no ptosis, no fatigable weakness, body mass index 24 kg/m2, mood euthymic with reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and fasting glucose all within normal limits, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 19 out of 24

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder presenting with hypersomnia and low motivation
options.rationale: Atypical depression does feature hypersomnia and leaden heaviness of the limbs, and it requires low mood or loss of interest, both of which are absent in a young man who is socialising, enjoying his hobbies and looking forward to the summer. Depressive hypersomnia also leaves patients unrefreshed rather than restored by a short nap. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Narcolepsy with cataplexy caused by loss of hypocretin signalling
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved awareness is cataplexy, which is close to specific for this condition and reflects intrusion of the muscle atonia of rapid eye movement sleep into wakefulness. Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are further manifestations of the same intrusion, and refreshing short naps distinguish this from the unrefreshing sleep of depression or sleep apnoea. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnoea producing fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea is an important cause of daytime sleepiness and characteristically occurs with obesity, snoring and witnessed apnoeas, none of which is described in a young man with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2. It also does not produce emotion triggered loss of tone or refreshing naps. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Focal epilepsy with atonic seizures and associated postictal confusion
options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt loss of tone and would be a reasonable consideration, but they impair awareness and are followed by confusion, whereas he remains fully alert throughout and recovers instantly. Reliable triggering by laughter rather than by anything else also fits emotional rather than epileptic physiology. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Delayed sleep phase disorder with chronic insufficient sleep on weeknights
options.rationale: Circadian phase delay is very common in this age group and produces sleepiness through simple sleep restriction, with normal sleep quality and duration when the person is allowed to choose their own hours. It offers no explanation for cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hallucinations at sleep onset. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood and is frequently misattributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits for years before diagnosis. The tetrad is excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, and the last three all represent intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep phenomena into wakefulness. Cataplexy, meaning sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved consciousness, is the feature that makes the diagnosis and separates it from atonic seizures and syncope. The mechanism in narcolepsy with cataplexy is loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, probably autoimmune. Diagnosis is confirmed by polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test.
key_points: Cataplexy is bilateral loss of tone triggered by emotion with fully preserved awareness and no postictal phase.
Short naps are refreshing in narcolepsy and unrefreshing in depression and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations reflect intrusion of rapid eye movement phenomena into wakefulness.
Loss of hypothalamic hypocretin neurons underlies narcolepsy with cataplexy.
Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day.
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether anything happens to the muscles when the patient laughs, because cataplexy is close to diagnostic of narcolepsy and patients rarely volunteer it, having usually interpreted their buckling knees as clumsiness rather than as a neurological symptom.

subtopic_detail: balancing the risk of refeeding against the risk of continued underfeeding in a severely malnourished adolescent
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 15 year old girl with anorexia nervosa who has lost 16 kg over eight months. She is on day two of admission to a specialist adolescent unit with continuous cardiac monitoring.

She was started on a nutrition plan yesterday and her intake is being supervised. Overnight her heart rate fell to 38 beats per minute while asleep and she has had one episode of dizziness on standing. Her weight for height is 68 percent of expected. She has no oedema and no confusion. Her phosphate was 1.10 mmol/L on admission and is 0.72 mmol/L this morning, her magnesium has fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L, and her potassium has fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms and no arrhythmia. The dietitian asks whether the energy intake should be held or reduced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38/min asleep and 46/min awake, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying and 74/46 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Emaciated with lanugo hair, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds, no peripheral or sacral oedema, no crackles, Glasgow coma scale 15, no confusion or weakness
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate fallen from 1.10 to 0.72 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), magnesium fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), corrected QT interval 440 ms, glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), thiamine given on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her nutrition?

options.text: Halve the energy intake until the electrolytes return to the normal range
options.rationale: Reducing intake in response to falling electrolytes is the traditional cautious approach and is now recognised to cause harm, because prolonged underfeeding produces its own syndrome of continued weight loss, worsening bradycardia and delayed recovery. The falling electrolytes are a predictable and treatable consequence of feeding rather than a signal to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Cease enteral intake entirely and commence parenteral nutrition instead
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition carries line sepsis and thrombosis risks and does not avoid refeeding syndrome, which is driven by the metabolic shift from catabolism to carbohydrate use regardless of the route. The gut is working and should be used. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Continue the current intake unchanged and recheck the electrolytes in 48 hours
options.rationale: Continuing to feed is correct, and a 48 hour monitoring interval is far too long during the first week when electrolytes shift rapidly and can fall to dangerous levels within a day. Daily or more frequent measurement is required while the risk period lasts. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Continue increasing energy intake with electrolyte replacement and daily monitoring
options.rationale: Falling phosphate, magnesium and potassium in the first days of feeding is the expected biochemical signature of refeeding, caused by an insulin driven intracellular shift, and it is corrected by replacing the electrolytes rather than by withdrawing the nutrition that is treating her starvation. Australian paediatric practice has moved away from prolonged low energy protocols because underfeeding prolongs medical instability, so intake continues to advance under continuous cardiac monitoring with at least daily electrolytes and prompt replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Maintain intake and give a fluid bolus to correct her postural blood pressure drop
options.rationale: Volume loading a severely malnourished adolescent risks precipitating cardiac failure, because the myocardium is atrophied and cannot handle a sudden preload increase, and fluid overload is a recognised component of refeeding syndrome. Her postural drop reflects starvation related cardiovascular adaptation and improves with nutrition rather than with boluses. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is reintroduced to a starved patient and insulin release drives phosphate, magnesium and potassium into cells alongside a shift from fat to carbohydrate metabolism, producing the falling electrolytes seen here. Thiamine is consumed rapidly in this process and must be given before or with the first feeds. The historical response was to feed very slowly, but that approach is now recognised to cause underfeeding syndrome, in which continued weight loss and persistent bradycardia prolong medical instability and lengthen admission, and Australian paediatric practice has moved towards advancing intake while replacing electrolytes aggressively. The decisive judgement in this case is that the falling electrolytes are an expected and treatable consequence of appropriate treatment rather than evidence that the treatment is wrong. Continuous cardiac monitoring, at least daily electrolytes and prompt replacement make that approach safe, and fluid boluses are avoided because the atrophied myocardium tolerates sudden preload poorly.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium is the mechanism of refeeding syndrome.
Thiamine must be given before or alongside the first feeds because it is consumed rapidly during refeeding.
Prolonged low energy protocols cause underfeeding syndrome and prolong medical instability.
Electrolytes require at least daily measurement with prompt replacement during the first week.
Fluid boluses risk cardiac failure because the myocardium is atrophied in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: Replace the electrolytes and keep feeding rather than cutting the calories when phosphate falls in the first days of refeeding, because the fall is the expected consequence of effective treatment and prolonged underfeeding causes its own syndrome of persistent bradycardia and delayed recovery.

sources.label: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders
