subtopic_detail: continuing or withholding an effective antipsychotic when a stable woman with schizophrenia conceives
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 30 year old woman with schizophrenia who has been well for three years on olanzapine 10 mg at night. She works part time, lives with her partner and has had no admission since her diagnosis at twenty four.

She tells you she is seven weeks pregnant and that the pregnancy is wanted and planned. She has read online that antipsychotics harm babies and has already missed four doses this week because she is frightened. She has no current psychotic symptoms, her sleep is normal and her insight is good. Her two previous relapses both followed her stopping medication, and the second involved a period of significant self neglect requiring inpatient care. Her booking bloods are normal and her body mass index is 26 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows euthymic mood, no hallucinations or delusions, no thought disorder, good insight, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin consistent with seven weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current antipsychotic with added fetal growth surveillance
options.rationale: The risk of relapse on stopping an effective antipsychotic is high and is itself harmful in pregnancy through self neglect, poor antenatal attendance and substance use, whereas olanzapine has not been shown to be a major teratogen. Continuing the agent that has kept her well for three years is therefore the safer course, with growth scans because of the association with large for gestational age infants and early gestational diabetes screening because of the metabolic profile. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic for the first trimester and restart it after organogenesis
options.rationale: Withdrawal through the first trimester is intuitively appealing and is the period of highest relapse risk following cessation, and by the time symptoms return the exposure has already occurred if it was going to. This approach reliably produces relapse without avoiding meaningful risk. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Switch her to a first generation antipsychotic with longer established safety data
options.rationale: Older agents do have a longer record of use in pregnancy, which is a genuine argument, and switching a woman who is stable risks destabilising her for a benefit that the comparative data do not support. Any switch also introduces a period of dual or inadequate cover at the least forgiving time. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Halve the dose for the remainder of the pregnancy to reduce fetal exposure
options.rationale: Dose reduction looks like a compromise and delivers the worst of both positions, since it leaves the fetus exposed while dropping the mother below the concentration that has maintained her remission. Increased volume of distribution and hepatic metabolism in pregnancy mean doses often need to rise rather than fall. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Replace the antipsychotic with regular psychological therapy for the pregnancy
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct in schizophrenia and improves function and adherence, and it does not substitute for antipsychotic medication in preventing relapse of a psychotic illness. Offering it as a replacement would leave her unprotected during a recognised period of vulnerability. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: The instinct to stop psychotropic medication in pregnancy usually does more harm than good in established psychotic illness, because relapse carries substantial risks to both mother and fetus through self neglect, disengagement from antenatal care, substance use and, at the extreme, suicide. Olanzapine and the other second generation antipsychotics have not been shown to be major teratogens, so the balance favours continuing an agent that has maintained three years of remission. Specific monitoring is added rather than the drug being changed: growth scans because of the association with large for gestational age infants, and early screening for gestational diabetes given the metabolic profile. Abrupt cessation, dose halving and switching agents each risk destabilising a well woman without a demonstrated safety gain. She also needs a plan for the postnatal period, which carries the highest relapse risk of all.
key_points: Relapse of psychotic illness in pregnancy carries substantial risk to mother and fetus.
Second generation antipsychotics have not been shown to be major teratogens.
Switching or reducing an effective agent in pregnancy risks relapse without a demonstrated safety benefit.
Olanzapine is associated with large for gestational age infants and gestational diabetes, warranting added monitoring.
The postnatal period carries the highest relapse risk and requires a documented plan made antenatally.
explanation.pearls: Address the fear rather than the prescription when a pregnant woman with schizophrenia starts missing doses, because relapse is the largest modifiable risk to her pregnancy and stopping through the first trimester exposes the fetus during organogenesis anyway while guaranteeing she loses her remission.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

subtopic_detail: classifying recurrent disproportionate aggression that resolves completely between episodes in an otherwise law abiding adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29 year old man referred by his general practitioner after he punched a hole in a plasterboard wall when his internet connection dropped during a video call.

He describes roughly fortnightly episodes over the past three years in which he becomes enraged within seconds over something he later agrees was trivial, shouts, and sometimes throws or breaks an object. The episodes last under twenty minutes and he is remorseful and embarrassed afterwards. Between episodes his mood is stable and he is described by his partner as gentle. He has never been arrested, does not deceive people or take their belongings, has never harmed an animal, and had no behavioural difficulties at school. He drinks two beers on Fridays and uses no other substances. He has no head injury, no seizures and no memory gaps around the episodes.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal between episodes with euthymic mood, reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and urine drug screen all within normal limits, electroencephalogram reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with a predominantly aggressive presentation
options.rationale: This diagnosis requires a pervasive pattern of disregard for the rights of others since age fifteen, including deceitfulness, unlawful behaviour and absent remorse, with evidence of conduct disorder before age fifteen. He was well behaved at school, has no criminal history and is consistently remorseful, which excludes it. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Bipolar affective disorder with recurrent irritable hypomanic episodes occurring
options.rationale: Hypomania requires a sustained period of at least four consecutive days of abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and associated features such as reduced need for sleep and increased goal directed activity. His episodes last minutes rather than days and his mood is entirely normal between them. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Intermittent explosive disorder with recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts
options.rationale: Recurrent outbursts of aggression grossly out of proportion to the provocation, impulsive rather than premeditated, not committed for any tangible gain, and occurring in someone whose functioning is normal between episodes, is precisely this diagnosis. The frequency criterion of verbal or minor physical aggression roughly twice weekly for three months, or three episodes of destruction or injury within a year, is met by three years of fortnightly destructive episodes. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Borderline personality disorder with affective instability and anger dyscontrol
options.rationale: Inappropriate intense anger is one of its criteria, so this is a genuine near miss, and the diagnosis also requires a pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, identity disturbance, abandonment fears, self harm and chronic emptiness. He has a stable relationship, a stable sense of self and no self harm, so the anger stands alone rather than sitting within a broader pattern. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Focal epilepsy of temporal lobe origin presenting with episodic ictal aggression
options.rationale: Ictal aggression is rare, undirected and stereotyped, and it is accompanied by impaired awareness, automatisms and postictal confusion with amnesia for the event. He has clear recall, directed behaviour, full awareness throughout and a normal electroencephalogram. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Intermittent explosive disorder is defined by recurrent failure to resist aggressive impulses, with outbursts grossly disproportionate to the provocation, impulsive rather than planned, and not undertaken for any tangible objective such as money or intimidation. The essential discriminator is that functioning between episodes is entirely normal, which separates it from personality disorders where the disturbance is pervasive and from mood disorders where the abnormality is sustained. Remorse after the event is characteristic and argues against antisocial personality disorder. Organic causes including epilepsy, head injury and substance intoxication must be excluded before the diagnosis is made. Cognitive behavioural therapy focused on relaxation, cognitive restructuring and relapse prevention is first line, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors having the best pharmacological evidence.
key_points: Outbursts are impulsive, disproportionate to provocation, and not committed for tangible gain.
Normal functioning between episodes distinguishes it from personality and mood disorders.
Remorse and embarrassment after episodes argue against antisocial personality disorder.
Organic causes including epilepsy, head injury and substance use must be excluded first.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors the best evidenced medication.
explanation.pearls: Establish what the person is like between episodes before diagnosing an anger problem, because completely normal interepisode functioning with genuine remorse points to intermittent explosive disorder, whereas pervasive instability across relationships and identity points to a personality disorder instead.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

subtopic_detail: distinguishing genuine autobiographical memory loss from feigned amnesia when a financial motive is present
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 44 year old man brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering in a coastal town three hundred kilometres from his home.

He cannot recall his name, his address or anything about his personal history, and he appears genuinely distressed by this. He is oriented to place and time, can tell you the date and the name of the prime minister, drove himself there and can operate his phone, read the newspaper and describe how to make a cup of tea. His wife arrives and tells you he had been served with bankruptcy papers the day before he disappeared and that his father died by suicide in similar financial circumstances. Computed tomography of his head is normal, his ethanol level is zero and his urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and cooperative, distressed affect, no thought disorder or psychotic phenomena, cranial nerves and peripheral neurological examination normal, no head injury, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the head normal, ethanol zero, urine drug screen negative, electrolytes, glucose, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Wernicke encephalopathy with confabulation from thiamine deficiency
options.rationale: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with some combination of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, usually with a history of alcohol dependence or malnutrition, and the amnesia that follows it is anterograde with confabulation. His cranial nerves and gait are normal, his ethanol is zero and he is forming new memories perfectly well. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue following overwhelming stress
options.rationale: Loss of autobiographical and identity memory with wholly intact semantic and procedural memory, purposeful travel away from home, and an immediately preceding overwhelming psychological stressor is the defining pattern of this disorder, and organic causes have been excluded. The financial motive raises malingering properly, but a malingerer typically presents with a vague global memory loss rather than this sharply selective sparing of skills, and genuine distress with a personally significant precipitant supports a dissociative process. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Transient global amnesia with dense anterograde memory loss and repeated questioning
options.rationale: Transient global amnesia causes profound anterograde memory failure with repetitive questioning, preserved personal identity and resolution within twenty four hours. He knows the date and can form new memories, and crucially it is his identity that is lost, which transient global amnesia characteristically spares. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Malingered amnesia motivated by avoidance of impending bankruptcy proceedings
options.rationale: External incentive is present and must be weighed seriously, but malingering is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires positive evidence such as inconsistent performance, dramatic presentation on demand or symptoms that do not follow any known memory architecture. His deficit is neuropsychologically coherent, he is distressed rather than indifferent, and the amnesia itself does nothing to prevent the bankruptcy proceeding. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Non convulsive status epilepticus producing a prolonged postictal confusional state
options.rationale: Non convulsive status causes fluctuating conscious state, impaired attention and automatisms, and it would be detected on electroencephalography. He is fully alert with intact attention and orientation, performing complex purposeful tasks such as driving and using his phone. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Dissociative amnesia involves an inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is too extensive to be ordinary forgetting and is not explained by a substance or neurological condition. The fugue subtype adds purposeful travel or wandering with confusion about identity. The diagnostic signature is dissociation between memory systems: autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic knowledge, procedural skills and the ability to form new memories remain fully intact. Organic causes must be excluded, which is what the imaging, toxicology and biochemistry accomplish here. Malingering deserves serious consideration whenever there is an external incentive, but it is not diagnosed merely because an incentive exists, and it requires positive evidence of feigning rather than the coherent selective pattern seen here.
key_points: Autobiographical and identity memory are lost while semantic and procedural memory remain intact.
Dissociative fugue adds purposeful travel away from home with confusion about identity.
Organic causes including head injury, substances, seizures and thiamine deficiency must be excluded first.
Transient global amnesia spares identity and causes dense anterograde failure with repetitive questioning.
Malingering requires positive evidence of feigning, not merely the presence of an external incentive.
explanation.pearls: Test procedural and semantic memory separately from autobiographical memory in any presentation of amnesia, because preserved ability to drive, read and name the prime minister alongside a lost identity is the pattern of dissociative amnesia, whereas feigned amnesia is usually globally and implausibly dense.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

subtopic_detail: establishing the nature of frequent prolonged events that have not responded to escalating anticonvulsant treatment
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old woman referred with events occurring up to four times a week for two years. She has been treated with three anticonvulsants at therapeutic doses without any reduction in frequency.

Her partner has recorded one on a phone. During the event she lies on the floor with her eyes tightly closed, her head turns rapidly from side to side, and her limbs move in an irregular asynchronous way that waxes and wanes over nine minutes. She resists having her eyelids opened. She has never been incontinent, has never bitten her tongue and has never been injured. Afterwards she is tearful but immediately oriented and can describe the room throughout. Her magnetic resonance imaging is normal, her routine interictal electroencephalograms have been normal, and her serum lactate taken twenty minutes after one event was normal.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal between events, normal gait and coordination, mental state shows anxious affect with no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal, three routine interictal electroencephalograms normal, serum lactate normal twenty minutes after a witnessed event, electrolytes glucose and calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Video electroencephalography telemetry to capture a typical event
options.rationale: Simultaneous video and electroencephalographic recording of a habitual event is the only way to establish whether the behaviour is accompanied by an ictal electrographic discharge, and it is the accepted standard for this diagnosis. Routine interictal studies cannot settle the question because they are frequently normal between genuine seizures as well, so capturing an event is what distinguishes the two. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Add a fourth anticonvulsant and reassess the frequency after three months
options.rationale: Adding further anticonvulsants is what happens to these patients for years before diagnosis, exposing them to teratogenic risk, cognitive adverse effects and occasionally intubation for presumed status epilepticus. Failure of three appropriately dosed drugs should prompt a review of the diagnosis rather than a fourth trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat the magnetic resonance imaging using a dedicated epilepsy protocol
options.rationale: A dedicated epilepsy protocol does improve detection of hippocampal sclerosis and focal cortical dysplasia and is worthwhile in drug resistant focal epilepsy. It cannot determine whether these particular events are epileptic, and a structural lesion would not by itself explain semiology this atypical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Measure serum prolactin immediately after the next witnessed event occurs
options.rationale: Prolactin rises after generalised tonic clonic seizures and was formerly used this way, and its sensitivity is poor, it is unhelpful after focal seizures, and it must be drawn within a narrow window against a baseline. A normal result would not exclude epilepsy and so cannot establish the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange cardiac monitoring with a prolonged implantable loop recorder inserted
options.rationale: Loop recorders are used where unexplained transient loss of consciousness may be arrhythmic, typically with abrupt collapse, brief duration and rapid full recovery. Nine minutes of asynchronous movement with retained awareness throughout does not fit a cardiac mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Psychogenic non epileptic seizures account for a substantial minority of patients referred to epilepsy services and are typically diagnosed after years of ineffective anticonvulsant treatment. Several features in the recorded event favour a non epileptic mechanism: forced eye closure with resistance to passive opening, side to side head movement, asynchronous limb movements that wax and wane, prolonged duration beyond a few minutes, retained awareness throughout, and the absence of tongue biting, incontinence or injury. A normal postictal lactate also argues against a generalised convulsion. None of these features is individually decisive, which is why video electroencephalography telemetry capturing a habitual event is the diagnostic standard. Diagnosis matters because the treatment is psychological therapy rather than anticonvulsants, and because these patients are otherwise at risk of harmful escalation including intubation for presumed status epilepticus.
key_points: Forced eye closure with resistance to opening is uncommon in epileptic seizures.
Asynchronous waxing and waning movements lasting beyond a few minutes favour a non epileptic mechanism.
Retained awareness with immediate orientation afterwards argues against a generalised convulsion.
Normal interictal electroencephalography occurs in genuine epilepsy and cannot exclude or confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment is psychological therapy, and anticonvulsants should be withdrawn once the diagnosis is secure.
explanation.pearls: Treat failure of three appropriately dosed anticonvulsants as a reason to question the diagnosis rather than to add a fourth, and arrange video telemetry, because these patients are otherwise escalated for years and occasionally intubated for presumed status epilepticus.

subtopic_detail: reconsidering a long standing anxiety label in a woman whose exhaustion follows social effort rather than preceding it
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 31 year old woman referred after a third trial of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor failed to help what has been treated as social anxiety disorder since she was nineteen.

She describes rehearsing conversations in advance, keeping a mental list of topics, and copying the facial expressions of colleagues so she appears normal. She says she is not frightened of being judged but finds the effort of appearing natural exhausting, and she sleeps for most of Saturday after a working week. She has an encyclopaedic knowledge of eighteenth century textiles and can talk about them at length. She reports that unexpected changes to plans leave her unable to function for the rest of the day, that certain clothing labels are unbearable against her skin, and that she has always counted steps when walking.

data_table.Examination: Limited spontaneous eye contact with effortful compensation, precise formal speech, mood euthymic, no psychotic phenomena, no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits, previous trials of sertraline, escitalopram and venlafaxine each at adequate dose and duration without benefit

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?

options.text: Treatment resistant social anxiety disorder requiring augmentation of her medication
options.rationale: Social anxiety disorder is driven by fear of negative evaluation and humiliation, and she explicitly denies fear of judgement, describing instead the effort of appearing natural. Three adequate medication trials without benefit is itself evidence that the original formulation was wrong rather than that more medication is needed. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with counting compulsions and an intense special interest
options.rationale: Compulsions in obsessive compulsive disorder are performed to neutralise a specific feared outcome and are experienced as unwanted and ego dystonic, whereas her counting and her textile interest are neither distressing nor aimed at preventing anything. The examination explicitly notes no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with camouflaging that has delayed her diagnosis
options.rationale: Rehearsing scripts, maintaining topic lists and consciously imitating the expressions of others is camouflaging, an effortful compensation that masks social communication difficulty and is far commoner in women, which is why they are diagnosed later and more often misdiagnosed with anxiety. The exhaustion following social effort rather than preceding it, alongside insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity to clothing labels and a circumscribed intense interest, completes the diagnostic picture. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Schizoid personality disorder with restricted affect and a preference for solitude
options.rationale: Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and little desire for social contact, so the person makes no effort to fit in. She works hard to appear natural and finds it costly, which indicates that she wants social connection and lacks the intuitive means rather than lacking the desire. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder producing fatigue, low motivation and social withdrawal
options.rationale: Chronic depression would involve pervasive low mood with anhedonia over at least two years, and her mood is euthymic on examination and she retains intense pleasure in her special interest. Her fatigue follows social effort specifically rather than being present regardless of activity. (Source: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition)
source_refs: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed substantially later than men, frequently after years of treatment for anxiety, depression or an eating disorder, because camouflaging conceals the social communication differences that diagnostic criteria were originally written to capture in boys. Camouflaging means consciously masking difficulty through rehearsed scripts, imitated expressions and prepared conversational material, and it is effortful in a way that produces characteristic exhaustion after social contact rather than anticipatory fear before it. That distinction is the key discriminator from social anxiety disorder, where the fear is of negative evaluation and precedes the encounter. The restricted and repetitive domain is present here as insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and a circumscribed intense interest. Recognition matters because it redirects care from repeated medication trials towards environmental adjustment, sensory accommodation and appropriate support.
key_points: Camouflaging masks social communication difference and is markedly more common in autistic women.
Exhaustion after social effort distinguishes camouflaging from the anticipatory fear of social anxiety disorder.
The restricted and repetitive domain includes insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivity and circumscribed interests.
Autistic special interests are pleasurable and ego syntonic, unlike the distressing compulsions of obsessive compulsive disorder.
Repeated failure of adequate medication trials should prompt review of the formulation rather than further augmentation.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the fear comes before the social event or the exhaustion comes after it, because anticipatory fear of judgement points to social anxiety disorder while post social depletion from effortful masking points to undiagnosed autism, and the distinction redirects care away from a fourth antidepressant trial.

sources.label: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition
Autism CRC: National Guideline for Autism Assessment

subtopic_detail: identifying the disorder behind repeated presentations for infant reassurance when screening for low mood is negative
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman with her 10 week old first baby. This is her fifth visit in three weeks, each time about a different symptom in the baby that has resolved by the time she arrives.

She describes checking the baby's breathing between eight and ten times each night and lying awake listening to the monitor even when the baby is asleep and settled. She has intrusive images of the baby stopping breathing that she finds horrifying and wholly unwanted, and she has never had any thought of harming the baby herself. She says her mood is fine, she enjoys the baby, she laughs with her partner and she looks forward to her mothers group. She is eating normally but is exhausted. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11, with the three anxiety items accounting for most of it and item 10 scored zero.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but engaged, interacts warmly and responsively with the baby, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no thoughts of harm to self or the baby
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with item 10 scored zero, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits, baby thriving on the 50th centile with a normal examination

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Postnatal anxiety disorder with prominent checking and intrusive unwanted images
options.rationale: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and frequently presents as repeated health seeking for the infant, excessive checking and unwanted intrusive images of harm coming to the baby, in a woman whose mood is preserved. Her Edinburgh score of 11 driven by the three anxiety items with a normal mood and preserved enjoyment fits an anxiety disorder rather than a depressive one, and the intrusive images are egodystonic and therefore not a risk to the baby. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Postnatal depression that the screening tool has partially failed to capture
options.rationale: Her total score is above the usual referral threshold, which makes this worth considering, and the diagnosis requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, and she reports preserved mood, preserved enjoyment of the baby and preserved social engagement. The elevated score comes specifically from the anxiety items rather than the depressive ones. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Postpartum psychosis with delusional beliefs about the baby's physical health
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency presenting within days to weeks with delusions, hallucinations, confusion and rapidly fluctuating mood, and it requires urgent admission. Her beliefs are not held with conviction, she recognises the images as unwanted products of her own mind, and there are no psychotic phenomena. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on another with fabricated symptoms in the infant
options.rationale: This involves deliberate falsification or induction of illness in the child to obtain attention through the sick role, and the presenting adult is typically calm and comfortable in medical settings. She is genuinely distressed, is seeking reassurance rather than investigation, and the baby has no fabricated findings. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Normal adjustment to first time parenthood requiring reassurance and sleep support
options.rationale: Some vigilance and worry is entirely normal in new parents, and this has crossed into disorder because it is producing insomnia when the baby sleeps, five medical presentations in three weeks and marked distress. Normalising it would leave a treatable condition untreated and reinforce the reassurance seeking. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is far more often missed, partly because screening and public awareness both centre on low mood. It commonly presents as repeated presentations about the infant, compulsive checking of breathing, inability to sleep when the baby sleeps, and unwanted intrusive images of harm befalling the baby. Those intrusive images are egodystonic, meaning the mother finds them horrifying and alien, which distinguishes them from the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis and means they do not indicate risk to the infant. Examining the subscale structure of the Edinburgh scale rather than the total score alone is what reveals the anxiety pattern here, with item 10 confirming absence of self harm thoughts. Treatment is psychological, with cognitive behavioural therapy first line and medication reserved for more severe or non responsive presentations.
key_points: Perinatal anxiety is at least as common as perinatal depression and is more frequently missed.
Items 3, 4 and 5 of the Edinburgh scale form an anxiety subscale that can drive an elevated total score.
Item 10 specifically screens for thoughts of self harm and must always be reviewed individually.
Egodystonic intrusive images of harm are distressing to the mother and do not indicate risk to the infant.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with medication reserved for severe or non responsive illness.
explanation.pearls: Ask a mother with intrusive thoughts of harm whether the thought is horrifying to her or feels reasonable, because egodystonic unwanted images indicate an anxiety disorder that responds to therapy while egosyntonic beliefs about the baby suggest psychosis requiring urgent admission.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

subtopic_detail: the oral cover required when a depot antipsychotic is started, which differs between preparations
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28 year old man with schizophrenia who has had two relapses in three years, each following a period of stopping his tablets. He has been well for four months on oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily and has agreed to move to a monthly injection.

He tolerates the oral medicine without akathisia, sedation or movement problems, and his most recent metabolic screen was unremarkable. He lives with his parents, who prompt him with tablets, and he is returning to study next month. The first injection of aripiprazole 400 mg is given today in the clinic. He asks whether he can stop the tablets now that he has had the injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rigidity, tremor or abnormal involuntary movements, weight stable over four months, injection site normal
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose, lipids, full blood count, electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 15 mg orally daily, aripiprazole 400 mg intramuscular given today

lead_in: What should you advise about his oral medicine?

options.text: Halve the oral dose today and stop it after the second injection next month
options.rationale: Halving the dose during the period of lowest injectable concentration is the worst of both options, giving inadequate cover for a fortnight while still requiring tablets. The oral dose is maintained in full and then stopped, not tapered. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose for three weeks, as required with the risperidone injection
options.rationale: Three weeks of oral cover is exactly right for the risperidone long acting injection, which releases nothing for about three weeks after administration. Applying that interval here gives a week of unnecessary double treatment and shows the cover period belongs to the preparation rather than to depots as a class. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Stop the oral dose today because the injection provides immediate therapeutic cover
options.rationale: One long acting preparation is designed to be started without oral cover by giving two loading injections a week apart, which is why this belief is common on the wards. That approach belongs to the paliperidone preparation and cannot be transferred to an agent that reaches therapeutic levels slowly. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose for fourteen days after this injection and then stop it
options.rationale: This preparation takes several weeks to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations after a single injection, so fourteen days of continued oral treatment covers the gap and is built into the product information. Stopping earlier leaves him subtherapeutic during the very period the change was made to protect. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose indefinitely because injections alone rarely maintain remission
options.rationale: Long acting injections maintain plasma concentrations at least as well as oral treatment and reduce relapse driven by missed doses, which is the problem he has had twice. Permanent dual treatment doubles his exposure and defeats the purpose of the change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Long acting injectable antipsychotics differ from each other in how quickly they reach therapeutic plasma concentrations, and the oral cover required at initiation follows the individual preparation rather than any general rule. Aripiprazole given monthly requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole after the first injection. The risperidone injection requires about three weeks of oral cover because it releases almost no drug for the first weeks. Paliperidone palmitate requires none at all, because the regimen uses a loading dose on day one and a second dose on day eight to reach therapeutic levels directly. Getting this wrong produces a relapse a few weeks after a change that was made specifically to prevent one.
key_points: Oral cover at initiation is determined by the individual preparation, not by depots as a class.
Monthly aripiprazole requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole.
The risperidone long acting injection requires about three weeks of oral cover.
Paliperidone palmitate requires no oral cover because of its day one and day eight loading.
Long acting injections reduce relapse driven by missed doses.
explanation.pearls: Write the stop date for the tablets on the prescription and in the clinic letter when you give the first injection, because the relapse that follows a depot change almost always happens in the first month and almost always traces back to the tablets being stopped on the day of the injection.

subtopic_detail: the interval required before an irreversible enzyme inhibitor can follow an antidepressant with an active metabolite
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44 year old woman with severe depression that has not responded to three adequate antidepressant trials. Your consultant has decided to move her to phenelzine and has asked you to organise the change.

She is currently taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily, which she has been on for eleven weeks with no benefit. She has no psychotic symptoms, is not suicidal, and lives with her husband who is supportive. She has no cardiac or renal disease, takes no other prescribed medicine and uses no over the counter preparations or herbal supplements. She has already been counselled about the dietary restrictions that go with the new medicine and is keen to start as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no clonus, no hyperreflexia, no rigidity, mental state shows low mood with reactive affect and no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: How should the change be made?

options.text: Switch to a two week course of sertraline first and then allow a two week washout
options.rationale: Bridging through a shorter acting agent sounds appealing and would shorten the final washout on paper. It requires the fluoxetine metabolite to be gone before the sertraline is stopped, which it will not be, so the total wait is no shorter and the patient takes an extra medicine for no reason. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

options.text: Cross taper the two medicines over ten days to avoid a period without treatment
options.rationale: Cross tapering is standard practice between most antidepressants and avoids both discontinuation symptoms and a treatment gap. It is specifically contraindicated with this class, because any overlap between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor risks life threatening serotonin toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

options.text: Stop the fluoxetine and wait five weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
options.rationale: Fluoxetine and its active metabolite have half lives measured in days to weeks, so serotonergic activity persists long after the last tablet and a standard two week gap is not enough. Five weeks allows near complete elimination before an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor is introduced, which is what prevents a severe serotonin toxicity reaction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Stop the fluoxetine and wait two weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
options.rationale: Two weeks is the correct interval after sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram or paroxetine, whose elimination is complete in that time. Applying it to fluoxetine ignores the metabolite that continues to inhibit serotonin reuptake for weeks afterwards. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Halve the fluoxetine for two weeks and then start the new medicine at a low dose
options.rationale: Reducing the dose shortens neither the half life nor the elimination time of the active metabolite, so the overlap risk is unchanged. A low starting dose of the new agent does not protect against a reaction that is driven by the combination rather than the dose. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Combining a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor can cause severe serotonin toxicity, with hyperthermia, rigidity, clonus and autonomic instability, which is why a complete washout is required rather than a cross taper. The length of the washout is set by the elimination of the drug and any active metabolites. Fluoxetine is the outlier among the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors because its metabolite has a half life of one to two weeks, so five weeks are needed after the last dose, against two weeks for the other agents in the class. Going the other way, two weeks are required after stopping an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor before a serotonergic drug is introduced, because new enzyme must be synthesised. Dose reduction does not substitute for time, since half life is unchanged by dose.
key_points: Serotonin toxicity presents with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia and autonomic instability.
A cross taper is never used between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor.
Fluoxetine requires a five week washout because of its long acting metabolite.
Other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors require two weeks.
Two weeks are needed after stopping the inhibitor before any serotonergic drug is started.
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine is the one antidepressant where the washout is measured in weeks rather than days, so before any switch involving it, check whether the incoming drug is serotonergic and count five weeks from the last tablet, not from the last clinic visit.

subtopic_detail: the monitoring schedule that must be arranged before a particular antidepressant is dispensed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38 year old man with a first episode of moderate depression whose main complaints are early waking and daytime fatigue. He has previously stopped two antidepressants because of sexual dysfunction and asks specifically about agomelatine, which a colleague at work takes.

He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and has no history of hepatitis, jaundice or alcohol related liver disease. He takes no other medication, has no known allergies and does not use recreational drugs. His weight is stable and his examination is unremarkable. He is engaged with a psychologist and is not suicidal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, body mass index 25
data_table.Investigations: No blood tests performed to date

lead_in: What must you arrange if you prescribe this medicine?

options.text: No specific monitoring, with review at two weeks to assess response and tolerability
options.rationale: Early review at two weeks is appropriate for any newly started antidepressant and should happen here as well. It is not sufficient on its own for this drug, because hepatic injury is usually asymptomatic until it is advanced and is detected only by scheduled blood tests. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Liver function tests before starting and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks
options.rationale: This drug causes dose related transaminase rises and rare cases of hepatic failure, so a baseline is taken before the first tablet and the schedule of repeats covers the period in which injury appears. Treatment is not started when transaminases are above three times the upper limit of normal, and it is stopped if they rise to that level on treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: A full blood count before starting and weekly for the first eighteen weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Weekly haematological monitoring of that intensity belongs to clozapine, where agranulocytosis risk is concentrated in the first months. No antidepressant requires this schedule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

options.text: Serum sodium before starting and again at two weeks, then every three months
options.rationale: Sodium monitoring in the early weeks belongs with the serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine in older patients, where hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is the recognised early risk. It is not the monitoring requirement that distinguishes this drug. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: An electrocardiogram before starting and again once the maintenance dose is reached
options.rationale: Baseline and follow up electrocardiography is the requirement for citalopram at higher doses and for antipsychotics that prolong the QT interval. This agent has no meaningful effect on cardiac conduction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Agomelatine is an antidepressant acting at melatonergic receptors with additional serotonin antagonism, and it is chosen partly because it is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain. Its distinguishing safety issue is hepatotoxicity, ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to rare hepatic failure, and this drives a mandatory monitoring schedule. Liver function is checked before the first dose and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks, and after any dose increase. Treatment is not started if transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and it is ceased if they reach that threshold during treatment or if the patient develops jaundice, dark urine or right upper quadrant pain. Regular alcohol intake and other hepatotoxic drugs increase the risk and are worth quantifying before prescribing.
key_points: Hepatotoxicity is the distinguishing safety concern with this drug.
Liver function is checked at baseline and at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks.
Transaminases above three times the upper limit of normal preclude starting or continuing.
It is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain, which is why patients request it.
Hyponatraemia monitoring belongs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine, not here.
explanation.pearls: Order the baseline liver function test before writing the script rather than with it, because the drug should not be started at all when transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and a result that arrives after the first week has already missed that decision.

subtopic_detail: a low neutrophil count on clozapine in a patient whose baseline count was always at the lower limit
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32 year old man of West African descent with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for seven months with a very good response, having failed two previous antipsychotics.

His monitoring bloods today show a neutrophil count of 1.4 x10^9/L. Looking back through the record, his neutrophil counts have run between 1.5 and 1.9 x10^9/L at every check since before clozapine was started, and a full blood count taken during an admission four years ago showed a neutrophil count of 1.6. His total white cell count has always tracked at the lower end while his lymphocytes are normal. He is afebrile, has no sore throat, mouth ulcers or other infective symptoms, and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No oral ulceration, no pharyngeal inflammation, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no focus of infection
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), lymphocytes 2.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and record it as a permanent contraindication for the future
options.rationale: Immediate cessation with a permanent bar is the correct response to a genuine red result, and it exists because agranulocytosis can progress rapidly to fatal sepsis. Applying it to a count that has always been at this level in this patient discards an effective treatment for treatment resistant illness on the basis of a reference range derived from a different population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Add lithium to raise the neutrophil count and continue the current clozapine dose
options.rationale: Lithium does raise the neutrophil count by demargination and has been used deliberately for this purpose in specialist settings. Using it to mask a count without first establishing why the count is low removes the very signal that monitoring depends on, and it is not an appropriate first response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Refer to haematology to confirm a constitutional low count and apply modified thresholds
options.rationale: A neutrophil count that sat at the lower limit for years before clozapine was ever started, with a normal lymphocyte count and no infections, describes a benign constitutional variant rather than drug induced marrow suppression. Haematology confirmation allows the monitoring service to register modified thresholds so that a patient who has responded to clozapine is not permanently deprived of it for a count that has never been abnormal for him. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the full blood count in one week
options.rationale: Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so halving the dose does not reduce the haematological risk while it does risk losing the response that has taken seven months to achieve. Dose reduction is not part of the response to an abnormal count. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine)

options.text: Continue unchanged and repeat the count at the next scheduled monitoring interval
options.rationale: Carrying on without action ignores a result that has fallen below the threshold at which the monitoring service requires a response, and it leaves the clinician with no documented basis for the decision. Increased monitoring frequency is part of the management even when a constitutional cause is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

explanation.summary: Clozapine monitoring exists because of agranulocytosis, and the thresholds that trigger cessation are derived from neutrophil reference ranges based largely on European populations. A substantial proportion of people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry have a constitutionally lower circulating neutrophil count, caused by a normal variant affecting neutrophil margination rather than by any defect in production or in immune function. Recognising this matters because otherwise these patients are excluded from the only effective treatment for treatment resistant schizophrenia on the basis of a count that has never been abnormal for them. The evidence for the constitutional pattern here is that the low counts long predate the clozapine, that the lymphocyte count is normal, and that there is no history of recurrent infection. Haematology confirmation allows modified thresholds to be registered with the monitoring service, and monitoring continues rather than stopping.
key_points: Clozapine neutropenia thresholds derive from reference ranges based on European populations.
A constitutional low neutrophil count is common in people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry.
Counts that predate the drug, with normal lymphocytes and no infections, suggest the variant.
Haematology confirmation permits modified monitoring thresholds to be registered.
Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so dose reduction does not help.
explanation.pearls: Look for a full blood count taken years before clozapine was ever prescribed, because a neutrophil count of 1.6 in an admission four years earlier is the single piece of evidence that converts a mandatory permanent cessation into a registered modified threshold.

subtopic_detail: an analgesic bought over the counter that alters the handling of a narrow therapeutic index drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for six years. She has come in about low back pain after moving house and mentions that she has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past ten days, bought from the supermarket.

Over the past four days she has felt nauseated, her hands have been shakier than usual, and she describes feeling unsteady on her feet. She has not vomited, has been drinking normally and has not had diarrhoea. She has had no recent dose change, no new prescribed medicines and no fevers. On examination she has a fine tremor that is coarser than her usual lithium tremor, and her gait is mildly unsteady with normal power and no focal signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild gait ataxia, normal power and reflexes, no clonus, no confusion, oriented and coherent
data_table.Investigations: No bloods taken yet today
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg orally at night, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for ten days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch the ibuprofen to regular celecoxib, which does not interact with lithium
options.rationale: Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors act on the same renal prostaglandin pathway and raise lithium concentrations in the same way, so the substitution offers no protection. Paracetamol is the safe analgesic in this situation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Refer her directly to the emergency department for consideration of haemodialysis
options.rationale: Dialysis is the treatment for severe toxicity, indicated by reduced consciousness, seizures, myoclonus or renal failure, or by very high concentrations. She is alert, oriented and haemodynamically well, so the level is needed before that pathway is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Lithium toxicity)

options.text: Continue both medicines and recheck the lithium level at her next routine appointment
options.rationale: Routine three monthly monitoring is appropriate for a stable patient with no new symptoms and no interacting drugs. Deferring here allows a rising concentration to continue toward the confusion, myoclonus and seizures of severe toxicity in a woman already showing neurological signs. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Stop the ibuprofen and take an urgent lithium level with electrolytes and creatinine
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatories reduce renal prostaglandin mediated blood flow and increase proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium, raising concentrations by up to half within days, and her tremor, nausea and unsteadiness are the early features of toxicity. Removing the interacting drug and measuring the level together establish both the cause and the severity before any dose decision is made. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Halve the lithium dose today and continue the ibuprofen until the back pain settles
options.rationale: Adjusting the lithium around an interacting drug that will be stopped in days creates a moving target and risks subtherapeutic concentrations and relapse once the anti inflammatory is finished. The interacting drug is the one to remove. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is cleared almost entirely by the kidney, so anything that reduces renal clearance raises the concentration quickly. Non steroidal anti inflammatories are the commonest culprit because patients buy them without mentioning it, and they can raise lithium concentrations by up to half within a week. The early features of toxicity are gastrointestinal upset, a coarsening of the usual fine tremor and unsteadiness, progressing to confusion, myoclonus, seizures and renal failure if unrecognised. The immediate response is to remove the interacting drug and measure the concentration alongside electrolytes and creatinine, since dehydration and renal impairment compound the effect. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazide diuretics interact by the same renal mechanism and deserve the same caution.
key_points: Lithium is renally cleared, so anything reducing renal clearance raises the concentration.
Anti inflammatories can raise lithium concentrations by up to fifty per cent within days.
Early toxicity presents as nausea, coarse tremor and ataxia before confusion appears.
Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors interact by the same mechanism and are no safer.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, receptor blockers and thiazides share the interaction.
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient on lithium what they buy at the supermarket, because ibuprofen and naproxen need no prescription, are not on the medication list you are reading, and are the commonest single cause of a lithium level that has climbed without any dose being changed.

subtopic_detail: separating the presence of mental illness from the capacity to refuse a specific medical treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the surgical ward to see a 45 year old man with schizophrenia who is refusing an appendicectomy. The surgical team has told you he lacks capacity because of his diagnosis and has asked you to authorise the operation under mental health legislation.

He has been on paliperidone for eight years and his last relapse was six years ago. He tells you he understands he has an infected appendix, that it may burst, and that this could kill him. He says he is refusing because his brother died under a general anaesthetic three years ago and he is frightened of the anaesthetic rather than the surgery. He repeats this account consistently and can explain the trade off he is making. He has no delusions about the surgical team, no hallucinations and no thought disorder on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, mental state shows no delusions or hallucinations, speech coherent and goal directed, oriented to time place and person
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), computed tomography showing an inflamed appendix without perforation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the surgical team?

options.text: Advise the team to proceed once he is sedated for pain, as consent will then be simpler
options.rationale: Sedating a person in order to remove their objection is a deliberate circumvention of a valid refusal and constitutes assault. Analgesia is given for pain on its own merits and never as a route around consent. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Document that he retains capacity for this decision and that his refusal must be respected
options.rationale: He understands the information, retains it, weighs it against a reason that is comprehensible and communicates a consistent choice, which is all that capacity requires. A diagnosis of schizophrenia does not remove capacity, and an unwise decision made for a reason a frightened person might genuinely hold is not evidence of incapacity. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Contact the guardianship board for an urgent substitute decision maker to be appointed
options.rationale: Substitute decision making is engaged when a person genuinely lacks capacity, and it is the correct pathway for non urgent treatment in that situation. Seeking it for a person who has capacity overrides a valid refusal through an administrative route and is not lawful. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Increase his antipsychotic dose and reassess his capacity again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Treating an illness that is currently in remission will not change a decision that is not being driven by psychotic symptoms, and forty eight hours in an inflamed appendix carries a real risk of perforation. Reassessment is appropriate when capacity fluctuates, which is not what is happening here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Authorise the operation under mental health legislation given the risk to his life
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness itself, not unrelated surgical conditions, so it provides no lawful basis for an appendicectomy whatever the risk. Surgical treatment of a person who lacks capacity proceeds through guardianship arrangements or the emergency doctrine instead. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision specific and is assessed against four elements: whether the person can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough to decide, weigh it in arriving at a choice, and communicate that choice. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself affect any of these, and the assessment must be made about this decision at this time rather than about the person in general. This man demonstrates all four elements and gives a reason for his refusal that is frightening but entirely rational in origin, so his refusal is valid even though the team considers it unwise. Mental health legislation cannot be used to authorise treatment of a physical condition unrelated to the mental illness. The useful clinical response is to address the specific fear, which is the anaesthetic rather than the surgery, ideally by having the anaesthetist discuss his brother's death with him directly.
key_points: Capacity requires understanding, retention, weighing and communication of a choice.
Capacity is specific to the decision and the moment, not to the person or the diagnosis.
An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness, not unrelated surgery.
Guardianship or the emergency doctrine applies when a person genuinely lacks capacity.
explanation.pearls: When a team says a patient lacks capacity because of a psychiatric diagnosis, ask which of the four elements is missing, because in most of these referrals the answer is none of them and the real problem is a specific fear that nobody has asked about.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

subtopic_detail: choosing an antidepressant when a concurrent medicine depends on a hepatic enzyme for activation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52 year old woman who finished treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eight months ago and now takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily. She describes two months of low mood, anhedonia and poor concentration that meet criteria for a moderate depressive episode, alongside troublesome hot flushes.

She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no suicidal thoughts and no psychotic symptoms. She has no cardiac disease, her blood pressure is normal, and she takes no other medication and no herbal preparations. She has already started with a psychologist and wants medication as well because the hot flushes are waking her several times a night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mental state shows low mood with restricted affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychosis, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Fluoxetine, which is well tolerated and can be given as a single morning dose
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is a potent inhibitor of the same enzyme and carries the same concern about reduced tamoxifen activation. Its long half life also makes any later switch slower and more complicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Venlafaxine, which has minimal effect on the enzyme that activates her other medicine
options.rationale: Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen effect, so an antidepressant that strongly inhibits that enzyme reduces its efficacy. Venlafaxine has minimal effect on this pathway and has the additional advantage of reducing hot flushes, which is the symptom troubling her most at night. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Paroxetine, which is effective for depression and also reduces vasomotor symptoms
options.rationale: Paroxetine does reduce hot flushes and is an effective antidepressant, which is exactly why it is prescribed in this situation by mistake. It is the strongest cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality when combined with tamoxifen. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Bupropion, which avoids sexual adverse effects and assists with fatigue and motivation
options.rationale: Bupropion has a favourable adverse effect profile in some respects but is also a strong inhibitor of the enzyme in question, so it shares the same problem. It is registered in Australia only for smoking cessation rather than for depression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Sertraline, which is first line for depression and is widely used after cancer treatment
options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable first line antidepressant generally and is only a moderate inhibitor of this enzyme, so it is safer than paroxetine or fluoxetine here. It still carries more interaction risk than the preferred agent and lacks the vasomotor benefit she specifically needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is inactive as given and relies on cytochrome P450 2D6 to produce endoxifen, the metabolite that provides most of its antioestrogen activity. Antidepressants that strongly inhibit this enzyme therefore reduce the concentration of the active metabolite, and observational data have linked paroxetine in particular with increased breast cancer mortality in women taking tamoxifen. Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are all strong inhibitors and are avoided, while sertraline is moderate and citalopram, escitalopram and venlafaxine have minimal effect. Venlafaxine is preferred in this setting because it combines negligible interaction with useful efficacy against vasomotor symptoms, which are common on tamoxifen and are a major cause of sleep disruption. The same interaction applies to other medicines requiring this enzyme for activation, including codeine and tramadol.
key_points: Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen.
Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are strong inhibitors of this enzyme and are avoided.
Venlafaxine, citalopram and escitalopram have minimal effect on the pathway.
Venlafaxine additionally reduces vasomotor symptoms.
Codeine and tramadol also require this enzyme for conversion to their active forms.
explanation.pearls: Check for tamoxifen before writing any antidepressant for a woman treated for breast cancer, because paroxetine is otherwise a sensible choice for hot flushes and it is the single worst option in this one situation.

subtopic_detail: aggression confined to one care task in dementia, where the trigger rather than the illness explains it
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked by a residential aged care facility to prescribe something for a 79 year old man with Alzheimer disease who has hit staff three times this month. The facility manager wants a regular antipsychotic started today.

The nursing notes show that every incident occurred during the morning shower, that all three involved the same two staff members, and that he is calm and cooperative at every other time of day including mealtimes and personal care in the evening. He has not been wandering, is sleeping through the night and has no hallucinations or persecutory beliefs described. He grimaces when his right shoulder is moved and has a documented rotator cuff problem. A urinalysis last week was negative and he is afebrile with no new medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Painful restricted right shoulder abduction, no delirium, attention preserved, no focal neurology, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative last week, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg orally daily, paracetamol as required for pain

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Regular analgesia with a changed showering routine and review after two weeks
options.rationale: Aggression confined to one task, at one time of day, with the same staff, in a man who grimaces on shoulder movement, is a response to pain rather than a symptom requiring an antipsychotic. Regular rather than as required analgesia and a modified approach to showering address the actual trigger, and trials show scheduled analgesia reduces agitation in dementia substantially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Prescribe as required oxazepam for staff to give before the morning shower
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, worsen confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation in older people with dementia, and their role is confined to brief use in severe distress. Sedating a man before a painful procedure treats the staff's difficulty rather than his pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Increase the donepezil dose to address the behavioural symptoms of his dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors have a modest effect on some behavioural symptoms over months and he is already at the maximum usual dose of 10 mg daily. Neither the timeframe nor the mechanism addresses aggression that occurs only during a painful task. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

options.text: Start regular risperidone at a low dose and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic registered in Australia for this indication and has a place for persistent aggression or psychosis that poses real risk after non drug measures have failed. Starting it first exposes him to an increased risk of stroke and death for a problem with an identified and treatable trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Send a urine sample and treat for infection while awaiting the culture result
options.rationale: New agitation in an older person does warrant a search for delirium and infection is a common cause, so the instinct is sound. His attention is preserved, the pattern is stable across weeks rather than fluctuating, he is afebrile and the urinalysis was negative, so this does not fit delirium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Delirium)

explanation.summary: Behavioural symptoms in dementia are usually a response to something rather than a random feature of the illness, and the first step is always to look for the pattern.
