Aggression confined to one care task, at one time of day, with particular staff, points to that task as the trigger, and in this man the painful shoulder explains why being washed and dressed provokes him when nothing else does. Untreated pain is one of the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia, and scheduled analgesia reduces it substantially in randomised trials, whereas as required dosing depends on a man with dementia asking for it. Antipsychotics in this population increase the risk of stroke and death and are reserved for persistent symptoms causing real risk after non drug measures have been tried. Delirium must always be considered, but it fluctuates, impairs attention and usually has an identifiable precipitant, none of which is present here.
key_points: Behavioural symptoms are usually triggered, so identify the pattern before prescribing.
Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia.
Scheduled analgesia works where as required dosing fails in a person who cannot ask.
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and follow failed non drug measures.
Delirium fluctuates and impairs attention, which distinguishes it from this stable pattern.
explanation.pearls: Read the incident times and the names of the staff involved before you prescribe anything, because aggression clustered around one task at one time of day is a pain or a care approach problem, and regular paracetamol fixes more of these than any antipsychotic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

subtopic_detail: choosing relapse prevention pharmacotherapy when the organ that clears one option is already damaged
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54 year old man on day nine of an inpatient admission who completed alcohol withdrawal management a week ago and wants medication to help him stay abstinent after discharge. He was drinking about fifteen standard drinks daily for twelve years.

He has established cirrhosis with a previous episode of ascites, and his most recent hepatic imaging showed a nodular liver with splenomegaly. He has no encephalopathy now and is fully oriented. His renal function is normal. He takes no opioids and has no chronic pain. He is motivated, has a supportive partner, has been linked with a community drug and alcohol service, and his aim is complete abstinence rather than reduced drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Spider naevi and palmar erythema, no ascites clinically, no asterixis, oriented with normal attention, no jaundice today
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 34 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.5 (0.8-1.2), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Thiamine 300 mg orally daily, no other regular medicines

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medicine should you start?

options.text: Disulfiram, supervised by his partner, given his stated goal of complete abstinence
options.rationale: Disulfiram works only with supervised administration and a clear abstinence goal, both of which he has, so it is not an unreasonable thought. It is hepatotoxic in its own right and has caused fulminant hepatic failure, which makes it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

options.text: No medicine, with counselling and community follow up arranged as the whole plan
options.rationale: Psychosocial treatment is the foundation of care and he is already linked with a service, so this is half of the right answer. Pharmacotherapy adds meaningful benefit on top of counselling and withholding it in a man with cirrhosis, for whom any further drinking is dangerous, is the wrong place to be conservative. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Naltrexone, which reduces heavy drinking days and is generally better tolerated
options.rationale: Naltrexone has at least equivalent evidence in alcohol dependence and would be a reasonable first choice in a man with a healthy liver. It undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, and his bilirubin, albumin and clotting all indicate significant synthetic dysfunction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Acamprosate, with the dose set by body weight and renal function checked beforehand
options.rationale: Acamprosate is eliminated unchanged by the kidney and is not metabolised by the liver, so it is the option that remains available when hepatic function is impaired, and his creatinine is normal. Dosing is by body weight and the contraindication to watch for is severe renal impairment rather than liver disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Baclofen at a low dose, titrated upward according to his response over four weeks
options.rationale: Baclofen is renally cleared and has been studied specifically in people with liver disease, which makes it a genuine second line option in this population. The evidence for it remains weaker than for the preferred agent and it carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own, so it follows rather than leads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

explanation.summary: Acamprosate and naltrexone are the two first line relapse prevention medicines in alcohol dependence, and choosing between them usually comes down to organ function and the treatment goal. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, while acamprosate is excreted unchanged by the kidney and is contraindicated instead in severe renal impairment. This man has cirrhosis with a raised bilirubin, low albumin and prolonged clotting, all indicating impaired synthetic function, so acamprosate is the appropriate choice and his normal creatinine confirms it is safe. Disulfiram is avoided because it is itself hepatotoxic. Concurrent opioid use is the other decisive factor, because naltrexone will precipitate withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks analgesia if they are needed later.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally excreted unchanged and is not metabolised by the liver.
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure.
Severe renal impairment is the contraindication to acamprosate.
Disulfiram is hepatotoxic and unsuitable in established liver disease.
Naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks later analgesia.
explanation.pearls: Let the failing organ choose the drug: acamprosate for the damaged liver, naltrexone for the damaged kidney, and neither before you have asked whether the patient is taking any opioid, prescribed or otherwise.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

subtopic_detail: the timing that determines whether the first dose relieves withdrawal or precipitates it
stem:
You are the registrar at a community drug and alcohol service starting a 29 year old man on buprenorphine with naloxone for heroin dependence. He has been injecting about half a gram daily for four years and has agreed to opioid treatment after a friend died of an overdose.

He arrives at 9 am having used heroin at 7 am this morning, saying he wanted to be comfortable for the appointment. He denies methadone or other long acting opioid use. He is not sweating, his pupils are small, he has no yawning, gooseflesh, abdominal cramps, rhinorrhoea or muscle aches, and he is comfortable sitting in the chair. His urine drug screen is positive for opioids only, and his hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus screening is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pupils 2 mm and reactive, skin dry and warm, no piloerection, no rhinorrhoea, no tremor, alert and comfortable
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for opioids only, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What should you do now?

options.text: Delay the first dose until objective withdrawal features are present, reviewing him later today
options.rationale: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with very high receptor affinity, so giving it while receptors are still occupied by a full agonist displaces that agonist and causes an abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Waiting until objective signs such as dilated pupils, gooseflesh, sweating and rhinorrhoea are present confirms the receptors are free enough for the first dose to relieve symptoms rather than provoke them. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Start methadone today instead, since the recent heroin use makes it the safer option
options.rationale: Methadone is a full agonist and does not precipitate withdrawal, so it can be started without waiting, which makes it a legitimate alternative for someone who cannot tolerate the wait. It carries a substantially higher overdose risk during induction because of accumulation over the first days, so it is a considered choice rather than the default when timing is the only obstacle. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Admit him for a naltrexone implant instead, given his high risk of fatal overdose
options.rationale: Naltrexone is an antagonist used after complete detoxification and requires a full opioid free interval beforehand, so it cannot be started today either. Relapse after antagonist treatment also carries a high mortality because tolerance has been lost. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any reaction
options.rationale: Symptomatic medicines take the edge off ordinary withdrawal and have a role alongside induction. They do not prevent or adequately treat precipitated withdrawal, which is far more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and frequently ends a person's engagement with treatment altogether. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Give a reduced first dose now and repeat it in four hours if he tolerates it
options.rationale: Dose reduction is used to make an induction gentler once the timing is right and withdrawal has begun. It does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, because the reaction is driven by displacement of the full agonist rather than by the size of the dose. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine binds opioid receptors with higher affinity than heroin or morphine but activates them only partially, so administering it while a full agonist is still bound displaces that agonist and drops receptor activation sharply. The result is precipitated withdrawal, which comes on within an hour, is more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and often destroys a person's willingness to try treatment again. The safeguard is timing rather than dose: the first dose is given only once objective withdrawal signs are present, typically six to twelve hours after short acting opioids and considerably longer after methadone. Objective signs such as dilated pupils, piloerection, sweating and rhinorrhoea are what count, since subjective craving and anxiety appear far earlier. This man used two hours ago, has pinpoint pupils and no objective signs, so dosing now would reliably produce the reaction.
key_points: Buprenorphine has higher receptor affinity than full agonists but only partial activity.
Dosing while a full agonist is bound displaces it and precipitates withdrawal.
Wait for objective signs, typically six to twelve hours after short acting opioids.
Longer intervals are needed after methadone or other long acting opioids.
Reducing the dose does not prevent the reaction, since displacement drives it.
explanation.pearls: Look at the pupils before the first dose, because a patient reporting that he feels terrible with 2 mm pupils and dry skin is anxious rather than in withdrawal, and dosing him then produces the one experience most likely to stop him ever coming back.

sources.label: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

subtopic_detail: Restarting clozapine for a man who stopped taking it for three days while unwell at home
stem:
A 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia attends your community mental health clinic. He has taken clozapine 400 mg at night for six years with good symptom control and no admissions in that time.

He had a bout of vomiting and diarrhoea over the weekend and did not take any clozapine on Saturday, Sunday or Monday. He restarted his usual night time dose last night of his own accord and now feels lightheaded on standing. He has no fever, no chest pain and no constipation, and his mental state is unchanged with no return of hallucinations. His full blood count today is normal and his observations show a postural drop in blood pressure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg lying with a fall to 84/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Clozapine 400 mg nightly for six years, no doses taken Saturday to Monday, full dose resumed last night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his clozapine?

options.text: Continue the current dose and monitor his blood pressure closely over the next few days
options.rationale: Continuing at the full dose after tolerance has been lost is the exact scenario that has caused deaths from cardiovascular collapse and seizures. Monitoring does not mitigate a dose the patient can no longer tolerate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the current dose and retitrate from 12.5 mg daily using the standard escalation schedule
options.rationale: Tolerance to the cardiovascular effects of clozapine is lost after more than 48 hours without a dose, so resuming the previous dose risks severe hypotension, sedation and seizures. Retitration from the starting dose rebuilds tolerance safely, and it can usually be done faster than an initial titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the current dose to 200 mg nightly and increase back to 400 mg over the next week
options.rationale: Any dose substantially above the starting dose carries the same tolerance related risk, and halving is an arbitrary compromise rather than a recognised approach. The safe restart point is the initial titration dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently and commence olanzapine at an equivalent antipsychotic dose
options.rationale: Abandoning an agent that has given six years of remission in treatment resistant illness would very likely lead to relapse. A missed dose interval is a titration problem, not a reason to change drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose and add fludrocortisone to manage the postural blood pressure drop
options.rationale: Treating the symptom leaves the underlying dosing hazard in place and adds a drug with its own risks. The hypotension is a signal that the dose is no longer tolerated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia and carries a set of hazards that require structured monitoring, including neutropenia, myocarditis in the first weeks, constipation progressing to ileus, seizures and cardiometabolic effects. A less well known but clinically critical hazard is the rapid loss of tolerance to its cardiovascular and sedative effects during a break in treatment. When more than 48 hours of doses are missed, the patient must be retitrated from the starting dose rather than resuming their previous maintenance dose, because reinstating the full dose has caused profound hypotension, respiratory depression, seizures and death. Breaks in treatment are common during physical illness, hospital admission and disruption to supply, so the question of how many doses were missed should be asked routinely whenever a patient on clozapine presents.
key_points: Tolerance to clozapine's cardiovascular effects is lost after more than 48 hours
A break of more than two days requires retitration from the starting dose
Retitration after a break can usually proceed faster than initial titration
Physical illness and admission are common causes of unplanned breaks
Ask specifically how many doses were missed at every presentation
explanation.pearls: The 48 hour rule is the one clozapine number that changes management at the bedside: beyond that gap the maintenance dose becomes unsafe and titration restarts at 12.5 mg regardless of how long the patient has been stable.

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first buprenorphine dose for a man who last used a long acting opioid the previous evening
stem:
A 34 year old man attends your addiction medicine clinic wanting to start opioid replacement treatment. He has been using illicitly obtained slow release oral morphine and last took a dose at 8 pm yesterday, about fourteen hours ago.

He is keen to take his first dose immediately and is frustrated at the suggestion of waiting. On examination he is mildly anxious and restless with a pulse rate of 92/min, but his pupils are mid-sized rather than dilated, he has no sweating, no gooseflesh, no lacrimation and no yawning. His objective withdrawal score is 5. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other sedating medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious and restless, mid-sized pupils, no sweating, gooseflesh, lacrimation or yawning
data_table.Assessment: Objective opioid withdrawal score 5, last slow release morphine dose fourteen hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his first dose?

options.text: Give the first dose now, since fourteen hours since his last use is a sufficient interval
options.rationale: The interval alone is not sufficient for a slow release preparation, whose duration of action extends well beyond that of immediate release opioids. The objective score rather than the clock determines readiness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any withdrawal symptoms
options.rationale: Symptomatic cover does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, which can be severe and prolonged and frequently causes patients to disengage from treatment. The timing problem is not solved pharmacologically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Wait until his objective withdrawal features score in the moderate range before the first dose
options.rationale: Buprenorphine has high receptor affinity with partial agonist activity, so giving it while substantial full agonist still occupies the receptor displaces that agonist and precipitates withdrawal. Waiting until objective withdrawal is established confirms the receptor is sufficiently free. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Start methadone today instead and reconsider transferring him to buprenorphine in a month
options.rationale: Switching agent avoids the timing issue but commits him to a drug with a narrower safety margin during induction and greater overdose risk. His preference and circumstances have not been shown to favour it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Give naloxone first to clear the receptor and then start buprenorphine an hour afterwards
options.rationale: Naloxone would itself precipitate severe withdrawal and has no role in planned induction. It is used for opioid overdose with respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial agonist at the mu opioid receptor, and this pharmacology explains both its safety advantages and its main induction hazard. Because it binds more avidly than most full agonists, giving it while the receptor remains substantially occupied displaces the full agonist and replaces a high level of activation with a lower one, producing abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Induction is therefore timed by objective withdrawal features rather than by the interval since last use, using a structured scale, and the required wait is longer after long acting preparations such as slow release morphine or methadone than after short acting opioids. Subjective distress alone is not adequate evidence of readiness, since anxiety and drug seeking can be present well before the receptor is free. Once established, buprenorphine carries a lower overdose risk than methadone because of its ceiling effect on respiratory depression.
key_points: Buprenorphine displaces full agonists because of its higher receptor affinity
Induction is timed by objective withdrawal features, not hours since last use
Long acting opioids require a longer wait than short acting ones
Subjective distress alone does not confirm readiness for the first dose
The ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes maintenance safer than methadone
explanation.pearls: Precipitated withdrawal from a too early buprenorphine dose can last many hours and is the single commonest reason a patient refuses to attempt opioid replacement again, so the wait for objective signs is a retention issue as much as a comfort one.

subtopic_detail: Prevention of further seizures in a man who had a witnessed fit thirty hours after his last drink
stem:
A 52 year old man is admitted under your team after a witnessed generalised seizure at home. He drinks about 20 standard drinks daily and his last drink was thirty hours before the seizure, having stopped because he ran out of money.

He has no history of epilepsy and has never had a seizure before. He is now alert and oriented with a mild tremor of the outstretched hands and is sweating lightly. His computed tomography brain scan is normal and there is no head injury. His electrolytes, glucose and magnesium are within normal limits, and his withdrawal scale score is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mild tremor of outstretched hands, light sweating, no focal neurological signs, no head injury
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes glucose and magnesium within normal limits, computed tomography brain normal, withdrawal scale score 12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent further seizures?

options.text: A loading regimen of oral phenytoin with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Antiepileptic drugs are ineffective for withdrawal seizures because the mechanism is receptor mediated central nervous system hyperexcitability rather than an epileptic focus. They are indicated when an independent seizure disorder coexists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: A loading regimen of oral carbamazepine with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Carbamazepine has some role in mild withdrawal in ambulatory settings in other countries but is not the Australian approach and is not adequate after a seizure. Benzodiazepine cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Oral haloperidol as required with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and would increase the risk of a further seizure. They are used only as an adjunct for hallucinations once benzodiazepine cover is adequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: A loading regimen of oral diazepam with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Long acting benzodiazepines are the only agents shown to prevent recurrent withdrawal seizures, and diazepam self tapers through its active metabolites. Parenteral thiamine precedes glucose because a glucose load in a thiamine deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Symptom triggered oral diazepam only when his withdrawal scale score exceeds 15
options.rationale: A symptom triggered threshold approach is reasonable for uncomplicated withdrawal but is inadequate once a seizure has occurred, since the seizure marks a higher risk course. Front loading provides immediate protection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur between six and forty eight hours after the last drink, are generalised tonic clonic, and usually occur singly or in a short cluster without focal features. A first seizure in this context still warrants imaging and biochemical assessment, since head injury, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance are common in this population and can coexist. Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice because they restore the inhibitory tone lost when chronic alcohol exposure is withdrawn, and conventional antiepileptic drugs do not prevent recurrence. A loading or front loaded regimen with a long acting agent gives immediate protection and a pharmacologically smooth taper, and is preferred to symptom triggered dosing once a seizure has occurred. Thiamine is given parenterally before any carbohydrate load, and having had a withdrawal seizure identifies a patient at higher risk of progressing to delirium tremens, which warrants closer observation over the following days.
key_points: Withdrawal seizures occur six to forty eight hours after the last drink
Benzodiazepines prevent recurrence and antiepileptic drugs do not
Loading with a long acting agent is preferred once a seizure has occurred
Parenteral thiamine precedes any glucose administration
A withdrawal seizure predicts higher risk of later delirium tremens
explanation.pearls: Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine to a chronically alcohol dependent patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so parenteral thiamine goes in first even when the blood glucose is low.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a primary psychotic illness from a substance related one in a man with psychosis persisting a month after stopping methamphetamine
stem:
A 25 year old man is reviewed on your inpatient unit. He was admitted five weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations after heavy daily methamphetamine use over the preceding six months.

He has been in hospital throughout with supervised urine drug screens that have been negative for four weeks. He was started on olanzapine on admission and his agitation settled within days, but he continues to describe a belief that a neighbour is transmitting messages about him, and he still hears two voices commenting on his actions. His family mention that in the year before he started using, he had withdrawn from friends, stopped attending TAFE and spent most of his time alone in his room. He has no fever, no confusion and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusion and third person auditory hallucinations persisting, no confusion, no fluctuation in conscious state, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Supervised urine drug screens negative for four weeks, full blood count electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic now, since his symptoms will resolve with continued abstinence alone
options.rationale: Symptoms that have already outlasted a month of abstinence are unlikely to be purely substance induced, and stopping treatment risks deterioration. Resolution within days to weeks is the expected pattern for a substance induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Record a firm diagnosis of schizophrenia now and counsel him that treatment will be lifelong
options.rationale: Committing to a lifelong diagnosis at this point overstates the certainty available and can be difficult to revise once documented. The duration criterion and longitudinal course still need to be established. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Switch to clozapine now, given that his symptoms have not resolved after five weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Treatment resistance requires failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials of sufficient dose and duration, and he has had only one. An adequate trial is generally considered to be at least four to six weeks at therapeutic dose. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Continue the antipsychotic and reassess the diagnosis after a longer period of abstinence
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting more than a month beyond confirmed abstinence exceeds the expected course of a substance induced disorder and raises the likelihood of a primary psychotic illness, particularly given the premorbid decline his family describes. Continuing treatment while observing over time is the approach that avoids both premature labelling and undertreatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing before altering treatment
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is suggested by confusion, seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability or a fluctuating conscious state, none of which is present. His examination and course do not fit that pattern. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Separating a substance induced psychotic disorder from a primary psychotic illness that has been unmasked or accompanied by substance use is one of the harder judgements in general psychiatry, and it usually cannot be made at a single point in time. The most useful discriminator is the course of symptoms during confirmed abstinence, since a genuinely substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks once the drug is cleared. Features favouring a primary disorder include symptoms persisting well beyond that window, a premorbid decline in function preceding the substance use, prominent negative symptoms, and a family history of psychotic illness. A substantial proportion of people given an initial diagnosis of methamphetamine induced psychosis are later rediagnosed with schizophrenia, so the safest position early on is to treat the symptoms, verify abstinence objectively, and let the longitudinal course clarify the diagnosis rather than committing prematurely in either direction.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks of abstinence
Persistence well beyond that window favours a primary psychotic illness
Premorbid functional decline before substance use is a key historical clue
Objectively verified abstinence is needed before the course can be interpreted
Many initial substance induced diagnoses are later revised to schizophrenia
explanation.pearls: Psychotic symptoms that persist beyond about one month of objectively verified abstinence from methamphetamine should shift the working diagnosis towards a primary psychotic illness, and the premorbid year is often where the answer already lies.

subtopic_detail: Mutism with waxy limb posturing and reduced oral intake in a young woman with known bipolar disorder
stem:
A 22 year old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted to your unit after four days of progressive withdrawal. She has not spoken since yesterday and has taken almost no food or fluid for two days.

She was started on olanzapine eight days ago by her general practitioner for elevated mood and reduced sleep. On examination she is awake with her eyes open and follows you around the room with her gaze, but does not respond to questions. When you lift her arm it remains in the position you leave it in. She resists passive eye opening and repeats your words back to you intermittently. She has no fever, her muscle tone is not rigid, and her creatine kinase is mildly raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mutism, waxy flexibility with limbs retained in imposed positions, negativism, echolalia, no rigidity, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 420 U/L (<200), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, computed tomography brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose and observe her response over the next forty eight hours
options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic therapy in catatonia risks converting it to the malignant form with hyperthermia and autonomic instability. The drug is a plausible contributor rather than the solution. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Commence dantrolene with active cooling and transfer her to the intensive care unit
options.rationale: This treats neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which requires fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and a markedly raised creatine kinase. She has none of these and her tone is not rigid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy before trying any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective and is the definitive treatment where the benzodiazepine trial fails or the malignant form develops, but a lorazepam challenge comes first. Sequencing rather than efficacy is the issue. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Give a parenteral lorazepam challenge and withhold the antipsychotic while she is observed
options.rationale: The combination of mutism, waxy flexibility, negativism and echolalia establishes catatonia, for which a benzodiazepine challenge is both the first line treatment and diagnostically informative. The antipsychotic is withheld because it can worsen catatonia and precipitate the malignant form. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and electroencephalography before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Investigation for an organic cause is reasonable in parallel but should not delay a treatment that is safe, rapidly acting and diagnostically useful. Her known mood disorder and classic signs make catatonia the leading diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis and occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and a wide range of medical and neurological conditions, with mood disorders the commonest psychiatric association. It is frequently missed because the immobile, mute patient is assumed to be depressed, uncooperative or sedated, and because clinicians look for a rigid patient rather than one with waxy flexibility and preserved alertness. Recognition rests on identifying several signs from the characteristic cluster, which includes stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypy. A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both treatment and diagnostic test, while antipsychotics should be withheld because they can precipitate malignant catatonia, which overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and carries high mortality. Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail, and the medical complications of immobility and poor intake, including dehydration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration, need active management throughout.
key_points: Catatonia is a syndrome seen most often with mood disorders, not only psychosis
Waxy flexibility with preserved alertness distinguishes it from a sedated patient
A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both first line treatment and a diagnostic test
Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and are withheld
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when benzodiazepines fail
explanation.pearls: A mildly raised creatine kinase without fever or rigidity reflects immobility in catatonia rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and mistaking one for the other sends the patient to dantrolene instead of the lorazepam that would have worked.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Polyuria and thirst with a normal lithium level in a man treated with lithium for twelve years
stem:
A 49 year old man attends your clinic reporting that he now passes urine four or five times each night and drinks constantly through the day. He has taken lithium for twelve years for bipolar I disorder and his mood has been stable throughout.

He has no polyphagia and has lost no weight. His fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin are normal, and his morning lithium level taken twelve hours after his dose is within the therapeutic range. His sodium is at the upper limit of normal and his creatinine has risen slightly compared with results from two years ago. He is passing large volumes of dilute urine and a urine dipstick shows no glucose, protein or blood.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 145 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.3% (<6.0), lithium level within the therapeutic range
data_table.Urine: Large volumes of dilute urine, dipstick negative for glucose protein and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that the symptoms are benign, since his lithium level is within range
options.rationale: This complication occurs at therapeutic levels and relates to cumulative duration of exposure rather than concentration, so a normal level offers no reassurance. It also carries a real risk of dangerous dehydration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Measure paired serum and urine osmolality and involve the renal team in his care
options.rationale: A dilute urine despite a high normal serum sodium indicates a failure of renal concentrating ability rather than excessive drinking, and paired osmolality demonstrates this objectively. Renal involvement guides whether lithium can continue and how the kidney is monitored. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start a fluid restriction of 1.5 litres daily and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Restricting fluid in a patient who cannot concentrate urine risks rapid hypernatraemic dehydration and lithium toxicity. His high normal sodium already indicates he is only just keeping pace. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add desmopressin and continue the lithium at the current dose with monthly review
options.rationale: The defect is renal resistance to antidiuretic hormone rather than a deficiency of it, so exogenous hormone is largely ineffective. Amiloride is the agent with a rational basis in this setting. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test and a water deprivation test on the same day
options.rationale: His glucose and glycated haemoglobin already exclude diabetes mellitus, and a water deprivation test is potentially hazardous here without renal supervision. Paired osmolality is the safer first measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Lithium acts on the collecting duct to reduce the responsiveness of the tubule to antidiuretic hormone, producing a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that affects a substantial minority of long term users. It presents with polyuria and compensatory thirst, is related to duration of therapy rather than to the serum level, and is therefore easily dismissed when the level comes back within range. The critical hazard is that the patient depends on continuous access to water, so any illness, surgery, fasting or heat stress that interrupts drinking can produce rapid hypernatraemic dehydration, which in turn reduces lithium clearance and precipitates toxicity. Diagnosis is by demonstrating an inappropriately dilute urine in the face of a high normal or raised serum sodium. Management involves renal input, ensuring unrestricted fluid access, considering amiloride which blocks the epithelial sodium channel through which lithium enters the tubular cell, and weighing whether to continue lithium against the difficulty of replacing it in a patient whose mood has been stable for years.
key_points: Lithium causes nephrogenic rather than central diabetes insipidus
Risk relates to duration of exposure, not to the serum level
Inappropriately dilute urine with high normal sodium confirms the diagnosis
Interrupted access to water can cause rapid hypernatraemia and lithium toxicity
Amiloride has a rational basis where desmopressin does not
explanation.pearls: A patient with lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus who is made nil by mouth for surgery can become dangerously hypernatraemic within hours, so the perioperative fluid plan matters more than the lithium level.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Choice of pharmacotherapy for a depressive episode in a man with an established diagnosis of bipolar disorder
stem:
A 36 year old man attends your clinic with eight weeks of low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia and poor concentration that have caused him to take leave from work. He has a documented diagnosis of bipolar I disorder following a manic episode requiring admission four years ago.

He stopped his mood stabiliser eighteen months ago when he felt well and has taken nothing since. He denies any current elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or racing thoughts, and there are no psychotic features. He has passive thoughts that he would rather not be here but no plan and no intent, and he agrees to a safety plan with his partner present. His thyroid function and full blood count are normal and he does not use alcohol or other drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Depressed mood with psychomotor slowing, no elevated mood or pressured speech, no psychotic features, passive thoughts of not wanting to be here without plan or intent
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits, no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly
options.rationale: An antidepressant without mood stabilising cover carries a recognised risk of switching him into mania or inducing rapid cycling, particularly given his bipolar I history. Antidepressants are not first line for bipolar depression. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Venlafaxine as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly
options.rationale: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors carry a higher switch risk than other antidepressant classes and the same objection applies with greater force. Noradrenergic agents are the least suitable choice here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Lithium at a low starting dose with review of his mood and a level taken weekly
options.rationale: Lithium is excellent for maintenance and reduces suicide risk but has more modest acute antidepressant effect, so it is slower to address the current episode. It is a reasonable addition once he has recovered. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Psychological therapy alone with review of his mood weekly and no medication started
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct but is not sufficient alone for a moderate to severe bipolar depressive episode with functional impairment and passive suicidal thoughts. He also currently has no prophylactic cover. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Quetiapine as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly
options.rationale: Quetiapine has the strongest evidence for bipolar depression and treats the episode while providing mood stabilising cover against a switch to mania. Monotherapy avoids the risk carried by an unopposed antidepressant in a patient with a documented manic episode. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Bipolar depression accounts for far more of the illness burden over a lifetime than mania does, yet it is treated differently from unipolar depression and the distinction is frequently missed when a patient presents during a depressed phase and does not volunteer a past manic episode. The central concern is that antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate a switch into mania, induce rapid cycling, or produce a mixed state, with the risk greatest in bipolar I disorder and with noradrenergic agents. Australian guidance therefore favours quetiapine, lurasidone, or lamotrigine, with olanzapine combined with fluoxetine as an alternative, rather than an antidepressant alone. Where an antidepressant is used it should be given under the cover of an adequate mood stabiliser and withdrawn once the episode resolves. Every depressed patient should be asked directly about past periods of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep and uncharacteristic risk taking, since the history determines the treatment far more than the current presentation does.
key_points: Bipolar depression causes more lifetime burden than mania and is treated differently
Antidepressant monotherapy risks manic switch, mixed states and rapid cycling
Quetiapine, lurasidone and lamotrigine are preferred first line options
Any antidepressant used should be covered by an adequate mood stabiliser
Ask every depressed patient directly about past elevated mood
explanation.pearls: Switch risk in bipolar I disorder is highest with noradrenergic antidepressants such as venlafaxine and with tricyclics, which is why an unopposed serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the least defensible of the antidepressant options.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Behavioural disturbance with visual hallucinations and marked motor slowing in an older man with fluctuating cognition
stem:
A 78 year old man is brought to your clinic by his wife because he has become distressed and occasionally aggressive in the evenings over the past two months. She describes him seeing small children in the lounge room who are not there, and says these episodes do not frighten him.

She reports his alertness varies markedly, with some days when he is sharp and others when he stares into space for long periods. He has become slower to move and has fallen twice, and he acts out his dreams at night with kicking and shouting. His examination shows symmetrical bradykinesia with mild rigidity and no tremor. His urine is clear, his electrolytes and thyroid function are normal, and his medication list contains no anticholinergic agents.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying with a fall to 118/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia with mild rigidity, no resting tremor, fluctuating attention, formed visual hallucinations without fear
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits, urine dipstick clear, no anticholinergic medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management of his behavioural symptoms?

options.text: Non-pharmacological measures with review of contributing medications and carer support
options.rationale: Marked antipsychotic sensitivity in this condition means even low doses can cause severe parkinsonism, sedation and a rise in mortality, so drug treatment is not the starting point. Environmental strategies and removal of aggravating drugs address the distress with far less risk. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Low dose oral risperidone at night with review of his symptoms after two weeks
options.rationale: This is among the least suitable choices because severe sensitivity reactions are well recognised with this class in this condition. It would be a more defensible option in Alzheimer dementia after non-drug measures failed. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Low dose oral haloperidol as required with review of his symptoms after two weeks
options.rationale: A typical antipsychotic carries the greatest risk of a severe sensitivity reaction and can produce irreversible deterioration. Its use in this setting is specifically cautioned against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Oral diazepam at night with review of his symptoms and falls risk after two weeks
options.rationale: A long acting benzodiazepine increases falls, confusion and daytime sedation in an older man who has already fallen twice. It treats none of the underlying features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Oral levodopa titrated upwards with review of his motor and behavioural symptoms fortnightly
options.rationale: Dopaminergic therapy may help the motor features but characteristically worsens visual hallucinations, which are his main behavioural problem. It is introduced cautiously only once behavioural symptoms are controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by a dementia with fluctuating cognition, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and it is commonly misdiagnosed as Alzheimer disease or delirium. Recognising it matters because of severe neuroleptic sensitivity, in which a standard dose of an antipsychotic can cause profound rigidity, sedation, autonomic instability and a marked rise in mortality. Management of behavioural symptoms therefore begins with identifying and removing contributors such as pain, infection, constipation and anticholinergic drugs, and with environmental and carer directed strategies. Cholinesterase inhibitors have better evidence in this condition than in most other dementias and can improve both cognition and hallucinations. If an antipsychotic becomes unavoidable for severe distress or risk, quetiapine at the lowest possible dose is generally preferred, with explicit discussion of the mortality risk and a defined review date.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment define the syndrome
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity can follow even a single standard antipsychotic dose
Reversible contributors such as pain, infection and anticholinergics are addressed first
Cholinesterase inhibitors have better evidence here than in other dementias
Levodopa improves motor features but worsens hallucinations
explanation.pearls: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder often precedes the cognitive decline of dementia with Lewy bodies by years, so a partner's account of dream enactment is frequently the detail that prevents a catastrophic antipsychotic prescription.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

subtopic_detail: Tremor and confusion at a lithium level reported as within range in a woman recently started on two antihypertensives, with the sample taken six hours after her dose
stem:
A 68 year old woman with bipolar I disorder is brought to your emergency department by her son with four days of worsening unsteadiness, slurred speech and intermittent confusion. She has taken lithium carbonate 500 mg twice daily for nine years with levels consistently between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L.

Three weeks ago her general practitioner started perindopril and hydrochlorothiazide for newly diagnosed hypertension. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea and no fever. Her son took her to a collection centre on the way in, where a lithium level was drawn at 2 pm; she took her morning dose at 8 am. That level is reported as 1.1 mmol/L. On examination she has a coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia and intermittent myoclonic jerks, and she is drowsy but rousable with no neck stiffness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, intermittent myoclonic jerks, drowsy but rousable, no neck stiffness, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 1.1 mmol/L drawn six hours after the morning dose, creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90) up from 72 two months ago, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), estimated glomerular filtration rate 32 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold the next lithium dose, observe overnight and repeat the level in the morning
options.rationale: Simple observation is adequate for mild toxicity with normal renal function, but her acute kidney injury means the drug will continue to accumulate rather than clear. Waiting allows the neurological injury to progress. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give activated charcoal and commence whole bowel irrigation to reduce ongoing absorption
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium at all, and gut decontamination has no role in chronic accumulation where the burden is already distributed to tissue. These measures address acute ingestion of a modified release preparation. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

options.text: Repeat the level timed correctly, start intravenous sodium chloride and discuss dialysis with the renal team
options.rationale: A level drawn six hours post dose understates the trough, so 1.1 mmol/L here represents substantially greater toxicity than the number suggests, and the neurological signs with acute kidney injury define severe chronic toxicity. Volume repletion restores clearance while the renal team assesses the threshold for extracorporeal removal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the lithium at a reduced dose, cease the thiazide and arrange review in one week
options.rationale: Removing the interacting diuretic is correct but continuing any lithium in the setting of established neurotoxicity with acute kidney injury is unsafe. The timeframe also fails to match the severity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to enhance urinary elimination and repeat the level in six hours
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation enhances elimination of weak acids such as salicylate, and lithium clearance is governed by sodium and volume status rather than by urine pH. The principle is misapplied to this drug. (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia)

explanation.summary: This presentation requires three separate errors to be recognised at once. First, lithium levels are only interpretable as twelve hour trough samples, so a level drawn six hours after a dose sits on the descending limb of absorption and understates the trough, meaning a reported 1.1 mmol/L represents a considerably higher true burden. Second, both perindopril and hydrochlorothiazide reduce lithium clearance, the thiazide by increasing proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption and the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor by reducing glomerular filtration, and their combination has produced an acute kidney injury that will drive further accumulation. Third, chronic toxicity causes neurological injury at far lower levels than acute overdose because lithium has already equilibrated into the central nervous system, so the severity of the clinical syndrome rather than the serum number determines management. Treatment is cessation of lithium and the interacting drugs, volume repletion with sodium chloride to restore clearance, and early renal consultation, since haemodialysis is indicated for severe neurological features or impaired renal clearance irrespective of whether the level crosses a particular threshold.
key_points: Lithium levels are interpretable only as twelve hour trough samples
Thiazides and renin angiotensin blockers both reduce lithium clearance
Chronic toxicity injures the brain at far lower levels than acute overdose
Clinical severity, not the serum number, drives the decision to dialyse
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and has no role
explanation.pearls: Haemodialysis in lithium toxicity is driven by neurological severity and renal function rather than by a level threshold, and a rebound rise several hours after dialysis as lithium redistributes out of tissue means a repeat level is always needed afterwards.

subtopic_detail: Electrolyte monitoring and supplementation in the first week of nutritional restoration for a severely underweight adolescent
stem:
A 16 year old girl is admitted under your team with anorexia nervosa. She has eaten almost nothing for eleven days and her weight has fallen to a body mass index of 13 kg/m2.

Her admission bloods show normal electrolytes including a phosphate at the lower end of the reference range. Her pulse is 42/min and she has a postural drop in blood pressure, and her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms. The dietitian proposes commencing nutritional restoration today and asks you to write the monitoring and supplementation plan for the first week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 42/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg lying with a fall to 76/48 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), magnesium 0.75 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), corrected QT interval 440 ms, albumin 36 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 13 kg/m2, cool peripheries, lanugo hair, no oedema

lead_in: What monitoring and supplementation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
options.rationale: Waiting for the level to fall means treating an established deficiency that can already have caused cardiac and respiratory compromise. The admission level offers no reassurance because the fall occurs after feeding starts. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun before the level falls below range
options.rationale: Her prolonged starvation and very low body mass index place her at high risk, and the phosphate falls only once feeding begins and insulin drives it intracellularly. Prophylactic supplementation alongside daily measurement prevents the fall rather than reacting to it. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Twice weekly phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
options.rationale: This frequency will miss the rapid fall that characteristically occurs within the first seventy two hours of feeding. Monitoring interval is as important as the decision to monitor. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Delay all nutritional restoration for 72 hours while daily electrolytes are observed for stability
options.rationale: Withholding nutrition in a severely malnourished patient carries its own mortality and does not reduce the risk once feeding eventually starts. Underfeeding is now recognised as a harm in its own right. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with a high carbohydrate feeding regimen to restore weight rapidly
options.rationale: A high carbohydrate load is the strongest driver of the intracellular shift and would increase rather than reduce the risk. Carbohydrate content is deliberately moderated during the early phase. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of metabolic disturbances that follows the reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, and hypophosphataemia is its defining feature. During starvation the body depletes intracellular phosphate, magnesium and potassium while serum levels remain deceptively normal, and when carbohydrate is reintroduced the resulting insulin surge drives these ions into cells along with glucose, producing a rapid fall in serum concentrations that can cause cardiac failure, arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and death. Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of minimal intake, recent weight loss and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, and this patient is at high risk on several counts. Contemporary practice has shifted away from cautious underfeeding, which carries its own mortality, towards starting adequate nutrition while monitoring electrolytes at least daily and supplementing phosphate and thiamine prophylactically in high risk patients. Thiamine is given before or with the first feed because carbohydrate metabolism consumes it and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
key_points: Serum electrolytes are deceptively normal during starvation despite intracellular depletion
The insulin surge after carbohydrate drives phosphate into cells within days
Risk is stratified by body mass index, duration of intake and recent weight loss
Prophylactic supplementation is preferred to reacting to a fallen level
Underfeeding is itself harmful and is no longer the recommended precaution
explanation.pearls: Thiamine must be given before or alongside the first feed in a severely malnourished patient, because the carbohydrate load consumes remaining thiamine stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within days of starting nutrition.

subtopic_detail: Baseline assessment required before a first stimulant prescription in an adult newly diagnosed with attention deficit disorder
stem:
A 29 year old man attends your practice having been newly diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by a psychiatrist, who has recommended a trial of a stimulant and asked you to complete the baseline assessment.

He has lifelong difficulty sustaining attention and organising tasks, documented from school reports, and he has lost two jobs because of missed deadlines. He drinks alcohol occasionally and uses no other substances. He tells you his father died suddenly at 44 while playing sport, and that the cause was never fully explained to the family. He has no chest pain, no palpitations and no history of syncope himself.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Normal heart sounds with no murmur, no signs of heart failure, normal peripheral pulses
data_table.History: Father died suddenly at 44 during exertion with no cause established, no personal syncope, chest pain or palpitations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before starting treatment?

options.text: Record his heart rate and blood pressure and commence the stimulant at a low dose
options.rationale: Baseline observations are necessary for every patient but are insufficient here, because a normal examination does not exclude an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy. The family history changes the threshold for investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange a urine drug screen and commence the stimulant once the result is confirmed negative
options.rationale: Substance use is worth assessing because of diversion and misuse risk, but he reports none and this does not address the cardiac question. It would not detect the risk that matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine instead, since it avoids any need for cardiac assessment beforehand
options.rationale: Non-stimulant agents also raise heart rate and blood pressure and do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment where the history warrants it. Changing drug class does not resolve the concern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an electrocardiogram and cardiology assessment before the first stimulant dose
options.rationale: An unexplained sudden death in a first degree relative under fifty raises the possibility of an inherited cardiac condition and is the specific trigger for cardiac assessment rather than routine baseline observations alone. Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so this must be resolved before treatment begins. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange thyroid function tests and commence the stimulant once the results are within range
options.rationale: Thyroid testing is not a routine requirement before stimulant treatment and would be prompted by clinical features of thyroid disease. It does not address the inherited cardiac risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Stimulant treatment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is effective but requires a structured baseline assessment because the drugs raise heart rate and blood pressure and are subject to misuse and diversion. Routine baseline assessment comprises pulse, blood pressure, weight, a cardiovascular history and examination, and a review of substance use and any comorbid psychiatric illness. Routine electrocardiography is not required for everyone, which makes it important to recognise the specific features that do warrant cardiac referral: a personal history of structural heart disease, exertional chest pain, palpitations or syncope, an abnormal examination, or a family history of sudden unexplained death in a first degree relative under about forty years of age. In Australia, stimulant prescribing is additionally regulated at state level with authority requirements, and ongoing monitoring includes pulse, blood pressure and weight at each dose change and periodically thereafter. Comorbid substance use disorder does not preclude treatment but influences the choice of a longer acting or less divertible preparation.
key_points: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so baseline observations are mandatory
Routine electrocardiography is not required for every patient
Sudden unexplained death in a young first degree relative warrants cardiac referral
Non-stimulant alternatives do not exempt a patient from cardiac assessment
State authority requirements apply to stimulant prescribing in Australia
explanation.pearls: A first degree relative who died suddenly and unexplained before about forty is the family history detail that converts a routine stimulant baseline into a cardiology referral, because inherited cardiomyopathies and channelopathies are often silent on examination.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing an expected bereavement reaction from a depressive episode five weeks after the death of a spouse
stem:
A 71 year old woman is brought to your practice by her daughter five weeks after her husband of forty six years died of pancreatic cancer. Her daughter is worried that she is depressed and asks you to start an antidepressant.

She describes waves of sadness that come when she finds his belongings or hears a particular song, interspersed with periods where she can enjoy her grandchildren's visits and laugh with them. Her sleep is broken and her appetite is reduced, and she has lost 2 kg. She says she misses him unbearably and sometimes hears his voice calling her name as she falls asleep, which she finds comforting rather than frightening. She does not blame herself for his death, retains her sense of her own worth, and says she wants to be here for her grandchildren.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband but able to be consoled and to engage warmly, no psychomotor retardation, normal cognition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant now with review of her mood and tolerability in two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have not been shown to benefit uncomplicated grief and medicalising a normal process can undermine it. They are indicated if a depressive episode emerges. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Commence a hypnotic for the disturbed sleep with review of her mood and function in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedatives risk dependence, falls and confusion in an older person and do not address the underlying process. Broken sleep is an expected feature of early bereavement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic at low dose to address the auditory experiences she has described
options.rationale: Hearing the deceased person's voice while falling asleep is a recognised and benign feature of bereavement rather than a psychotic symptom. Treating it would expose her to significant risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Refer urgently to the older persons mental health team for specialist assessment this week
options.rationale: Urgent specialist referral is reserved for suicidal ideation, psychotic depression, severe functional decline or failure to eat and drink, none of which is present. Her presentation can be managed in primary care with review. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue supportive review with practical bereavement support and no antidepressant at this stage
options.rationale: Her reactivity of mood, preserved self worth, absent suicidal ideation and comforting rather than distressing perceptual experiences are characteristic of uncomplicated grief rather than a depressive episode. Planned review allows a depressive illness to be identified if the pattern changes. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Grief and depression overlap substantially in their surface features, since sadness, tearfulness, disturbed sleep, reduced appetite and weight loss occur in both, and the distinction rests on qualitative features rather than on symptom counting. In uncomplicated grief the dysphoria comes in waves triggered by reminders, with preserved capacity for pleasure and connection between those waves, whereas depression produces a persistent and pervasive lowering of mood with global anhedonia. Self esteem is characteristically preserved in grief, while worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the death and self loathing point to depression, and fleeting perceptual experiences of the deceased person are common in bereavement and are not psychotic. Any active suicidal ideation, marked psychomotor retardation, or persistent functional collapse should prompt treatment for depression. Prolonged grief disorder is a separate diagnosis requiring persistent intense yearning and preoccupation with functional impairment beyond six to twelve months, and it responds to specific psychological therapy rather than to antidepressants.
key_points: Grief produces waves of dysphoria with preserved reactivity between them
Depression produces persistent pervasive low mood with global anhedonia
Preserved self worth favours grief while worthlessness and guilt favour depression
Fleeting perceptions of the deceased are common and not psychotic
Prolonged grief disorder requires impairment beyond six to twelve months
explanation.pearls: Active suicidal ideation with a wish to die rather than a passive wish to be with the deceased is the feature that should move a bereaved patient out of the grief category and into treatment for depression, irrespective of how recent the loss was.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Matching alcohol relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to a goal of reduced drinking rather than abstinence
stem:
A 45 year old carpenter attends your general practice asking for help with his drinking. He describes about ten standard drinks most evenings, morning shakiness that settles once he has a drink, and two failed attempts to cut down on his own.

He is clear that he does not want to stop completely at this stage but wants to get the amount down, and he will not consider an inpatient admission. He takes no regular medication, uses no opioids and has never injected drugs. His liver enzymes are mildly raised at twice the upper limit of normal with a normal bilirubin and normal synthetic function, and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no asterixis, no peripheral neuropathy
data_table.Liver function: Alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L (less than 45), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin and international normalised ratio within normal limits
data_table.Other: Renal function within normal limits, no current opioid use, declines inpatient withdrawal

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate to offer him now?

options.text: Acamprosate started once he has completed a supervised withdrawal
options.rationale: Acamprosate works by maintaining abstinence once it has been achieved and requires the patient to have stopped drinking first, which he has declined to do. It has little effect on the quantity consumed in someone still drinking. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Disulfiram with supervised dosing arranged through his pharmacy
options.rationale: Disulfiram depends on an aversive reaction to any alcohol at all and therefore requires a committed abstinence goal with supervision, making it unsuitable for someone who intends to keep drinking. Using it here would risk a deliberate and dangerous reaction. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Naltrexone started now while he continues to drink at a reduced level
options.rationale: Naltrexone blocks the opioid mediated reward of drinking and reduces heavy drinking days and the quantity consumed, so it suits a harm reduction goal and does not require prior abstinence. His mildly raised transaminases with preserved synthetic function are not a contraindication, and he uses no opioids. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Baclofen at high dose titrated against his reported craving levels
options.rationale: Baclofen is a later option used mainly where liver disease precludes the first line agents, and the evidence for it is weaker with a risk of sedation and of a withdrawal syndrome on abrupt cessation. His liver function does not force that choice. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Topiramate titrated slowly as first line pharmacotherapy for craving
options.rationale: Topiramate has some supporting evidence but is not registered for this indication in Australia and carries cognitive slowing and paraesthesiae that limit tolerability. It sits behind the established first line agents. (Source: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

explanation.summary: Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder is chosen by matching the drug to the patient's stated goal rather than by ranking the drugs against each other in the abstract. Naltrexone reduces the reinforcing effect of alcohol and therefore reduces heavy drinking days, which makes it the agent of choice when the goal is reduced consumption or when the person is still drinking at the point of prescribing.
